Upon their arrival, they were not unkindly received, but initially found more entry and enjoyed more signs of generosity and indulgence—allowing them to prepare for themselves a permanent dwelling and seat in the heart of our Land—than prudence, built on a prior careful investigation of matters, would have allowed. # PREFACE

Who could have thought otherwise, than that all the Members of this Congregation <note>original: *Gemeente*; referring to the local Reformed church body.</note> would have accepted the Paternal warning of the Reverend Consistory <note>original: *Eerw: Kerkenraats*; the governing body of a local Dutch Reformed church, composed of the minister and elders.</note> in love and with thanksgiving to God for the watchful attentiveness of their Overseers. And, as evil usually finds the most entrance, so has also this slander (forgive me that I must use that word <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "ken," indicates the word "gebruiken" (to use) continues on the next page.</note>—

*or an even worse fate befell various honest families, recently lured to Moravia by certain deceivers who were called Mähr-Broeders (that is, Moravian Brethren): These men knew how to disparage all the toils to which one was subject here in order to support oneself through housekeeping, claiming that in their own Land a better order was maintained. They said they had a sort of Monastery, or dwellings in the Land, where everyone, as much as he wished, did a little of one thing or another, and that furthermore every good order was kept regarding their way of life. Many gullible people, selling their possessions in Holland, traveled upcountry <note>original: *na boven*; literally "to the top," a common Dutch expression for traveling inland toward Germany or Central Europe.</note> with Wife and children, led by these Moravian Brethren; but once they arrived in Moravia, they were locked up and put to the loom, spinning, and hard labor—after they had handed over all their fine money to these superiors of the Moravian Brethren. Being unaccustomed to such tyranny, and seeing that they were looked upon with disfavor, they received no other comfort than being told they must remember they were still like the Israelites in the Wilderness; but if they wished to murmur like Moses' people, they would only enjoy the sight of the Land of Canaan, but never the possession thereof, etc. These sermons displeased our deceived Dutchmen so much that, turning their backs, they fled from that place, leaving everything behind; some were given a little money, but of the remainder, the MORAVIAN DECEIVERS remained the owners.*

## ->P R E F A C E<-

Do not think, kind reader, that I only now have begun to collect what you will see brought together in this writing. No, but from that time when I had acquired the Moravian <note>original: *Herrnhuthsche*</note> High-German Hymnal, and had begun to leaf through it with some attention, and saw from it as clear as noon, and to the complete persuasion of my mind, where these people belonged and under what sort of people they must be counted—namely, among those *Enthusiasts* and *Fanatics* <note>original: *Geestdryvers*; a derogatory term used by orthodox theologians to describe those who prioritized subjective spiritual experience over established church doctrine and scripture.</note> who, for a century or two now, have disturbed so many places in Germany and have torn and laid waste to so many previously flourishing congregations—I have made a beginning of rummaging through the writings of those High-German erring spirits, as many as I could get hold of, to compare the system of the confused, falsely-named "Theology" of these people with what the Moravian Hymnal teaches in many places.

But because I could not find all those books here in this Country <note>Referring to the Netherlands.</note> that I dearly wished to consult, I soon noticed that I could succeed nowhere better than in the writings of such Lutheran theologians who lived in those times, or in those places, where *Enthusiasm* was most active and had established itself. Here, the learned writings of those theologians who adhere to the <term>Augsburg Confession<gloss>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, established in 1530, used here as a standard of orthodoxy against which the Moravians were measured.</gloss></term> have been of wonderfully good service to me—not only in their entire books, but also in specific academic treatises called *Dissertations* (of which I have collected a fair supply) which have either pointed out the rise and progress of the *Enthusiasts* in a *historical* manner, or their errors from their own writings...

### TO THE READER.

[...various] members, of whom perhaps even the least are known to me by sight, in public or in private, to declare so unconditionally that it *consists of those purchased by the blood of the Lamb*. <note>original: "beſta uit gekochte door het bloet des Lams"</note> God forbid me even more, that I should attempt to make suspect, or even accuse, any of my Brothers—let alone the majority of the theologians <term>Godgeleerden: Literally "God-learned," referring to the established Dutch Reformed clergy and academic scholars.</term> of our country, who are convinced in their consciences on good grounds that the Herrnhutters <term>Herrnhutters: The Moravian Brethren, followers of Count Zinzendorf.</term> are guilty of dangerous and far-reaching errors—as if they were opposing, or sinning against, those *purchased by the blood of the Lamb*. That goes too far; I could never answer for that before God, before my conscience, and before the Church of God.

I know that the self-interest of the Herrnhutters requires that they praise their Sect with great fanfare as a Congregation of the living God, and call their cause the cause of God, in order to frighten off the credulous, and especially to ensure they harbor no suspicion against them, much less undertake anything against them by the discovery or refutation of their chief errors. It reaches quite a height when one hears this language: *That their Congregation is a power of Jesus Christ himself, just as her cause is his cause.* And when one dares to testify: *that the power of such a Community is that awe-inspiring quality, which is inherent to rightly ordered gatherings here, which also works upon the hearts of those who come in from the outside, whether out of curiosity or with an evil intent.* They are not infrequently, in a manner they do not understand, suddenly seized by a reverence that bows them in their hearts, and even—as the hidden things of the heart are made manifest to them—causes them to acknowledge the presence of God, and fall down— <meta>catchword: fall-</meta>

...to judge the Congregation. # TO THE READER.

...bear it, and hand it over to Him who is no respecter of persons, but who, as the searcher of hearts, will judge according to truth.

I know that many sincere people, who are not yet entirely devoted to the party of the **Herrnhuters** <term>Herrnhuters: Another name for the Moravian Brethren (Moravians), a Pietist Christian movement following the lead of Count von Zinzendorf</term>, will perhaps think that some passion might be driving this—that one should be so zealous against the growth of the **Herrnhuter sect** and warn against it repeatedly. They might point out that learned, discerning, and pious theologians in Germany and elsewhere not only testify that they see no danger, but even give ample and favorable testimonies in their favor. I know this, and it is through such testimonials that they have found so much entry among others who have less insight. I profess to have all high regard for the judgment of sensible and godly men, whose learning and piety I shall continue to prize; however, (while maintaining all respect for those persons), I cannot bring myself to hang my seal upon their judgment through a blind consent. Since I began to use my understanding and judgment (according to my modest measure) in a reasonable manner, and to obtain some small experience of matters, I have never been inclined to close my own eyes, or to pluck them out, and to see through the eyes of another. The *prejudice of authority* <note>original: *Præjudicium auctoritatis*</note>, that is, the *prejudice built upon human authority*, I already sought to resist to the best of my strength in my youth, and I can surrender myself to it even less now than then. All the more because I know that already in earlier days, other renowned theologians were misled by enthusiasts to give them overly favorable testimonies. ### TO THE READER.

*to be among the number of those* (who by progressing write, and by writing progress) <note>original Latin: "qui proficiendo scribunt, & scribendo proficiunt"</note> *who write while making progress, and who progress by writing. Therefore, if anything has been set down by me, whether imprudently or unlearnedly, which can be lawfully rebuked not only by those who have eyes to see it, but also by myself (since I, at least, if I progress, must see it later), one should not wonder at this, nor pity me, but excuse me and congratulate me; not because I have erred, but because I have rejected the error. For he who loves himself too much through a perverse self-love wishes for others to err so that his own error remains hidden. For how much better and more useful is it, when someone has erred, that at least others do not err, through whose instruction he can be brought back from his error; so that, if he does not wish for such correction, he at least has no companions in his error.*

Make use, as lovers of the pure truth and the <term>simplicity that is in Christ Jesus: A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:3, emphasizing a straightforward, sincere faith in contrast to the complex or deceptive doctrines the author is attacking.</term>, of this my meager labor, which is dedicated to you out of love for the <term>Sanctified Truth: "Geheiligde Waarheit," referring to the divine truth that sets the believer apart for God and leads to a holy life.</term>. If you see what abominable secrets lie hidden beneath seemingly beautiful words, do not for that reason immediately reject every manner of speaking, nor condemn those who use them in a healthy sense; but neither let yourselves be misled by any honey-sweet words and fair speech. If you learn anything for your instruction and warning, seek to preserve it in the thoughts of your heart, so as to henceforth guide your paths only according to the rule of God’s holy Word, which alone leads to <term>Salvation: "Zaligheid," often translated as "blessedness" or "salvation," referring to the ultimate state of grace and eternal life.</term>. <margin>Introduction to this writing, and to the account of the proceedings of the Amsterdam Consistory.</margin>
It is the **Pastoral and Paternal Letter**, published at the end of last year by the Ministers and Elders of the Reverend Consistory of this famous and populous city, for friendly instruction and faithful Pastoral and Paternal warning regarding those people known by the name of Herrnhuthers <note>The Herrnhuthers, also known as the Moravian Brethren, were a Pietist Christian denomination. In the 18th century, their emotional and often mystical focus on the physical wounds of Christ caused significant controversy among the more traditional Dutch Reformed clergy.</note>, who are attacked in that *Anonymous writing* (which we now examine in the fear of the Lord, to fulfill the request and command of the Reverend Consistory): and in such a way that not only the faithfulness and sincerity of the Reverend Consistory—in quoting passages from that very notorious High German Hymnal of the Herrnhuther Congregation <note>original: "Hoogduitsche Gezangboek"</note> within the Pastoral and Paternal Letter—is made highly suspicious, to the injury of the honor and name of a Church Assembly as prominent as that of the Consistory of Amsterdam: but also even the manner of proceeding by that Reverend Assembly in this entire Herrnhuther matter, and particularly in the publication of the

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of an anonymous pamphlet that challenged the Amsterdam Consistory. The author highlights inconsistencies in the critic's writing and announces his intention to provide a truthful, firsthand account of the church's dealings with the Herrnhuthers.</meta>

**Pastoral and Paternal Letter**, held to be less cautious and faithful, is criticized from the sidelines—or at least some improper suspicion regarding it is instilled in the minds of the readers, who do not know, nor can they know, all the particulars of the ecclesiastical proceedings. For when, in the Preface of that writing, *p. 3*, the title of the **Pastoral and Paternal Letter** is mentioned as *Written by the Ministers and Elders*, the Author places an asterisk* there and adds at the bottom for clarification, *Though not with the consent of all*. And in the conclusion of that writing, *p. 39*, the Author speaks thus in the singular: *Meanwhile, one wishes for the* AUTHOR *of this P. and P. L.* <note>Abbreviation for "Pastoral and Paternal Letter."</note> *that the Lord may not impute to* HIM *the evil it may cause, and the offense it has already given to many pious people.* Yet after that follows again in the plural: *that they may humble themselves before the Lord because of their imprudence, and remember, etc.* Whether this is to be considered a writing or printing error, or whether it was set down thus with some specific intent <note>The author suggests the critic may be intentionally trying to imply that the Letter was the work of a single person rather than the whole Consistory.</note>, we leave undecided. 

It is at least certain that just as the Letter itself was not received equally favorably by everyone—despite the Godly wish and tender-hearted aim of those Members of the **Consistory** <note>The Consistory, or *Kerkenraad*, was the governing body of the local Dutch Reformed Church, consisting of ministers and elders.</note> who felt compelled in conscience, by virtue of their office and duty, to watch over truth and unfeigned piety—so also the judgments and prejudices regarding the manner of handling the case of the **Herrnhuthers** <note>Also known as the Moravian Brethren, the Herrnhuthers were a Pietist group whose emotional and mystical practices were often viewed with suspicion by the orthodox Dutch Reformed clergy.</note> by the Reverend Consistory, caused by more than one coincidence, are varied and in many ways not according to the truth. I have therefore judged it my duty, and not unhelpful to the public, to share with the impartial reader the entire course of the proceedings held by the Reverend Consistory in the aforementioned case, truthfully yet concisely. This account is drawn partly from the Acts <note>The official recorded minutes and legal documents of the church council.</note> of the Reverend Consistory, and partly from what I myself, along with others among my honored colleagues, have noted from the oral negotiations that occurred both in the Committee meetings <note>original: "Commissoriale," referring to smaller committees appointed by the Consistory to investigate specific matters.</note> and Consistory meetings; however, all this is shared without mentioning anyone's name.

-># The Moravian Brethren. Section I.<-

<margin>Preparations within the Consistory for the careful observation and monitoring of the activities of the Moravians, from June 5th to August 22nd, 1738.</margin>
When, on June 5th of last year, a book entitled *The Hidden Man of the Heart* <note>original: "De Verborgene mensch des harten"; likely a Pietist or mystical devotional work</note>, etc., reprinted in 1737 by J. Hartig, was brought before the Reverend Assembly for examination, it was decided on that occasion to keep a watchful eye on strange conventicles <note>Private, unofficial religious gatherings held outside the oversight of the state church.</note>, and to discuss the matter further in an extraordinary meeting. On the 26th of the same month, it was resolved that fourteen days later, in an extraordinary session of the Consistory <note>The *Kerkenraad*, the governing body of the local Dutch Reformed Church.</note>, they would hear whether any of the Members had anything specific to report regarding harmful books and assemblies. On July 10th, in that extraordinary meeting, it was determined with sufficient unanimity to watch closely against the progress of Mysticism <note>original: "Mystikery," often used dismissively by the orthodox to describe inward-focused or ecstatic spiritual practices.</note> and the publication of mystical books. It was also decided to keep an observant eye on the members of the Moravian Assembly, and to request information regarding their doctrine and conduct by writing letters, in the name of the assembly, to the Reverend Consistory of Ysselstein <note>A town where the Moravians had established a significant community.</note> and to the Reverend Mr. Manger, a worthy Minister in The Hague (as they were judged to be able to provide the most direct reports). This was subsequently done. 

On July 31st, two letters were brought in and read to the Assembly: one from the Reverend Mr. Manger, sent in reply to the Reverend Assembly, which included an Extract from the Acts of the Christian Synod of South Holland concerning the proceedings of that Highly Esteemed Assembly in the case of the Moravians. (And thus, that extract—to which we referred in our **Pastoral and Paternal Letter**—came into the hands of our Assembly directly from the President <note>original: "Præses"</note> of the South Holland Synod). The second was a letter from the Reverend Consistory of Ysselstein, containing weighty reasons for concern regarding the Assembly of the Moravians; however, it also indicated that their Reverences could provide no specific details, as those people associated as little with them as they did with any other denomination, though they allowed free access to all kinds of sects and Separatists <note>Those who had withdrawn from the official Reformed Church.</note>. Both of these letters are recorded word-for-word in our Consistory Acts. On August 7th, it was decided to hold an extraordinary Consistory meeting in fourteen days to discuss the matter

<margin>The proceedings of the Commission, appointed to investigate the Doctrine and the Existence of the Moravians.</margin>
This Commission met several times in the fear of the Lord. They weighed every point and every passage from the Dutch Moravian writings with the greatest care, examining them in their proper context within the books themselves. Each member's advice was sought on whether a particular passage could serve as proof for the point it was cited for. Everything concluded by a majority vote was finally compiled and organized under specific headings (as will soon be shown). A copy was then placed in the hands of each respective Member of the Commission, with an explicit request that everyone, for themselves and in the fear of God, should once more maturely weigh and consider everything, in order to bring their reflections on the matter the following week, when the Commission would meet again. # Enthusiasm Unmasked, etc.

In the 34th letter, page 93, these words appear: *“It is not something strange to us, but rather common in the congregation here, that a soul, when the light begins to dawn for her, and she begins to notice her darkness and corruption (where previously she was not accustomed to such a melting <note>A common Pietist term for a heart becoming softened and receptive to God’s grace.</note>) that such a soul is* SO CONVINCED <note>original: "ZO OVERTUYGT"</note> *from all sides, and enters into such distress (without it* EVEN BEING URGED BY ANYONE WITH THAT INTENT<note>The author is highlighting that the Moravians believe spiritual conviction happens spontaneously rather than through deliberate preaching of the Law.</note>*) that she does not know what she wants, or what her condition is, or whether she shall stay or run away, until she finally finds her rest in the wounds and merits of the Savior, and also finds her heart within her, etc.”* 

When it was subsequently pointed out to His Reverence <note>A formal title for a clergyman, likely referring here to the member of the commission who defended the Moravians.</note>, in part, that the Commission’s draft did not state that the Moravians are against convictions, but rather that "discovering and convincing means" <note>This refers to the "Law" in traditional Reformed theology, which was used to "discover" a person's sin to them and "convince" them of their need for a Savior.</note> are not considered very necessary; and in part he was asked whether His Reverence could judge that this passage was contrary to our position, especially since it is said of this Moravian conviction that it happens to someone *without it even being urged by anyone with that intent.* 

Upon this, His Reverence folded his paper together, and being most kindly requested to share the remainder with us, His Reverence said that all his other remarks were of that nature, and continued to refuse to provide any more. This is what happened, and those who were also in that Commission can, if it pleases Their Reverences, bear witness to this. 

This now being as it is, I must in good conscience ask everyone what should be judged of the claim made in a certain writing: *“That whatever was brought forward in the Commission, appointed to the investigation of these matters, by one of the Members of that Commission—tending to cause almost everything in the Draft to be dismissed—nevertheless, no place was given to any of those representations.”*

The Herrnhuters, Part I

# ACTS OF THE COMMISSION
### Regarding the investigation into the case of the Herrnhuters.

Mr. I. Le Long <note>Isaac Le Long (1683–1762) was a noted Dutch bibliographer and historian who documented the history of various religious groups, including the Moravians.</note> was requested to appear before the Commission; he entered and was asked:

**A.** How he had come by the pieces and documents making up the First Volume of the *History of the Moravian and Bohemian Brethren*, and whether those pieces could be considered authentic? He answered that he had received them from the hands of a Herrnhuter traveling to Suriname <note>The Moravians began a mission in Suriname in 1735, which became one of their most significant overseas endeavors.</note>, and that the authenticity of the documents themselves was not doubted, although the Lord Count <note>Referring to Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader and protector of the Moravian community at Herrnhut.</note> had shown himself dissatisfied with the publication and the order [in which they were arranged].

**B.** Whether there was any substantial change in the second edition? He answered no, but that he had only corrected some errors therein.

**C.** Whether the Second Volume of the *Memorable Account of the Moravian and Bohemian Brethren*, which is still at the press, could be considered an authentic document of the Herrnhuters? He answered yes: because it consisted partly of the Lord Count’s own hand-written papers and partly of documents already printed in Germany.

**D.** Whether he could also give any report regarding the publisher and printer of the collection of *Herrnhuter Letters with the Supplements*? He answered that he could say nothing of that with certainty. Nevertheless, for various reasons, the Commission made no difficulty in considering them to be authentic documents (a).

**E.** The small Hymnals (b) were judged as not to be placed to the account of the Herrnhuters.

---

(a) Especially since a Member of the Commission, being very well-informed on Herrnhuter matters, declared those Letters with their appendices to be authentic documents, and would make no exception to them.
(b) Namely, those printed at Leeuwarden in the Year 1738 by... <note>The entry cuts off, likely continuing on the next page.</note>

# Enthusiasm Exposed Nakedly, etc.

I. That the Herrnhut Congregation, as it declared itself in Tübingen and Stralsund, belongs to the Lutheran Church, provided they maintain their specific arrangements and Church Discipline. See *Memorable Narrative* <note>original: "Gedenkw. verhaal" refers to J.C. Rieger’s *Gedenkwaardig verhaal van de Herrnhuthsche broeders* (1742), a key source for the history of the movement.</note>, Part 2, pages 188, 191, 192. Thus, it agrees with the Lutheran Church, as long as it goes no further.

A. In the matter of Universal Grace <term>Universal Grace: the theological belief that God's saving grace is offered to all humanity, contrasting with the Reformed view of grace for only the elect</term>, compare this with the words the Count <note>Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the charismatic leader and bishop of the Moravian Brethren.</note> spoke to the Reverend Mr. Manger <note>Samuel Manger (1700–1768) was a Dutch Reformed minister who scrutinized the Moravians.</note>, according to the *Acts of the Synod of South Holland*, which is found in the *Memorable Narrative*, Part 2, page 135. In which matter of Universal Grace, they furthermore:

a. Condemn the doctrine of Particular Grace <term>Particular Grace: the Calvinist doctrine that Christ died only for the "elect," or those chosen by God for salvation</term>, calling it a "Horrible doctrine." See *Acts of the Synod of South Holland*.

b. Call it an error, from which those who join them are converted. See *Memorable Narrative*, Part 2, pages 207 and 205.

B. In the matter of the Sacraments in general, they consider them means to work Grace in the heart. See *Memorable Narrative*, Part 2, page 144. In particular:

a. Concerning Baptism, stating that man receives rebirth therein, but that he must lose that baptismal grace again. See *Acts of the Synod of South Holland*.

b. In the Lord's Supper, they go further than the Lutherans. See *Memorable Narrative*, page 149, Part 2.

II. Furthermore, regarding Indifference in Religions <term>Indifferentism: the stance that specific denominational dogmas are secondary to personal piety or "heart religion," often viewed as a threat by established churches</term>, it was found:

A. That the Congregation refuses to declare itself for any specific denomination. See *Preface to the Letters*, page 4 (a), and will not allow itself to be guided by sectarian boundaries alongside the Scripture. See *Memorable Narrative*, Part 2, pages 212, 213.

The Commission for drafting the Pastoral and Patriotic Letter delivers said Letter to the Assembly, and what was then decided on October 16 and 30.

The Commission for drafting the Pastoral and Patriotic Letter, having carried out their mandate as quickly as was possible for a matter that had to pass through so many hands, delivered the Pastoral and Patriotic Letter on October 16 in an Extraordinary Meeting called for that purpose, and read the same aloud distinctly before the numerous Assembly. And it was resolved in that meeting—notwithstanding that many members voted they felt such satisfaction with the letter as read that they found no objection to it being published immediately (upon which one of the members declared that if such should be the conclusion of the Reverend Assembly, to publish the Letter before everyone had had the freedom to read and examine it, that his Reverence would then be forced to protest against that resolution)—to leave that Writing in the Chamber for 14 days, so that it could be read and examined by everyone. For this purpose, each member was once again invited and heartily exhorted by means of a sealed note, written by the Reverend Scribe <term>Scribe: The "Scriba," the official secretary of the Church Council responsible for records and correspondence.</term>, sent around to the houses of all the respective members. It was also decided that the citations of the passages from which the grievances <term>grievances: "bezwaarnissen," or formal theological objections and points of concern regarding the Moravian doctrines.</term> were drawn should be noted either at the bottom or in the margin when the Letter was judged fit to be issued in print (since in the Writing laid upon the Table of the Church Council, the passages were not indicated, although they were all—and many more besides—contained in the transcript used by the Commission). ### Of the Moravians. Part I.

The Letter was to be signed by the Honorable President <note>original: "Præfes"</note> and Secretary <note>original: "Scriba"</note> of that time.

Finally, on October 30, in an Extraordinary Meeting that was well-attended for that purpose, the publication of that drafted Pastoral and Patriotic Letter—which had been available for the closest examination—was discussed, and it was decided by a very large majority of votes (among which were several of the senior Honorable Members who, being unable to be present due to illness, declared their consent through written advice, which was read publicly after the members present had voted orally) that the Pastoral and Patriotic Letter, without any the slightest change, in the manner planned on October 16, be handed over to the printing press; the execution of this was left to the Honorable Members who had served on the Commission. In this Meeting, everything was unanimous, except that, in part, one of the Reverend Ministers and one of the Honorable Elders were of the opinion that the publication should be delayed for another eight days. But, in part, and this is what it primarily concerns, three Honorable Members present opposed the publication of that Pastoral and Patriotic Letter, each giving reasons, and finally protesting against the publication. *Scripture cannot be the only or primary rule of Christians: for then there would be no distinction between the Law and the Gospel—for the Law and the Gospel differ in this, that the Law, written from without and externally, brings condemnation, but has no life for Salvation: while the Gospel not only reveals the evil, but is also that which is inward and powerful, and gives to the soul the strength to obey, and sets it free from evil—The Law or the letter that is outside of us, kills: but the Gospel, which is the inward and spiritual Law, gives life, for it consists not so much in words as in power etc: Let an understanding person compare these matters with one another, and note especially that the externally written word of the Gospel is distinguished from that which is primarily inward; and this Gospel that is inward is the inward word, entirely distinct from the externally written word. And that this is the sentiment of the Moravians, in agreement with the Bevers* <note>The "Bevers" likely refers to the followers of Jakob Böhme (Bohmists), whose mystical ideas about the "Inner Word" heavily influenced radical Pietism and the Moravians.</note>*, is taught to us by the 3rd Supplement at the end of the Moravian Letters, where on page 187 the Anointing* <note>term: "Zalvinge" (Anointing) - refers to the Holy Spirit's internal guidance as described in 1 John 2:27.</note>*, which is nothing other than the inward Word and the inward Jesus (as shall be abundantly shown to us), is called an* **INWARD GOSPEL-LIGHT**, *kindled in the soul. In what follows, this matter shall be clearly demonstrated.*

<header>Enthusiasm Unmasked, etc.</header>

Regarding this artificial distinction, we present to the consideration of sensible and God-fearing people: (1) what kind of "word" that might be, which God ordained from the beginning (when man was still in the state of righteousness), as distinct from the Law and the Gospel, or existing as an unseparated and undivided whole within them both? Should anyone desire the key to unlock these expressions according to the sense of the Mystics, let him read what the notorious <term>Pierre Poiret<note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher whose "Divine Economy" was influential among Pietists but often criticized by orthodox theologians for its focus on internal illumination over external scripture.</note></term> says about it in his *Divine Economy*, Book 3, Chapter 7, § 8. (2) What does it mean that God, after the Fall, divided the word into Law and Gospel? (3) Does it not give pause that Jesus is said to have "first" brought the Gospel from the Father’s bosom? I know that Jesus, who is in the Father's bosom, proclaimed the Gospel to us; but I also know that both the Father and Jesus, through the Holy Spirit, had already proclaimed that Gospel of salvation to the <note>Old Testament</note> Fathers before Jesus came in the flesh from the Father's bosom. And all those know this along with me who understand the difference between the teachings of the <term>Socinians<note>A non-trinitarian Christian group that denied the pre-existence of Christ; the author is accusing the Moravians of sharing their "heretical" views by suggesting the Gospel didn't exist until the Incarnation.</note></term> and the orthodox Church. Yet I wish to draw no conclusions; if anyone, through leniency, can bear all this and interpret it in a good sense, I shall not build an accusation upon it—especially since that Song, in its continuation, seems to speak of the Word of God in a completely different manner than the corrupt Mystics.

<margin>Among the Moravians, internal preaching precedes external preaching.</margin>

We have something that comes closer and shall teach us how that Gospel—taken as distinct from the Law—is preached, and by whom, according to the sense of the Moravian [Herrnhuth] Hymns. We find an opening for this in Hymn 159, being the second that deals with the office that preaches reconciliation. There we find a threefold preaching and three distinct preachers. The first preaching is presented thus:

I do not ask here whether these manners of speaking, each on their own, might not be excused by Biblical phrases. *The beholding of Jesus*, compared with what is written in <note>Luke 22:61, where the Lord turned and looked at Peter, leading to his repentance.</note> Luke 22: 61. *The witness of the Father*, through which one goes to Jesus, compared with the <term>drawing of the Father<note>The concept from John 6:44 that no one can come to Christ unless the Father "draws" them.</note></term> in John 6: 44. I shall also not ask whether the order of the work of Grace is not reversed here, according to the <term>economic operations<note>In theology, the "economy" of the Trinity refers to the distinct roles played by the Father, Son, and Spirit in the history of salvation. For there, the Spirit begins the work of Grace with the conviction of sin (John 16: 8), which is here attributed to the beholding of the Son, etc. 

But this is the point upon which everything depends: you hear here of three sermons following one another in succession, brought under the *office* that *preaches reconciliation*; but what kind of sermons are they? They are such as are performed immediately by the Triune God, where until now not the slightest mention is made of the means of the *written* and *preached* Word of God contained in the Bible. ...[proven]. Whether we have acted so faithlessly in this matter, like those who, *carried away by passion and prejudice, bear witness against the truth*, regarding that we leave the judgment to the impartial reader.

<margin>
...[ness] of the expressions of the Author, shown. <note>This marginal note is a continuation from the previous page, likely concluding a point about the "clarity" or "truthfulness" of the author's words.</note>
</margin>

But before we move on from here to the following point that our Anonymous Author <note>A common strategy in 18th-century religious debates was to respond to "Anonymous Authors" to avoid direct personal attacks while still dismantling their arguments.</note> objects against us, we cannot let it pass unnoticed that our man does not seem fully at ease in his conscience regarding the explanation he gave for the expression, *to bind the heart to words* <note>original German: "das hertze an worte binden"</note>. Namely, his claim that *a soul full of the internal peace of God here testifies that it knows not how to express its condition with any words*, does not hold up so infallibly; which is why, on that same page 6, he immediately follows with: *Or if one wishes to see here some Precept or precepts of Words? then they shall be* **HUMAN PRECEPTS**, to which such a soul declares itself unable to be bound. You see clearly, our author admits that one could at least understand the expression in the song over which there is a dispute as referring to some *precept of words*. But we shall not dwell on that any longer; yet what does it mean that *a soul (namely, one that has tasted or is full of internal peace of the soul)* declares it cannot bind itself to *human precepts*? By which "human precepts" we can, according to the nature of the matter, understand nothing other than *Confessions of Faith, Formulas of Concord* <note>The 'Formula of Concord' (1577) is a fundamental Lutheran document that settled doctrinal disputes; the author here defends its authority against Moravian "emotionalism."</note>, and all that belongs to the *external institutions* in a congregation, which bind and must bind for the preservation of good order and the edification and unity in the doctrine of faith. To what extent these *precepts* may be called *human*, being drafted by men, and what binding force they possess insofar as they are drawn from the Word of God, and how necessary it is to be bound to them—not because those precepts are from men, but because they rest upon the infallible Word of God and agree with God’s ordinance, who being a God of order, wills that everything happen with order and for edification—we shall not recount here. We say only that our Anonymous Man has truly [found/hit upon] the right

sense of the **Moravian Community** <note>Original: "Herrnhuthische Gemeente." (a) It may seem obscure to some what the author of this Hymn means here by this *garden*, in which the soul waits for the voice of the anointing in the *Spirit*. Most will, I think, understand it to mean the Church and the Assembly, in which a believer, under the means of the Gospel, waits for the voice of the Anointing. But that is missing the trail; the garden here is the *heart*, the innermost *ground of the soul* <term>ground of the soul: a mystical term (Seelengrund) referring to the deepest, most essential part of a person where they can experience direct union with the Divine</term>, in which that anointing, *that internal Jesus*, and that internal word, dwells, to teach from within. This is evident from the explanation we find in the Hymn itself; for everyone is the interpreter of their own words. In the first verse it says:

# The Fanaticism Unmasked, etc.

It is beyond dispute that the act of turning within oneself, of which God's Word speaks, consists in a person bringing a matter to their heart with composure, coming to their senses, examining their heart, living close to their heart, and paying attention to its impulses; see Isaiah 46:8, Luke 15:10, Deuteronomy 4:39, Chapter 6:6, and elsewhere. Anyone desiring an orthodox and godly description of this may find it in the work of the great theologian Voetius, *On the Exercises of Piety* <note>original: "De Exercitiis Pietatis", a seminal work by Gijsbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a leading Dutch Reformed theologian known for his strict orthodoxy and interest in practical godliness.</note> Chapter 2, page 38, etc. One may also compare this with that alert champion of truth and godliness, Hoornbeek, in *Practical Theology* <note>original: "Theol: Practic:", referring to Johannes Hoornbeek (1617–1666), another prominent Dutch theologian.</note> Volume 1, Book 4, Chapter 11, *On the knowledge of oneself* <note>original: "De notitia ſui ipſius"</note>; and Volume 2, Book 8, Chapter 2, *On the examination of oneself* <note>original: "De examine ſui ipſius"</note>.

However, the corrupt *mystical inwardness* <term>Inwardness: (Dutch: 'inkeringe') The practice of withdrawing from the external world to focus on the internal spiritual state.</term> differs violently from this. Among them, it is: *the exercise of a person through which they seek and awaken God, Christ, and the Word in the innermost ground of their soul—believing them to be already essentially present and innate there. Through this, all active effort gradually falls away, and the person is brought into an entirely passive state, with a complete absence of sense and will, until they finally enter fully into the essence of God, sinking in and being swallowed up within it.* We shall not yet observe the effects and consequences of this inwardness, but regarding the inwardness itself, we shall now cite a few examples from the Moravian Hymnal <note>The "Herrnhuthſche Gezangboek" refers to the hymns used by the Moravian Brethren, often criticized by contemporary orthodox theologians for their emotional and mystical language.</note> as well as other mystical and fanatical <note>The author uses "Enthufiaſtiſche" here, which in the 18th century referred to "enthusiasm"—a derogatory term for religious fervor believed to be based on private revelations rather than scripture.</note> writers.

# The Moravians. Section II. Chapter I.

**He** will not **WASTE** the **GRACE** (a),

**He** shall not **SQUANDER** the **GRACE** (a),

(a) I cannot neglect to mention here how remarkable it is that the Herrnhuters <note>A Pietist Christian denomination (the Moravians) founded by Count von Zinzendorf in the 18th century, often criticized by the orthodox Reformed church for their mystical language.</note> play with words and seek to hide themselves behind them. For what is expressed here in this Song: *He will not waste the GRACE*, was previously expressed in an earlier edition of the Herrnhuter Hymnal with the word **PEARL**: *He will not waste the Pearl*. I learned this from *M. Oetinger* <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782), a prominent German theosophist and prelate who attempted to reconcile Pietism with the mystical theories of Jacob Böhme.</note> in his *High-German Defense of the Herrnhuter Hymnal*, where on page 52 he cites this same verse and uses *Pearl* instead of *Grace*. You may ask, what purpose does this change serve? We say with great boldness that it serves to throw sand in the eyes of simple souls, to mislead through words, and to better cover themselves behind secretive terminology. For it was all too well known in Germany what the most dangerous <term>Enthusiasts: A derogatory term used by the orthodox to describe radical mystics who believed in direct divine inspiration or an "inner light" over the authority of Scripture.</term> understood by that *pearl* hidden in the "ground of the soul"—namely, that *in-created word*, *light*, and *Jesus*. This was as clear as day, even from the title of a book published by the "Father of the Enthusiasts," the notorious *Theophrastus Paracelsus* <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist whose mystical philosophy heavily influenced later radical pietism.</note>, which reads as follows:

> *Theosophical booklet, regarding the true remaining **SEED** of God in us, which remained after the fall, and from which the holy Fathers and Prophets became such great men, through which children of God are still born daily. Published for the purpose that we might seek and learn to recognize that **LITTLE PEARL** hidden within us.*

That is to say: *Theosophical* (this is what the corrupt Mystics call what we would call Theological, for they love the name of *Theosophers* or "God-wise." See *G. Arnold* <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a historian whose work "Unbiased History of the Church and Heretics" was controversial for being sympathetic to those the church labeled as heretics.</note> *in History of Mystical Theology, Chapter 1: §. 8, 9. p. 5.*)

> *booklet, regarding the true remaining **SEED** of God in us, which remained after the fall, and through which the holy Fathers and Prophets became such great men, and through which children of God are still born daily. Published for this purpose, so that we might seek and learn to recognize that **PEARL** hidden within us.*

Now, so that everyone might not immediately notice that they mean this Paracelsian *Pearl*, they have placed **GRACE** in the place of that word in the new and allegedly improved edition of the Hymnal. Yet even this excuse cannot help them, for by doing so they not only fail to change the meaning, but they also cannot [hide] themselves under that word.

<note>The original text provides this poem first in German and then in Dutch. The German "Seelen-grund" and Dutch "zielen-grond" refer to the "ground of the soul," a central concept in Rhineland mysticism suggesting a spark of the divine exists at the human core.</note>

-> In the center, one remains still. <-
-> The world is but a wheel, an ever-turning circle; <-
-> If you enter with desire, you will be caught in the turning; <-
-> GOD IS THE CENTER; return to the *ground of the soul*. <-

Abominable secrets indeed. What do you think, reader who loves truth and godliness, of such an "inward-turning" into oneself, and into the innermost ground of the soul, to find there the Treasure and the Pearl—the true Divinity—which lies hidden there in all people? This is that deceptively beautiful expression by which so many simple souls (who do not understand what is meant by it until they are already deeply enough entangled in the snare and this secret is revealed to them) are miserably led astray. They imagine that because they hear the language of the Bible, they are also hearing a Biblical truth, though it is far from it.

<margin>On the agreement of the Moravians in this matter with other corrupted Mystics.</margin>
It is not obscure from which wells the Moravians <note>The "Herrnhuthers," or Moravian Brethren, a Pietist Christian denomination.</note> and their predecessors have drawn this murky water. We shall not even mention that the Platonists posited that a part of the Divinity dwelt within man (a), but only say that the most corrupted among the corrupted Mystics speak of such an *in-turning into oneself*, through which one *finds the essence of Divinity in its center or the innermost ground of the soul*. Out of a multitude of proofs, which—

---

(a) Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, *Meditations*, Book 3, Section 5: <note>original Latin: "Deus qui in te residet"</note> "The God who resides in you." And Book 5, Section 27: <note>original Latin: "Cum Deis vivendum..."</note> "One must live with the gods; and he does this who shows his soul to be constantly satisfied... and does whatever that PROTECTING SPIRIT <term>Genius: In Roman religion, a personal guardian spirit; here used to describe the divine spark within.</term> wills, which Jupiter has given to each as a protector and guide, a particle of himself." Also Book 12, Section 26: <note>original Latin: "Oblitus es..."</note> "You have forgotten that the mind of every person is God, and has flowed down from Divinity." Compare on this passage the notes of the most learned Gataker.

There he declares himself openly and clearly enough, and he does so no less in Book 3, Chapter 10, §. 16: *Faith, as far as its light is concerned,* **IS GOD HIMSELF** *in the* **CENTER-POINT OF THE HEART**—striving to work, and that which proceeds from this (namely a sincere desire to please God) **IS THE WORK OF FAITH.** Compare with that his more detailed treatise on Faith in Book 5, Chapter 4, § 26 and following: How far the disguised Alethophilus <note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth," frequently used by various 18th-century polemical writers.</note> agrees with this has been pointed out and refuted by the learned Mr. Cremer in the *Chain of Morals* <note>Original Dutch: *Zeden-keten*.</note> page 193, etc.

What do you think, Reader, of such a theology, which teaches us the order and manner of the most important part of the work of reconciliation? I have wished to set that down here, partly to unwrap the sought-after ambiguity of the convoluted expressions of the presumed Bishop of the falsely-named Moravians <note>A biting reference to Count Zinzendorf, who claimed the title of Bishop of the Renewed Moravian Church.</note>, and partly to give you the key in hand to unlock the true secret of many seemingly beautiful <term>Herrnhut</term> <note>Another name for the Moravian Brethren, named after their community, Herrnhut ("The Lord’s Watch").</note> expressions, primarily in their Hymnbook and Letters, so that no one might be led astray by fair speech regarding reconciliation, justification, and faith.

# Enthusiasm Revealed Nakedly, etc.

<margin>The inward word alone is sufficient.</margin> Let this be enough for now regarding the first matter: namely, that the Moravians <term>Herrnhuthers; followers of Count Zinzendorf’s Pietist movement</term> elevate the *inward word* above the *externally written word*. Indeed, they do so to such an extent that they judge the former alone to be sufficient for salvation—even if the latter is not added to it—along with all the consequences of that view. Anyone who might not yet be fully convinced of this should, for further evidence, compare it with **Hymn 741**, which is the first under the title of *Orderly Conduct*, verses 30–33. And especially **Hymn 185**, where it is clearly stated *that they need nothing else but that inward light*.

### The Moravians. Part II. Chapter I.

<margin>Literal knowledge is held in very low regard by the Moravians.</margin>

B. The second point that we promised to investigate, we shall now unfold a little more closely, yet somewhat more concisely—namely, that **Biblical knowledge**, the **knowledge of the truth**, and the means to achieve it, the **investigation of the Scriptures**, along with other means of grace <note>In 18th-century theology, "means of grace" (Dutch: *middelen der genade*) refers to the external instruments through which God communicates grace, such as the Bible, preaching, and the sacraments.</note>, are held in very low regard by the Moravians. This was proven in our *Pastoral and Fatherly Letter* <note>original: "Herd. en Vad. Brief"</note> on pages 16, 17, or 18, 19. This is what our Anonymous Writer calls *accusations formulated from their own words to gain traction* (page 7). Meanwhile, he refutes not a single one of those points which—in order to support that well-founded accusation—are cited not only from the *Acts of the Highly Honorable South Holland Synod*, but also from the *Preface and the Appendix of the Moravian Letters*, and from Le Long’s *Memorable Account* (these being authentic Moravian documents). Therefore, we assume them to be proven facts. His only observation concerns the citation from the **544th Hymn**, which we have already abundantly resolved. We could, therefore, let the matter rest here; but to leave no debt unpaid, here is a further addition to prove what we were meant to prove: namely, that *the knowledge of the truth is truly not held in high regard by them.* I read the following words on page 91 of the first volume of the *Memorable Account, etc.*, published by I. Le Long <note>Isaac Le Long (1683–1762) was a historian and bibliographer who wrote extensively on the Moravians, initially with interest but later with significant criticism.</note> (others have also read it and did not let it pass unnoticed, just as it must not and should not be overlooked, because it reveals to us the true nature of the Moravians in more than one respect). When the great influx to that Community—of many hundreds of people (whether this be an exaggerated expression, I leave to the Author’s account)—with various motives was mentioned, he continues his narrative in this manner: *Those who still* **GAPED AT ONE OR THE OTHER SECT** <note>original: "VERGAAPTEN"</note> (the Reformed and Lutherans certainly belong among those; and to be a Moravian, one must stop "gaping" at those sects) *or were still too attached to* **MAN**, *or those who through not enough—*

...careful deliberation of matters, had fallen into **HARMFUL SCHISMS**; (which these are, they are cunning enough to hide) have here, through the grace of the Lord, committed themselves to a desired stillness, and embraced a general unity; **CONSIDERING THEMSELVES NOW HAPPY, HERE IN THEIR SIMPLICITY, TO KNOW LITTLE OF JESUS, BUT TO PRACTICE MUCH LOVE AND FAITH.** What say you, reader? This is surely clear and distinct enough. Those who have laid aside all infatuation with one Sect or another, and having embraced the general Moravian <term>Herrnhuthsche</term> <note>Referring to the Herrnhuters or Moravians, followers of Count Zinzendorf who settled on his estate, Herrnhut ("The Lord's Watch").</note> unity, consider themselves happy in their simplicity *to know little of Jesus*, these can surely set no high price upon that Biblical knowledge, (*in which the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy, and in which all the Scriptures, which must be searched, testify of Him,*). Because I have no desire to dispute with these people, as they also declare they do not wish to engage, I shall not ask how someone could be said to practice much love and faith regarding Jesus, of whom he considers it a happiness to know little? This, at least, cannot coexist with a reasonable love and a true faith, for *unknown makes unloved* <note>original: "onbekent maakt onbemint," a common Dutch proverb meaning that one cannot love what one does not know.</note>; indeed, those who know God as He has revealed Himself in His word, through the light of the spirit paired with that word, they alone can truly love Him. But to believe in Him of whom one has not heard, and thus does not know much about, is impossible according to Paul in Romans 10:14. Yet for the Moravians, it is a happy state; for blind faith is for them the safest, and also the most necessary (though for us the most lamentable) to preserve the general unity, or rather to carry away poor blinded souls through cunning deceptions. I do not know if we could find any better explanation, in the sense of the Moravian Congregation, regarding these words cited from I. Le Long <note>Isaac Le Long (1683–1762) was a Dutch bibliographer and historian whose works on the Moravians were often used by critics to highlight the group's perceived errors.</note>, than those which I discover, partly in the 580th Hymn, verse 15, concisely, and partly in the 765th Hymn of the *High German Hymnal*, somewhat more extensively. ### The Moravian Brethren, Part II, Chapter I.

<margin>The view of Zinzendorf is brought to the test.</margin>
E: Letter following the Defense of Mr. Watteville <note>Johannes von Watteville (1718–1788) was a prominent bishop in the Moravian Church and Zinzendorf's son-in-law.</note>, p. 4. There are, he says, certain FUNDAMENTAL TRUTHS <note>original: "GROND-WAARHEDEN"</note> (these are none other than those we call Foundational truths, which concern the foundation of salvation; for the Count immediately distinguishes from these FUNDAMENTAL TRUTHS, *speculations* and *allusions*, in which one can and may freely feel according to their own understanding without harming the foundation of salvation,) IN WHICH NO HUMAN ERRS <note>original: "DAAR GEEN MENSCH IN DWAALT"</note> (namely: whether he be Heathen, Turk <note>In the 18th century, "Turk" was a common general term for Muslims.</note>, etc., for it is stated here in a completely indefinite sense) *out of a lack of understanding, but solely from the temptation of his dead, uncrushed heart, never washed in the blood of the Lamb; and to err thus is the worst sin, and the actual matter against which the preaching of the Holy Spirit (John 16: 8, 9) is directed.* But there are other errors, which solely concern the SPECULATION OF THE UNDERSTANDING, *which God overlooks in His children, and which one must therefore also tolerate in one another.* Anyone who has paid attention to all that we have treated extensively in the preceding will now, if he is not blinded by prejudice, clearly learn from these words that there must be something in all people—even in those who do not have the Word of the Gospel—that so clearly convinces them, not just of one thing (namely: that there is a God, Creator, and Sustainer, etc.) but of several *Fundamental and Foundational truths* touching the foundation of salvation, so that not one of all humans *can err* regarding them *out of a lack of understanding*—that is, because he is completely ignorant of those fundamental truths. But what is it then, that is in him, which so clearly convinces him of those Fundamental Truths touching the Foundation of salvation? That cannot be the light of reason and conscience of which Paul speaks in Romans 1 and 2; for that does not teach the most essential fundamental truths leading to salvation. This also cannot be the written Word of God; for not all people have that. What then? It is *the inward light, enlightening every person coming into this world; this is the inward word, the seed, yes, the inward Jesus Himself.* <note>The author is accusing the Moravians of holding beliefs similar to the Quakers, suggesting that an "inward light" provides divine knowledge independent of Scripture.</note> But how does it happen then, that people still err by that light, when they [do not err] out of a lack of understanding regarding those fundamental truths—

And that is the chief sin of man, according to the Lord Count <note>The author refers to Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader of the Moravian Brethren.</note>, that man does not give ear to that inward calling voice of the word in the center of his heart, by turning inward to the soul’s ground, and of this he is convicted by the Spirit, when the anointing gains the upper hand, John 16: 8, 9: that he has committed this chief sin, and has not listened to the inward word, nor been faithful to his light.* This is, in a brief summary, the secret of the system of the Count's theology, just as it is also the system of all Fanatics <note>original: "Geestdryvers," a pejorative term used in the 18th century for radical spiritualists who claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit outside of traditional church structures.</note>. <margin>What the Moravians hold regarding the means, etc.</margin>
Since Biblical knowledge is judged to be so little necessary, how can the means of grace—through which man, *as means ordained by God, is brought to the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, and is outwardly convinced*—be held in high esteem? This has been shown in our *Pastoral and Fatherly Letter*, page 17 or 19. And therefore all outward things concerning the outward ceremonies of religion, along with everything that binds outwardly (including all formulas and bonds of unity, as we saw above), are of little use or necessity. At the very least, they are to be valued no higher than *scaffolding on a house being built, which, when it is fully built and the Congregation has become a complete building, is dismantled*. See our *Pastoral and Fatherly Letter* at the cited place. I will now only briefly note one or two things regarding this.

<margin>*Meanwhile, their exercises are judged absolutely necessary, even in defiance of any prohibition by the government.*</margin>
Who does not see what this aims at? Especially when, from the 16th verse onwards, the Moravian Congregation <note>original: "Herrnhuthsche Gemeente"</note> is set up as if it were Zion <note>In biblical terms, Zion represents the true city of God or the faithful remnant.</note>, that small flock, against the entirety of Babel <note>A common polemical term for the established churches, implying they are sites of confusion and corruption.</note>, comprising all other denominations. Indeed, this was necessary; everything had to be torn down if the Moravian Sect was to be built up. Upon the ruins of all other denominations, the building of this new Congregation had to be established, provided God did not intervene. Therefore, as much as the public worship of other denominations is disparaged, the assemblies of the Moravians are highly exalted. This is despite the fact that in those meetings—aside from singing from this Hymnal, which in many ways contains mysteries of godlessness and the depths of Satan—little is performed that resembles a rational service of God. Such secret gatherings, which they wrongly call *Exercises* and *Christian Conversations*, but are much more rightly termed forbidden *Conventicles* <term>Conventicles: Private, often illegal religious meetings held outside the authority of the established state church.</term> and clandestine assemblies, are nevertheless esteemed by these people far above the public worship of the Reformed and Lutheran churches. For this reason, the Count <note>referring to Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, the leader of the Moravian Brethren.</note> has not only written an entire book to recommend them (which has been translated from High German and published in Nijmegen this year by H. Heymans), but they are judged so necessary that a Moravian is obliged to renounce the obedience owed to his lawful government, under whose protection he lives, rather than neglect attending these so-called *private exercises*. Hear the very words of the Lord Count, in a High German writing titled *Reflections and Special Circular Letter, etc.* <note>original: "Bedenken und besonder Sendschreiben"</note>, where he says on pages 44 and 45:

> No authority, if IT WISHES TO BE CALLED A CHRISTIAN AUTHORITY, can [prohibit] the private meetings

Forgive me for saying that anyone who dares to use and write such language must either see through the eyes of others—having lent both his eyes to someone else and *pawned his heart to the Herrnhutters*—or he must believe that all his readers are so blinded by prejudice that, upon his word, they will also want to give their eyes to him. Does it mean that those words, which we cited in our Pastoral and Paternal Letter, are not there? *But that only the further words are found?* If it is to be understandable language, that must be the meaning. But we cannot believe that he means it in that sense, for the words cited by us are expressed all too clearly there. Or does it mean that the sense of those words was poorly captured by us, and that those words must be understood in another sense, which is the sense of the <term>Congregation<note>The "Gemeente" or "Unitas Fratrum," the official self-designation of the Moravian Brethren.</note></term>? # Enthusiasm Revealed in its Nakedness, etc.

...kept back? This seems to us the most likely meaning that the man, with his dark, convoluted words, intended to convey (unless he meant to instruct me otherwise). To that, I shall answer: I believe the good man must not have even taken the trouble to look up those words in the book of the <term>Moravian Letters<note>original: *Herrnhuthsche Brieven*. These were collections of correspondence and reports from the Moravian community at Herrnhut, used by critics to find evidence of unorthodox teachings.</note></term> and *Supplements*. (I have noticed this more often in this matter: that those who blow the loudest spend the least time investigating the facts, but content themselves with seeing through the eyes of others and, as if by commission, spreading many tales.)

For in the third part of the <term>Treatise on the Anointing<note>original: *Verhandelinge van de Zalvinge*. In this context, "Anointing" refers to the indwelling and teaching of the Holy Spirit.</note></term>, from which our words were taken, three distinct stages of the anointing are presented, and three kinds of ways and means are indicated to reach each of these three stages. The title placed above that third section could have convinced him of this, had he taken the trouble to look at the book, for it reads thus: *How one comes to the Anointing, understands it, and becomes sure and certain in it.*

First, to come to the Anointing and obtain it, the means is to repent and believe in *Jesus Christ*. Then one is showered with it.

Second, to *understand* the Anointing once one has already obtained it through conversion—for he who has it does not understand it immediately—the means is *the soft, quiet waiting*, etc.

Finally, to become sure and certain in it, which is a higher stage than the two preceding ones, a third means is indicated, which is also distinct from the two preceding means: *obedience without contradiction*, etc.

Now I ask you, truth-loving reader, judge whether our anonymous rebuker even knows and understands what he intended to say with his contrived, dark language, except perhaps to arouse a prejudice in the minds of simple and gullible readers.

I am well aware that God’s word frequently speaks of a *drawing* <note>The concept of "drawing" (*trekkinge*) refers to the theological idea of God attracting the human soul toward Himself, as seen in the Song of Solomon 1:4 and John 6:44.</note> (Song of Sol. 1:4; John 6:44). I also agree, with all orthodox members of our Church, that a <term>prevenient grace<note>Prevenient grace is a theological term for divine grace that precedes human decision, "coming before" any action on the part of the believer.</note></term> is necessary, both in the first conversion and in all further exercises of the Believers, who also gladly acknowledge that they can do nothing without Jesus (John 15:5). But such a "pulling," in which the human remains merely passive, and lets God do with them as He will—that I do not recognize. Instead, I set my seal to the words of Paul, in which the middle path of righteousness is shown to us in this matter: ***Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work, according to (His) good pleasure.*** (Phil. 2:12, 13). 

The <term>Herrnhuters<note>The Herrnhuters, or Moravian Brethren, were a Pietist group whose focus on emotional, internal experiences of Christ’s suffering often drew criticism from more traditional Protestant theologians.</note></term> use the latter verse as a cloak, but they lose the former entirely from sight and heart when they praise that *idle-quiet-waiting* as a means to understand the Anointing. # Enthusiasm Laid Bare, etc.

...simple, but even to sensible Members of our and other Congregations, among whom some, to our deep sorrow, have gone so far as to pass judgment on the Pastoral and Fatherly Letter, and on its Authors and other Members of the <term>Consistory<note>Original Dutch: *Kerkenraat*. The governing body of a local Reformed church, typically composed of the minister and elders.</note></term>. These judgments do not at all accord with the love and esteem they ought to bear toward their Teachers, who sought to warn them out of love and faithfulness, even if they had erred as men. The paths that have been taken to instill a belief in the imagined treacherous dealings of the Congregation’s Consistory are many; some are somewhat more secret, others more public. It has been seen fit to make simple folk believe that in the cited Hymn it stated that a believer testified *to be able and to will to do nothing without* JESUS; that has come to my attention several times. Afterward, some copies of this verse, along with other Hymns, were secretly slipped into the hands of various people. Subsequently, a small Hymn-book was clandestinely printed, in which some of the best Hymns from the High German <term>Moravian Hymnal<note>Original Dutch: *Herrnhuthſche Gezang-boek*. The official collection of spiritual songs used by the followers of Count von Zinzendorf, known for their emotional and sometimes controversial imagery.</note></term> were translated and set into Dutch rhyme, with the intent to make the innocent believe that the Moravian Hymnal must truly be a holy and precious book of songs. The title of this translated Hymn-book is: *Evangelical Hymns, translated from the High German. Containing especially the grace of the Gospel, in the Reconciliation of the blood of the Lamb; and how one obtains a part therein. Along with the heartfelt declaration of the Savior toward us, and of hearts toward the Savior, flowing therefrom. Printed at Amsterdam 1738.* The name of the Printer is not mentioned, just as the Translator and Publisher hide themselves (although it is not unknown to me who the first is, and to whom the copies were delivered, and who distributed them partly to Friends and partly sold them). In the Preface, the Publisher declares that these Hymns are only a beginning, and that more will follow. And among other things, he testifies: *One is so near...*

...we remain limited to that which we have brought this verse to in the Pastoral and Fatherly Letter, to prove the *passive-inactive-quiet-waiting*. <note>The author is critiquing the Moravian concept of "stillness," where a believer does nothing but wait for God to act, which orthodox critics saw as dangerous spiritual laziness.</note> For

of that kind, I shall not speak. But I appeal only to one of the most prominent Defenders and Leaders of the Moravian <term>Conventicles<note>A "conventicle" was a private religious meeting held outside the established state church. In the 18th century, these were often viewed with suspicion by the authorities.</note></term> in this City, whose name I spare out of discretion, though I would name him if necessary. I have in my hands an authentic copy of a Confession that he gave to a person well known to me, who, after learning that Confession by heart, was baptized by him. In it, this is the 3rd Question: *Since one is baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, what do you believe first of the Father?* The answer to that Question is: *That he is* THE ONLY, ETERNAL, *omnipresent, omniscient, almighty and merciful* SUPREME BEING, *who possesses all blessedness and perfection in and of himself, who is the Creator of heaven and earth, and who maintains and governs everything through his wise providence.* When in the 4th Question it is asked, *what do you believe of the Son?* the answer contains various honorary names given to the second person as the Son of God (just as the <term>Rijnsburg Meeting<note>The Rijnsburgers, or Collegiants, were a Dutch religious group known for their rejection of strict dogma and their leanings toward Socinianism—the denial of the Trinity.</note></term> is accustomed to piling them up), yet in the entire answer it is not said in plain words that he is the *self-existing and mono-essential true God with the Father;* <note>The author is suspicious because the Moravians use beautiful titles for Jesus but avoid saying he is "of the same substance" as God the Father.</note> yet because this answer can be twisted, I will not dwell on it. The 5th Question, dealing with the power and fruit of Christ's death and suffering, is also quite obscured and complicated. But in the 6th Question, the Socinian sting reveals itself clearly again. Thus it is asked, *what do you believe of the Holy Spirit?* the answer is: *That* HE IS THE POWER OF THE MOST HIGH, *who goes out from the Father, and is shared through the Son to all who believe in him and his Father.* And regarding the Sacraments, when in the 13th Question it is asked: *what do you hold regarding this ceremony?* namely: *the Holy Supper.* The answer is: *That the same must be maintained in the Christian Church* (1.) *as a grateful remembrance of the suffering and death of our Savior.* Luke 22:19, 20. Matthew 26:26, 28. 1 Corinthians 11:26. (2.) *as a testimony of our communion with the Lord.* 1 Corinthians 10:16. (3.) *As a sign of mutual love and communion of the believers, as members of one body.* 1 Corinthians 10:17. ...that extravagant rule **OF HAVING TO FOLLOW JESUS**, does not change the sense of *knowing nothing, knowing nothing, wanting nothing, and doing nothing* <note>These four "nothings" are central to the doctrine of Quietism, which the author is attacking. ---

(a) Here our Writer seems to be knowledgeable in the Greek Language, and wishes to conclude from the nature of that language that those little children of whom Jesus speaks in Matthew 19:14 must be newly-born infants, still wrapped in swaddling clothes and carried in arms, who were brought to Jesus, by comparing Luke 18:16 and 1 Peter 2:2. However, whether he succeeds all too happily in this linguistic observation of his, we wish to leave to the judgment of those more knowledgeable in the Greek language than he. In Matthew, it says *the children* <note>original Greek: *τα παιδια* (ta paidia)</note>, and that word, just like the word *child* <note>original Greek: *παις* (pais)</note>, is of a general meaning, expressing all sorts of children of both sexes, not only the young and newly born, as in Matthew 2:11 and Luke 2:21, but also children who can already walk and run, even twelve years old, Mark 5:39, 40 and Matthew 21:15; and such children who are capable of instruction, which is why a teacher of such children is called a *pedagogue* <note>original Greek: *παιδαγωγος* (paidagogos), a tutor or guardian of children</note>. Meanwhile, it does not lead to honor to be like such children in ignorance regarding matters of which one ought to have knowledge, as Paul says:

> *Brothers, do **NOT BE CHILDREN** in understanding; but be children in malice, and in understanding be mature*, 1 Cor. 14:20.

We present this passage to our Anonymous Writer and to those whose supposed childlike simplicity he wishes to gloss over. Thus, our good man cannot yet find anything in those words used by Matthew with which he can justify his interpretation. The comparison with the 16th verse of Luke 18, to which he appeals, does not help him in the least, for there the same word appears, *the children* <note>original Greek: *τα παιδια* (ta paidia)</note>. But I see well enough where he is going; he has incorrectly cited the 16th verse, and he seems to mean the 15th verse, where it says *the infants* <note>original Greek: *τα βρεφη* (ta brephe)</note>, and of that word *the infant* <note>original Greek: *το βρεφος* (to brephos)</note>, Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Greek scholar and archbishop noted for his commentaries</note> remarks that it signifies *a first-born child* that is still being nursed by a wet-nurse. And in Luke 2:12, the first-born child Jesus appears as *an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes* <note>original Greek: *βρεφος εσπαργανωμενον* (brephos esparganomenon)</note>. Compare Acts 7:19. <note>The OCR reads Acts 17:19, but the context of infants suggests Acts 7:19, regarding the exposure of newborn babies in Egypt.</note> Indeed, that word is even sometimes used for a child in

We answer to this: That Song 221, being the last under the title, *Of the Good Walk*, deals with and makes much of *humility*, is true, and can be seen from the 4th verse; yet that this *humility* could or might be called the *true humility* with any appearance of truth, and that it is the desirable *Child-likeness* <term>Kinder-geſtalte: Literally "child-form," referring to a spiritual state of infancy or innocence</term> which Jesus wishes to commend through the example of the children brought to Him, is what we deny with much boldness and on good grounds. But that the alleged Moravian *humility*, everywhere praised by them under the glittering name of *childlike simplicity*, is understood by it, is also true; which *childlike simplicity* is fundamentally nothing else among them but an absolute *passive inactivity*, and inactive passivity, which differs as much from the true *humble child-likeness* that Jesus commends, as darkness from light.

On used in the mother's womb. Luke 1:44. However, this meaning is not so universal that the word *brephos* <note>original Greek: βρέφος, usually meaning an infant or unborn child</note> is not also used for a child who can already exercise his understanding. For when Paul testifies of Timothy that *from a child* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ βρέφους (apo brephous)</note> he *had known the Holy Scripture*; 2 Timothy 3:15. This certainly cannot be said of him when he was still a first-born infant *wrapped in swaddling clothes*. I know what the linguist Hakspanius <note>Theodor Hackspan (1607–1659), a Lutheran theologian and orientalist known for his work on biblical philology</note> has brought against Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a reformed theologian famous for his Bible translations and commentaries</note>, who understands it thus with us, to assert that *from a child* means as much as *after his childhood*; concerning which we leave the judgment to the learned, who can read it in his: Learned Theological-Philological Notes, Part 3, pages 352, 353. The passage from 1 Peter 2:2, which our Anonymous Writer wishes to have compared, is cited by him entirely out of context; for there the word *brephos* does not stand alone, but another word is added that determines the sense: *newly born infants* <note>original Greek: ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη (artigennyta brephe)</note>, and not the one word alone, as our good man in his simplicity believes, is thus translated. Let this be enough for the instruction of our self-imagined Linguist, and of those who might have helped him in this, and to show that the presupposition—that it was newly born children who were carried in arms and brought to Jesus—is without sufficient ground.
