This is a most strange, yet common way of God with the soul—at least in the mind of the corrupt Mystics. First, God takes away everything He has given. This includes not only that grace which the soul already possessed before its actual conversion—which is precisely what the Herrnhuters understand by the loss of <term>Baptismal grace</term><note>The theological idea that the initial grace of baptism is withdrawn to test the believer or to prepare them for a "higher" spiritual state.</note>—but among all that God has given are also included the rational powers of the soul: the <term>rational understanding</term>, judgment, and will, along with the internal and external senses. 

As will shortly be shown, through this process a person comes completely *away from themselves*. Indeed, they are *robbed of self* (this refers to the Mystical concepts of *attachment to self, selfhood, and "I-ness"*<note>The Dutch terms "eigenheit, zelfsheit, ikheit" refer to the individual ego which these mystics sought to annihilate.</note>, which encompasses not just the sinful self, but all natural and rational selfhood as well). Thus, a person falls into a Mystical *death*, in which they can grasp neither God, nor comfort, nor grace. 

And then there is nothing else to do—indeed, according to that foundation, nothing else *can* be done—except to remain in a mindless silence and *let God work upon you, allowing yourself to be purely exercised and used by Him*. One must be so in such a manner as we humans use our hand, which does not move without the signal and influence of the soul, and also like a limb devoid of all reason that cannot move itself and merely allows itself to be used. While this last part is not in the Hymn itself, I find the explanation for it in the booklet *The Spiritual Flower-Garden*<note>original title: "Geiſtliches Blumen-gärtlein," a popular devotional work by the mystic Gerhard Tersteegen.</note>, where on page 9, number 32, I read these words:

Sometimes one does not follow God, sometimes one runs ahead too fast,
One is too sluggish, the other too busy:

We have, in this part, drawn the matters somewhat closer together, and have not expressed the full verses of all the cited hymns, partly because we see that we must be brief, lest all these citations become tedious to the reader, and so that our work does not become too extensive and fall too far behind; and partly to make you understand more clearly the structure of this <term>passive, idle waiting</term> <note>original: "lydelyke-werkeloze-wachten"; a central concept in Quietism where the soul remains "passive" (lydelyke) to allow God to act without human interference</note>. And if it is still not clear enough to you where this passivity leads, it has been shown: namely, to take away entirely all that is rational within man, so that he allows himself to be governed by the internal Divinity as a <term>mere instrument</term> <note>original: "enkel werktuigig"</note>, as one who finds himself outside of himself, beyond time and place. Or do you think that some expressions in the cited hymns could still be twisted? We do not deny this, especially when one uses scriptural language to hide the most irrational errors behind it. We are in a position to present the matter to you in such a way that no concealment will be possible, and you will be forced to be convinced of the true sense of the <term>Moravians</term> <note>original: "Herrnhuthers", a Protestant Moravian community known for their emotional and mystical piety</note>, and that from the *Spiritual Little Flower-Garden of Inward Souls* <note>original: "Geistliches Blumen-Gärtlein inniger Seelen", a highly influential collection of hymns and poems by the mystic Gerhard Tersteegen</note>, which is so highly esteemed by them and their followers. <meta>This page continues the critique of the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuters) and other "Enthusiasts," specifically attacking the mystical practice of "passive waiting" and self-annihilation. It links these modern groups to the ancient writings of Pseudo-Dionysius and the later works of Valentin Weigel.</meta>

->Enthusiasm Unmasked, etc.<-

Those who understand **Mystic Theology** know that all Mystics, **Enthusiasts**, and **Quakers**, in this matter of **passive waiting**, of the **loss of senses and will**, and the resulting **lack of feeling**, teach exactly the same things that we have reported from the **Moravian writings**; therefore, to prove this, we do not need to be extensive. The Patriarch of the corrupted Mystics, the fictional **Dionysius the Areopagite**, right at the beginning of his treatise *On Mystic Theology* <note>original: *De Mystica Theologia*</note>, Chapter 1, Section 1 (found in his *Complete Works*, Volume 2, page 2), gives his Timothy this advice: *“But you, my beloved Timothy, in these mystical contemplations, through intense practice, abandon both your senses and the operations of your intellect, and all that is sensible and intelligible, and all that is, and all that is not, so that you may ascend in an unprovable or incomprehensible way to union with Him who is above all being and knowledge, as far as it is attainable. For through the free, absolute, and pure withdrawal of yourself from all things, having stripped away everything and being unencumbered by all, you shall be lifted up to that supernatural ray of the Divine darkness.”* (a) **Weigelius** <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and astronomer whose mystical writings influenced later Pietism.</note> expresses himself thus on the matter, in Part 2 of his *Postils*, page 86: *“Betake yourself to your inward prayer (that is, the passive prayer), frequently in a **silentium** (silence) rest in God, and keep the Sabbath; surrender yourself entirely to God, inwardly and outwardly; enter into a forgetting of yourself, so that God may find place and room to work, and to en- light-”*

---

(a) The specific words, as the editor of the works of Dionysius has translated them from the Greek, are these: *“But you, dear Timothy, in mystical contemplations, through intense exercise, leave behind the senses and intellectual operations, and all sensible and intelligible things, and all things that are and are not, so that you may rise up unknowingly <note>original Greek: ἀγνώστως (agnostos)</note> toward union with him who is above all essence and knowledge, as far as is permitted. For indeed, through the free, absolute, and pure withdrawal of yourself from all things, you will be carried up to that supernatural ray of Divine darkness, having cast off all things and been released from everything.”* <note>This footnote provides the Latin translation of the original Greek text by Pseudo-Dionysius, which the main Dutch text had summarized.</note>

# Of the Herrnhuters. Section II. Chapter II. Part I.

...kind of joy, peace, and resignation to experience under these or those circumstances. All that we can think of God by ourselves, desire, or grasp with the imagination—all that we can imagine for ourselves of His light, beauty, joy, pleasures, and of all His perfections—are nothing but mere fictions and phantoms of the brain, unworthy of God, who is infinitely exalted above all the ideas and fictions of our own activity. In this way, we only stir or smudge the canvas, or the ground of our soul; and thus we prevent God from sketching His Divine and living image therein, while we constantly seek to paint our own disorderly trifles upon it. From this it is evident once again how **ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY IT IS THAT THE POWERS OR FACULTIES OF THE SOUL, EVEN THE HIGHEST ONES—NAMELY THE UNDERSTANDING AND THE RESIGNATION—REST AND BE STILL.** And §. 24. is finally this conclusion: *The desire having come this far, is accepted by God the Father, strengthened, expanded, and JOINED AND UNITED WITH HIS OWN, IN SUCH A WAY THAT THEY CONSTITUTE BUT ONE SINGLE DESIRE.* Then the **DESIRE** *of man*, being as it were animated by God’s desire, becomes **ENTIRELY DIVINE**; and then natural faith is changed into a *supernatural*, **DIVINE**, living, and saving faith, which, though infinite, nevertheless grows daily without end.

### What true prayer is.

> True prayer is **TO CLING TO GOD IN THE GROUND** (a) **WITH LOVE**,

## PART II.

(a) This is the *Ground of the soul* <note>original: *Zielen-grond*; a mystical concept referring to the deepest, most inward part of the human spirit where God is said to dwell.</note>, and in the turning inward into the same, and the clinging in love to that *God of the heart*, the essence of prayer is found here. This is how Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who edited the works of Antoinette Bourignon and promoted Quietist ideas.</note> names that *Divinity*, which has His seat in the center-point of the heart of all men. And to cling to Him in love, through turning inward into oneself—just as it constitutes the essence of prayer here—so it is for Poiret the essence of *true and Divine Religion or Worship*: namely: **A HEART BURNING WITH LOVE AND RESIGNED OR SURRENDERED TO GOD**, in his *Divine Economy* <note>original: *Goddel: Huish:*, referring to Poiret's *L'Oeconomie Divine*.</note>, Book 3, Chapter 10, §. 2.

(b) These words might appear to an inattentive person as if they meant to say that someone praying in distress and suffering often does not mean it sincerely. However, on the contrary, the contrast with the following line—*of someone who does not pray when he seems to pray much*, and thus actually is—(which, considered on its own, is a truth) clearly shows that the meaning is that someone, through a passive prayer <term>passive prayer: Dutch *lydelyk gebed*; a mystical state where the believer remains entirely inactive or "passive," allowing God to work within the soul without any effort from the human will or intellect.</term>, can pray at a time when he himself does not even know that he is praying.

### The Moravians. Section II. Chapter II. Part II. ###

...only this: that we investigate in what manner the Moravian Hymnbook speaks of that refining and melting, so that everyone may draw their own conclusion as to whether this is the same refining of which the Word of God speaks in the cited and other passages, or whether it is a refining drawn from the wells of corrupt Mystics. It is evident that in the Moravian Hymnbook, very many expressions occur that are not drawn from the pure river of God’s Word, but from the unclean wells of the fictional *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy and Hermeticism.</note> and of *Theophrastus Paracelsus* <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who integrated mystical and chemical concepts.</note>, and which are taken from the technical terms <term>konstwoorden; specialized jargon or "art-words" used by practitioners of a specific craft</term> of those foolish Gold-makers, called *Alchemists*, who, while seeking the Philosopher’s Stone, become fools. We have already heard *M. Oetinger* <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782), a German theologian who attempted to reconcile Pietism with the "chemical" philosophy of the time.</note> confess in the first Section that there are indeed expressions in the Moravian Hymnbook that sound somewhat *Chemical*, but which are nonetheless beautiful. One does not need a lantern to search for them; they appear everywhere. Aside from the entirety of Hymn 358, we currently present for the consideration of the sensible reader only the expression used regarding the souls of the faithful who have departed from the body, found in Hymn 1068, verse 2.

But here the author of the Hymn must either be playing with the Biblical expression of the *old Adam* <note>In traditional theology, the "Old Adam" refers to the fallen, sinful nature of humanity that must be overcome by faith.</note> to hide behind it, or this line has neither point nor purpose in connection with the preceding 2nd and the beginning of the 3rd verse. However, the former is all too true; for *the old man, who must be completely melted away and annihilated and die the Mystical death*, is not the sinful corruption that exists in man by nature and which must be subdued by grace through daily crucifixion <note>The act of "mortifying the flesh" or suppressing sinful desires.</note> until man, at physical death, is completely freed from the "body of sin and death" <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul's words in Romans 7:24.</note>, and not a moment before. No; instead, "the old man," according to the style of these corrupt Mystics <note>A derogatory reference to those who sought direct, emotional union with God, often bypassing traditional church doctrine.</note>, is the entirety of human nature with all its parts and faculties—not even excluding reason—and everything within a person that, according to their warped view, is not the Divine part or the Divine nature itself. This is partly evident from what has already been said in the previous section, and will become abundantly clear from what will be said before we conclude this Part.

But I ask you, discerning Reader, to observe the wretched blindness of our Anonymous Man; take note of the sequence of events to understand what is meant by *that which must completely turn to annihilation*. Here, the author seems to be alluding to the binding of Isaac, and to the binding of that goat <note>original: "bok," referring to the ram provided by God as a substitute for Isaac.</note> which was laid in his place upon the wood of the Altar and consumed by the flame, and thus *annihilated*, or rather burned to ashes. Here, that which was bound and laid upon the Altar was nothing other than Isaac, Abraham's beloved Son, and thereafter, in his place, a young goat—a pure sacrificial animal—which was also immediately consumed on the Altar by the holy fire. Now, the author of the Hymn translates this, in his own way, into a Spiritual sense and applies it to himself, wishing that God would make him *quiet and sluggish* <note>original: "stil en slom." "Slom" implies a heavy, passive state of indifference or stillness sought in certain radical Pietist traditions.</note> under suffering (which suffering here represents the fire of the Altar, howsoever...

These passages are currently sufficient for us to know how the Moravians <note>original: *Herrnhuthers*; a Pietist Christian denomination known for their emotional and mystical devotion</note> speak of entering and coming into the wilderness. But I remain certain that many readers, who do not understand the secret language of the corrupt Mystics, will not yet clearly grasp what this Wilderness may be. Many will understand it as that spiritual solitude in which a soul occupies itself through active meditations, in the contemplation of God and his virtues and ways, etc., and thus converses familiarly with God. Others will think of that state in which Jesus found himself in the Wilderness, active in fasting and prayer, to prepare himself, as it were, for his public Mediatorial ministry, for which he had already been solemnly consecrated through Baptism and the testimony from Heaven—in which wilderness the tempter also came to him (Matthew 4:1, etc.). Others will think something else of it. But the true sense can only be clarified from the writings of the corrupt Mystics, for whom the wilderness, the Divine Chaos, <term>Sabbath</term> <note>In this mystical context, a state of total spiritual rest where all human striving and mental activity ceases</note>, <term>silence</term> <note>original: *stilte*; a technical term for 'Quietism,' the silencing of the will</note>, etc., is nothing other than that state of the soul in which it arrives after many repeated purifications and turning inward to the <term>soul-ground</term> <note>original: *zielen-grond*; the 'Seelengrund,' the deepest part of the inner self where the mystic seeks a direct union with the Divine</note>. This occurs when the soul is robbed of everything that is not God himself within it, and is so emptied of sinfulness—and even of its entire rational nature—that, in place of internal and external senses, understanding, and will, etc., nothing but a complete emptiness of all ideas and a perfect desolation is found within it. Whereby, however, according to their judgment, the perfection of the soul is not harmed, but rather increased, while the essential Divine light fills the place. # Enthusiasm Revealed in its Nakedness, etc. #

*Few souls are elevated to this* **PASSIVE** and **INFUSED PRAYER**; <note>original: *lydelyk en ingestort gebed*; technical terms in Quietist mysticism. "Passive" prayer means the soul does nothing but receive, while "infused" prayer is gifted directly by God rather than achieved through human effort.</note> because few are made receptive to the *Divine influences* through a **TOTAL NAKEDNESS** and the **DEATH** of their **ACTIVITY** and **FACULTIES**. And that state he calls immediately thereafter, a **PERFECT NAKEDNESS**. Again in Chapter 20, § 194: <note>The author is quoting from *The Spiritual Guide* by Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696), a key figure in the Quietist movement who emphasized internal silence.</note> *Clothe yourself with this* **NOTHINGNESS** *and misery, make of it your food and dwelling, sink into the* **NOTHING**, *and God will be your all*. § 196. *Sink into your nothingness and do not disturb yourself over any thing*. § 198. *Along this path* **OF NOTHINGNESS** *one goes* **TO LOSE ONESELF IN GOD**, *and one climbs to the highest step* **OF PERFECTION**: *for thus* **LOSING** *oneself, is winning oneself*. And this state he calls first thereafter *a somber and deep dwelling*. § 201. he says again: *Drown yourself in the* **NOTHINGNESS**, *and you shall find therein a harbor, and a certain shadow, against all winds and fearsome storms*. And finally, he shall pull the knot tight <note>An idiom meaning to bring the argument to its conclusion or to reveal the core truth.</note> and show that in all this consists the true *Mystical* (and also the *Moravian*) **ANNIHILATION**. § 203. *Walk upon this certain path, seek* **TO SUBMERGE**, **to LOSE** *and* **to DROWN** *yourself in the* **NOTHINGNESS**, *if you wish to* **ANNIHILATE**, *unite, and transform yourself*. Now I believe that you will have understood somewhat more clearly what it consists of when the soul—according to the style of the Moravians <note>original: *Herrnhuthers*</note> and those from whose wells they have drawn their water—is said to enter and come into the wilderness, where it is entirely empty, and where all faculties of the soul, senses, thoughts, etc., are rooted out, and thus **ANNIHILATED**, which not only truly belongs to the passive existence, but is the highest step of passivity, in which only then the infused and passive prayer can truly take place. No wonder, for this Mystical <term>NOTHING</term> <note>In mystical theology, "Nothing" (Latin: *Nihil*) refers to God as being "nothing" of what we can perceive or describe with human language—a state of being so pure it is "no-thing."</note> is the Divine Being itself, which is the unlocking of this secret that we shall now lay open as clear as the midday sun.

I assume that many of my readers will not imagine so much evil coming from this <term>NOTHING</term>, and from this "entering into the <term>NOTHING</term>." Others might possibly think that it expresses the same thing that Paul intends to convey when he testifies *that he who thinks he is something, becomes nothing* <note>A reference to Galatians 6:3.</note>; and that this entering into the <term>NOTHING</term> means nothing other *than that deep humility and abasement of a soul convinced of its total nothingness and impotence, which cries out with Abraham: I have undertaken to speak with you, though I am dust and ashes.* <note>A reference to Genesis 18:27.</note> We wished from the bottom of our soul that we could interpret it in that sense. 

But those who understand even a little of the secret language of the corrupted Mystics know that—however complexly they speak and in how many turns they twist themselves—they nevertheless eventually come to the point that this <term>NOTHING</term>, as well as the <term>UNIVERSAL BEING</term> and the <term>ONE</term>, is nothing other than the <term>DIVINE BEING ITSELF</term>. They believe that man, by entering into this <term>NOTHING</term> (after the total turning toward *annihilation* <note>The mystical process of *annihilatio*, where the individual's will and ego are completely extinguished.</note> in the <term>Mystical DEATH</term>), *sinks and loses himself into the being of God, just as a drop of water falling into the sea unites itself therewith, becoming therefore called God the Universal Being.* This is the *entering into the ONE*, in which lies the ground of *deification* <note>Also known as *theosis*: the transformative process of a human becoming one with God.</note> and the *receiving of the Divine nature*, according to the peculiar style and the clearest testimonies of the so-called Mystical writers. The latter will be abundantly clear to us in the entire 4th Chapter, but first we must show that this <term>NOTHING</term> is God himself to these men of a corrupted understanding. The notorious Jacob Böhme <note>Jacob Böhme (1575–1624) was a German Christian mystic and theologian whose ideas on the nature of God and evil deeply influenced later Pietism and Romanticism.</note> says in his book called the *Signatura Rerum* <note>Latin: *The Signature of All Things*, one of Böhme's most influential works on the relationship between the spiritual and physical worlds.</note> Cap. 6: §. 8.: *God has made all things out of nothing, AND THAT SAME NOTHING IS HE HIMSELF*, as a love-desire dwelling within Himself, in which there is no affect. ### The Moravians, Section II, Chapter II, Part II. ###

...firm confidence that my DIVINE-ALL will finally consume my SIN-ALL, and bring me in deed and entirely into that NOTHING which I now only possess in faith and in part. I cannot omit adding here, as a conclusion, a passage from that notorious booklet named *German Theology* <note>original: *Duitſche Theologie*. This refers to the *Theologia Germanica*, a 14th-century mystical treatise influential among Pietists, which argues that the soul must be emptied of "selfhood" to let God act through it.</note> (although the learned Mr. Cremer has already cited it in his *Chain of Morals* <note>original: *Zeden-Keten*. > *And thus man becomes entirely poor (the greatest shadow that has ever been) and also becomes NOTHING in himself, and in him and with him ALL becomes SOMETHING, that is, all created things; and then, for the first time, a true inward life arises there, and then henceforth* GOD HIMSELF BECOMES THE MAN, *so that there is nothing more that is* NOT GOD *or* GOD’S OWN, *and also that there is nothing there that assumes anything for itself;* SO GOD IS, LIVES, RECOGNIZES, EMPOWERS, LOVES, WILLS, ACTS, AND LEAVES, *that is the* ETERNAL ONE, *completely* ALONE.

<margin>The conclusion of this Part.</margin>
See there, the deeply hidden mystery of iniquity is opened; this is the end and goal at which all those purifications and meltings aim, until all that is called nature—not only the sinful but also the rational, or if you will, all that is and is called <term>Creature: (Dutch: Schepzel) a term used to distinguish anything that is not God. In this context, the author argues the mystics want to destroy the very status of being a created being.</term>—is entirely melted away, and the human being, having turned entirely toward annihilation, sinks and falls into that *Mystical NOTHING*, into that immeasurable *Divine Essence*, through which man then is nothing, and God is the *General-All*. Thus, in that highest stage of <term>passivity: (Dutch: lydelykheit) the state of being "acted upon" by God, where the human will is completely silent.</term>, it is no longer the human who thinks, works, etc., but God himself (who then, oh horror! *becomes the man, and the man becomes God*) thinks and works everything. What think you, God-fearing Reader, of such a *becoming nothing*, wherein the imagined deepest humiliation raises the void Creature to the very highest, above all nature of the Creature, and makes it equal to God, yes, is made into God himself? What think you, from whence such a falsely named Theology has its origin? I cannot [ho-]

# CHAPTER III.

->On the Perfection of the Saints in this life, in general.<-

<margin>The connection of this doctrine with the preceding one, and our purpose indicated.</margin>
When we take up the matter again where we left it in the previous section, it is not only that the thread provided to us by the Anonymous Writer—whom we have resolved to follow throughout—leads us to the main section on the *Perfection of the Saints in this life*: but also the natural order of what is called Moravian and Mystic Theology obliges us to arrive there. For among them, *purification* and *melting* <note>original: "louteringe en smeltinge" — these are alchemical metaphors used by mystics to describe the refining of the soul by burning away worldly desires.</note> serve to completely melt away everything that *is called* or *can be named nature*, until man is *entirely annihilated*, reaching an absolute *emptiness* of all senses and movements of the soul, having entered the *wilderness*, until having become that *Nothing* <note>original: "Niets" — referring to the mystical concept of the "divine nothingness," where the soul loses its individual identity to merge with God.</note>, which is God Himself; then, nothing remains in him but the *Divine nature*. Upon this, nothing else can follow but *Mystical Perfection*, which these people attribute to their saints, while still in *this life*, to such a degree and rank that the true distinction between the Church militant <note>The church on Earth struggling against sin.</note> and triumphant <note>The church in Heaven.</note>, between Heaven and Earth, and between time and eternity, is effectively removed. If there is one error that has been charged against the Moravians <note>original: "Herrnhuthers"</note> until now, which they not only do not deny, but which they—though with some glossy distortion of the actual state of the dispute to mislead the inattentive—manfully come forward with, it is this: and indeed in such a way that they, according to their *childlike simplicity*, do not fail to sharply attack the sacred Doctrine of the Reformed Church, and of all those who do not favor the whole or half-Pelagian heresy <note>Pelagianism is the historical belief that human nature is not fundamentally corrupt and that humans can take the first steps toward salvation without divine grace—a view the Reformed Church strongly opposed.</note>, making it hated by those who lend them an ear. This is done to better draw toward themselves all those who are simple enough that, through lack of understanding or observation, they allow themselves to be led away from the true state of the dispute and be blinded by some seemingly beautiful words, to

In this, we shall not dispute with the Moravians, nor defend the Doctrine of our Church, but act only in an exposing manner, so that at least simple, upright souls who wish to listen to good counsel will not let themselves be further misled by fair speech.

->De Naakt ontdekte Enthusiaſtery, enz.<-
<note>Enthusiasm Unmasked, etc. In the 18th century, "Enthusiasm" was a derogatory term for religious groups who claimed direct, personal divine inspiration, often viewed by the established church as fanatical or delusional.</note>

In his remarks on the 19th Letter, pages 53 and 54, he makes a comment in which he wants us to believe that the *Moravians* <note>original: "Herrnhuthers," the followers of Count von Zinzendorf's renewed Moravian Brethren.</note> are far from **PRESUMPTUOUSLY IMAGINING** that one can be without having sin within oneself. For, he says, to become **WHOLE PEOPLE**, and to be **PERFECT IN HIM**, does not mean that upon reaching that state, one therefore ceases to be a sinner in oneself, or ceases to have that sinful nature which is a constant cause for *humiliation* <note>original: "verootmoediginge," a religious term for the humble recognition of one's own unworthiness before God.</note>. It is very pleasing to us that the maker of this remark calls the matter by its own and true name, namely an **ARROGANCE** *to imagine* (let alone to say and openly testify) that one **CAN BE** *without having sin within oneself*. It is truly a most abominable arrogance, born from a prevailing corruption of the heart—namely pride—and arising from a deep ignorance of the true condition of the heart, and of the nature of the indwelling corruption that often keeps itself hidden and quiet. It is a foolish imagination, even to allow such deliberations to arise and take place in one’s thoughts: *that one could ever, as long as one is in this life, be without having sin within oneself*. Indeed, it is not only a foolish and vain, but even a lying **ARROGANCE** to imagine or say such a thing. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. 1 John 1:8. If this is how the matter stands, then one *Moravian*, or one of *Moravian* mind, pronounces judgment upon the other, and precedes us in that judgment. For if it is an **ARROGANCE** merely to imagine such a thing, then it is surely a high-reaching **ARROGANCE** not only to plead for this **ARROGANCE**, but to despise in a mocking way all those who do not favor this *presumptuous imagination*, but instead contradict it in the most modest manner or warn against it—as all orthodox Protestants, both Reformed and Lutheran, do. In a legal or sacrificial context, it refers to an animal without physical defects.</note> is generally used for offerings, as well for lambs and calves as for sheep and cattle. And thus a firstborn child can just as well be said to be *perfect* as a full-grown man. Consequently, it is a strange linguistics that Mr. von Watteville employs when he says that, according to the literal translation, that expression must be translated as a *whole Man*, which is why he also had those words printed in capital letters. And he adds: *this is plain language, which still must count for the most under the Gospel.* It is truly plain language, but it proves nothing less than what that Gentleman seeks to prove with it. That *perfection*, which God commanded to Abraham, the Father of the faithful, and also to all who follow in the footsteps of the faithful Abraham, is a *perfection* that consists in *unfeigned sincerity*, which rejects all *craftiness*, *hypocrisy*, and everything that looks like insincerity. In that perfection there is place for a spirit in which there is no guile, Psalm 32:2; truth in the inward parts, in which God takes delight, Psalm 51:8; and after which His eyes look, Jeremiah 5:3.

From that inward and perfectly sincere foundational principle is born a walk corresponding to it, being an *entirely upright walk*, *a walking in one’s integrity, and in simplicity of heart*, maintaining in everything an *inoffensive conscience* <term>conscience (conscientie): the inner sense of right and wrong, which the author argues must be kept "inoffensive" or clear before God and people.</term> before God and before men, and that constantly and at all times. And *he who thus walks in his integrity, walks surely, but he who behaves perversely in two ways shall fall on one.* <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 10:9 and 28:18, emphasizing that a divided or hypocritical life leads to ruin.</note> *And whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be revealed in the Congregation.* So it stands with true *Evangelical Sincerity*, which can never be praised enough—

...can have any will to sin, since all sin is *condemned through Jesus' death.* The Lord Baron <note>Referring to Count von Zinzendorf, the leader of the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuters). ### Of the Moravians. Section II, Chapter III, Part I.

...[won]derful simplicity; the Lord Baron <note>Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, the leader of the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuters).</note> will make this somewhat clearer when he immediately adds these words: *“Thus we hold it as a settled matter, that they (namely: the believers) are to be viewed as those who have no further connection with sin, no longer standing in that old bond wherein it had dominion over them. That old bond is broken, and sin cannot and may not rule over them, for grace by no means allows that.”* Rom. 6:14. etc. When I read these words, as well as all the others his Honor allows to follow on pages 21 and 22, I stood amazed, not knowing whether to regard them as being born from ignorance of the true state of the dispute, or from an inexcusable cunning, with a bold design to—by twisting the state of the dispute—not merely make the teaching of the Reformed Church <note>The established Dutch Reformed Church, which followed traditional Calvinist doctrine.</note> suspect, but to slander it.

Who, among those who understand and profess the foundations of the Reformed doctrine, has ever denied that believers are released from the *dominion of sin*, and that they no longer stand in that old bond with sin as they did in their natural state <note>term: "natural state" (natuurstaat) refers to the condition of humanity before spiritual conversion or "grace."</note>, before their conversion? This would remove all distinction between nature and grace entirely. Is that the point on which we declare ourselves to differ from the Moravians? Is that why we are, with good reason, concerned that they *exalt the perfection of the Saints in this life to the highest peak*? <note>The author argues that while Reformed Christians believe sin no longer *rules* a believer, the Moravians go further by claiming believers can reach a state of absolute "perfection" where sin is entirely absent.</note> 

If that is not the state of the dispute—as indeed it is not—then how does this Lord come to such an unaccountable distortion of that state of the dispute, upon which he builds all his following arguments? What is his purpose? Does he seek to hide the true sense of the Congregation to mislead the simple-minded? That is surely not acting faithfully, nor as those must act who have the truth before them. Or does he not understand the sense of the Congregation, and how it is expressed in the Hymnal <note>gloss: "Gezangboek"</note> and others of their writings? How then can he write a Defense in the sense of the Congregation? We cannot [expect] that from a Representative of the Brethren, who [is] the closest...

### The Herrnhuthers. Part II. Chapter III. Section I.

[which] Mr. de Watteville <note>Baron Friedrich von Watteville (1700–1777) was a close friend of Count Zinzendorf and a prominent leader in the Moravian movement.</note> applies. When Paul speaks of *condemning sin in the flesh* <note>A reference to Romans 8:3: "God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh."</note>, then that is certainly not *that flesh of man*, in which, according to the opinion of the Herrnhuthers <note>term: "Herrnhuthers" (Moravian Brethren). They were named after Herrnhut, the estate of Count Zinzendorf where the community was established.</note>, *sin, banished from the heart, must remain*; rather, it is the *flesh of Jesus*, who bore our sins in his body on the tree <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:24, often used in Reformed theology to emphasize Christ’s substitutionary atonement.</note>, as anyone can see who merely casts a fleeting eye upon the passage. How then is this passage relevant here, and what is it supposed to prove? At least *not* that *sin*, moving out of the heart, *must remain in the flesh*. Yet according to the Herrnhuth citations of Scripture, it is sufficient if only one word or another appears in the text that serves their purpose, even if it contradicts the intent of the Holy Writer. Here, the words sin and flesh appear—indeed, *sin in the flesh*—and that is enough for them.

Furthermore, *that faith purifies the heart* is a truth to which we fully set our seal, according to the Scriptures; but the conclusion that the Lord Baron, in his name and that of his Brethren, draws from it—namely, *that sin is thereby driven out, no longer to have its seat in the heart, but that it must remain in the flesh*—is language that is very ambiguous, and entirely intended to mislead simple and less attentive souls through fine speech. When *sin is said to be driven out of the heart*, is that to say that the heart is so purified by faith that nothing *called sin* remains in it, but that *all sin and all remnants of sin are entirely banished and driven out*? That surely cannot be true; for from whence come those thoughts of vanity, which are sin, and the first welling up of desires? These must then either not be sin, or the Believers among the Herrnhuthers must have climbed to a much higher step in Sanctification <note>term: "Sanctification" (Heilighmakinge) is the process of being made holy; the author argues that Moravians claim a level of perfection that even the Apostle Paul did not claim.</note> than Paul, and than all the Saints, such that they are not tormented by them—or they imagine such a thing through idle conceit. One will say that it is explained how the Herrnhuthers understand it, namely, that sin is driven out in such a way *that it no longer has its SEAT*

When it is proposed that *the newborn life is essentially God Himself, and that it therefore wants to return again into that source (from which it flowed, namely the essential Godhead), which source is nothing other than God Himself, this being the seed (namely that which lies in the innermost ground of the soul <note>Dutch: *zielen grond*. Or is it *he* who is more active in this regard, who through **Arrogant Grandeur** allows himself to claim—nay, even boasts—that this enemy has already been so suppressed and rooted out...

Among these, already in the first two centuries, there reared their heads the so-called Gnostics, Basilidians, Carpocratians, and others, followed by the Valentinians, Marcionites, Montanists, and others of that sort. These people, under the pretext of possessing a higher degree of holiness, separated themselves from others, calling themselves *pneumatikoi* and *teleioi* <note>original Greek: πνευματικες and τελειες, meaning "Spiritual ones" and "Complete" or "Perfect ones."</note>, **Spiritual and complete or perfect**, and claiming that they were free and pure from all stains of sin. A 4th-century sect known for their belief in perpetual prayer and their claim that the Holy Spirit could be physically perceived.</note> (**that is, bidders or those who pray** <note>original Greek: ευχομενοι, *euchomenoi*.</note>), who may rightly be regarded as the Patriarchs of the Enthusiasts and Fanatics <note>original: *Geestdryvers*, literally "spirit-drivers," a derogatory term for those claimed to be driven by private revelations rather than Scripture.</note>, just as Theodoretus already called them *Enthusiasts* in his time. (*c*) For which he gives this reason:

> *They are called Enthusiasts for this reason, because they are driven by the impulse of a certain spirit (daimonos tinos <note>original Greek: δαιμονος τινος.</note>), and they judge the same to be the presence of the Holy Spirit.*

Which Euchetes proudly pretended that, having climbed to the summit of perfection, they could not sin even in thought or out of ignorance: as the Church Father Jerome <note>original: *Hieronymus*.</note> charges against them. (*d*) This same path was taken by the schismatic Novatians in the third century, who distinguished themselves from

His eighth proposition is one that he presents in a brief summary on pages 185 and 186 as follows: *“In those in whom this holy and immaculate birth is perfectly brought forth, the body of sin and death is crucified and removed, and their hearts are subjected to the truth and united with it: to the extent that they obey no inspirations or temptations of the Devil, and are delivered and set free from actual sin and the transgression of God’s law, and in that respect become perfect. This perfection, however, always allows for growth and increase; and the possibility of sinning always remains in part, if the mind does not watch and wait upon God with the utmost diligence and industry.”* <note>The author is quoting Robert Barclay’s "Apology for the True Christian Divinity," a foundational text for Quakerism.</note> In the following pages (pp. 188–194), he attempts to confirm this proposition in his own manner; moreover, he does not fail to denounce the orthodox doctrine of the Protestants as not only unseemly but even blasphemous, using the same kinds of distortions regarding the true state of the controversy as those employed by the Moravians <note>original: *Herrnhuthers*</note> and their advocates. He teaches that the inward turn into the ground of the soul <term>inkeringe in den zielen grond</term> <note>A mystical practice of looking inward to find the "divine spark" or the direct presence of God, bypassing external scripture or ritual.</note> is the means to reach this perfection (p. 196). Yet, even here, he wishes to keep a "back door" open by positing that a *possibility of sinning* nonetheless remains. Indeed, he cannot do otherwise because, according to his own system—and in conformity with other Fanatics <term>Geeſtdryvers</term> <note>original: *Geestdryvers*, a pejorative term used for those who claimed direct, personal revelation from the Holy Spirit.</note>—the falling away of the saints <term>afval der heiligen</term> <note>The theological concept that a person who has attained a state of grace can lose it and eventually be damned.</note> is not impossible, as he attempts to prove in the following ninth proposition on page 204, etc. This could not exist without the *possibility that believers could sin.*

As for Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystical theologian whose works were influential in the Netherlands.</note>, he goes even further. Anyone who pays attention to the stages of what he calls *passive purification* or *cleansing* <term>lydelyke louteringe</term> will immediately notice that everything leads toward this *perfect holiness in this life*. He presents this (according to an analogy forged in his own imagination of a wax statue that has fallen into the mud, where the filth has penetrated the inside as well as covered the outside) in the 5th Book of the *Divine Economy*, Chapter 5, Section 16, etc. <note>Refers to Poiret’s multi-volume work *L’Économie Divine* (The Divine Economy), which systematized mystical thought.</note> For according to him, the soul must first [cease] *from doing evil*...

*After this, the soul is seized by the clear and radiant fire of Divine love.* § 18. *Further, when the fire of purification penetrates to its innermost parts, then all its faculties and powers—its understanding, its will, its reason, etc.—are mixed together into a dark, chaotic mass, where one perceives nothing everywhere but disorder, misery, and a general impurity and stench, etc.* § 19. *Whereupon the Divine fire, through its Divine movements, touches everything found in the soul, down to the very smallest detail; it separates the pure from the impure everywhere, drives this impurity together into a heap, and casts it out.* § 20. *Thus the interior is purified, down to the smallest parts; but then the soul remains a while longer with the fire, not only to cleanse it of the very smallest impure specks <note>original: "fierties." This refers to tiny particles or dregs of sin that remain even after the initial purging.</note> that might still remain, but also to grant it a certain firmness.* § 21. *Then the soul is now and then removed from the fire, when it finds itself in a state of dryness <note>In mystical theology, "dryness" or "aridity" refers to a spiritual state where the believer feels no emotional or spiritual comfort, testing their faith and patience.</note> and seems to have no warmth nor movement toward the good.* § 22. *After that, finally, God brings the soul back into the clear and radiant fire of His love, yet without pain, and pours it thus into the mold of His most perfect and Divine will—into the form of God Himself and of the Holy Spirit, who fashions it, works upon it, and gives it such shape and firmness as it must have to be a Divine, perfect, and God-pleasing image. And from that time on, the soul is born again and has become a new creature, in which everything is new: knowledge, will, inclinations, senses, conduct, heaven and earth—finally God, Christ, and everything. And thus this work is a perfect work, even though in the future it must still grow in perfection.* § 23. See, this is, in a brief summary, the path along which a soul is born again and purified of all impurity, so that nothing unclean may be found in it anymore; which is also the meaning of the Moravian <note>original: "Herrnhuthsche"</note> hymns examined by us in § 2 and 3. Upon such a foundation, Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystical philosopher and theologian who lived in the Netherlands; his work "The Divine Economy" was highly influential on Pietists and Moravians.</note> further elaborates on the state of perfect holiness of believers in this life, when he, in the same [Book] V.

The Book, in the 8th Chapter, speaking of *Justification* (which for him, as for other Mystics, does not differ from sanctification <note>In mainstream Protestant theology, justification is God's legal declaration of righteousness, while sanctification is the gradual process of becoming holy. Mystics like Poiret often merged these into a single internal transformation.</note>), explains itself thus in §. 2: *“When the Divine light (which is God Himself) has driven the darkness out of the soul, restored its evil and perverse inclinations <note>original: "ploeyen," literally "folds" or "bends," referring to the distorted character of the fallen soul</note>, and DESTROYED AND UPROOTED SIN DOWN TO THE INNERMOST TENDENCIES OF THE HEART; then the first thing which this light subsequently works in the soul is that it shines and glows therein, pure and without clouds. Which is properly called illumination, which is said to be a consequence of purification. This illumination, revealing to the soul the ground of its state, makes it see that THERE IS NOTHING MORE REMAINING IN IT WHICH DISPLEASES GOD OR IS DAMNABLE, BUT THAT EVERYTHING THEREIN IS JUSTIFIED AND RESTORED.”* This last part is, for him, true justification in the most proper sense. He expresses this more closely in §. 22: *“That the soul, down to its innermost ground, IS PURIFIED AND CLEANSED IN THE DEEPEST MANNER FROM ALL THE ROOTS AND TENDENCIES OF SIN, SO THAT THERE IS NOTHING MORE IN THE SAME WHICH CAN BE JUDGED OR DAMNED, etc.”* And upon that same foundation, he continues to build his reasoning in the following Chapter IX, where, after having again devised and presented an allegory <note>original: "gelykenisse," meaning a parable or similitude used as an instructional tool</note> in §. 26 and applied it in his own manner in §. 27, he subsequently draws this conclusion in §. 28: *“It is firm and certain on the one hand, that IN THE HEART OF ONE WHO IS REBORN THERE IS NO MORE CONCUPISCENCE <term>Concupiscence: In this theological context, it refers to the internal leaning or desire toward sin that remains in humans after the Fall.</term>, THAT NOT A SINGLE EVIL DESIRE IS BORN ANY MORE FROM THE GROUND OF THE SAME—THAT FINALLY THERE IS NOTHING EVIL LEFT IN HIS HEART TO BE FOUGHT.”* But all enemies are on the outside, and from there they hardly dare to attempt an attack. *“Therefore, it is necessary that every reborn person, throughout his whole life, continually struggles against his external enemies—the Devil, the world, and his own flesh and sensitivity <note>original: "gevoeligheit," referring here to the physical senses and emotional impulses that can lead one astray from spiritual focus</note>—or at least that he is always ready to struggle against them, even though those enemies all seem to retreat and [leave] him in peace...”*

Just as these people have sought to excuse themselves using the words of an <term>orthodox Poet<note>Likely referring to a traditional Reformed or Lutheran songwriter whose work the Moravians adapted.</note></term>, contrary to the clear explanation of that famous man; so our Anonymous Writer tries to hide behind *Scriptural expressions*, which he brings forward, though unfortunately quite apart from their actual purpose. On page 19, the three last passages from Philippians 3:20, Psalm 73:25, and Colossians 3:12 do not touch upon the point of dispute at all. For when Paul testifies that the *citizenship of believers is in heaven* (<note>original Greek: "πολίτευμα" - politeuma, referring to one's state or commonwealth</note>), he by no means implies that *the heaven of believers is already here*. The contrary is taught by that same Paul in Hebrews 13:14, compared with 2 Corinthians 5:1–5. To have *nothing besides God in heaven, etc.* <note>A reference to Psalm 73:25</note> directly contradicts *already having one’s heaven here*; just as to *seek the things that are above* <note>Colossians 3:1</note> does not, after all, mean to already have heaven here on earth. Only the first passage remains, from Ephesians 2:6, which has some appearance of support. But it all comes down to the expression *seated together in heaven* (<note>original Greek: "ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις" - en tois epouraniois</note>) in Christ Jesus. That the Greek word refers just as much to heavenly things as to heavenly places is abundantly well known. That believers are said to be *seated together in heaven in Christ Jesus* essentially indicates their legally obtained right, which they have to heavenly things and places, acquired for them by Christ, and the grounded expectation they have for it through a living hope, and the <term>firstfruits<note>A theological term (from the Greek 'aparche') referring to a small initial installment of a spiritual blessing that guarantees the full amount will follow later.</note></term> and the foretaste which they are sometimes permitted to enjoy. The Dutch reader can look this up in the Learned and Godly treatises of both the late Mr. Dinant <note>Pieter Dinant (1665–1732), a Dutch Reformed minister known for his devotional and theological works.</note>, Volume I, page 426, etc., and the Learned and Godly Mr. Royaards <note>Albertus Royaards (1701–1753), a prominent Dutch theologian and preacher.</note>, also Volume I on the Ephesians, page 488, etc. Whether this is the same as the expression *to already have one’s heaven here*, in the sense of the Herrnhuters as previously defined by us, we let every godly and impartial person judge.

But all counter-arguments will entirely vanish when we observe the distinction the Herrnhuters <note>The Moravian Brethren, a pietist Christian movement led by Count von Zinzendorf, often criticized by the orthodox for their ecstatic and sometimes graphic religious language.</note> make between *time* and *eternity*, and how they boast of being here below already in eternity, *outside of all time and place*. But we say only that our translator makes a mistake when he translates the fourth line: *Du hast -- mich gäntzlich* **AUSGESOGEN** <note>original German: "You have -- me completely sucked out"</note>, as *You have -- me completely* **PULLED OUT** <note>original Dutch: "uitgetogen"</note>. Whether our man did not know the difference between those two German words *Aussaugen* and *Ausziehen*, or whether he sought to soften the harshness and unscriptural nature of that expression—where Jesus is said to have *completely sucked out a soul that has flown up to him*—he himself will best know. Yet that way of speaking, however unscriptural, is nonetheless very typical of the Herrnhuters; I have noted it once more from Hymn 667, where it appears in verse 2, in which a soul says to Jesus the Bridegroom:

We must state beforehand that the Honorable <note>The abbreviation "E." stands for "Edele" or "Eerwaarde," a formal honorific for committees and councils.</note> Commission for the drafting of the Pastoral Letter did not overlook the expression of verse 9 in this Hymn, but very well foresaw that excuses would be sought for it; and therefore this matter was taken into ripe deliberation, and the Honorable Commission, after having well-weighed and considered the connection of matters and the expression itself, decided that this passage indeed proved that for which it was cited in the Pastoral Letter. And when, in the Honorable Church Council on October 30th of the past year, that same counter-objection was raised by one of the Honorable Members, according to what we have mentioned above on page 25...

The primary reason that strengthens our suspicion—that the Herrnhuthers are not free from these misconceptions regarding <term>Sophia <note>In mystical tradition, Sophia is the personification of Divine Wisdom, often viewed as a feminine aspect of God or a celestial bride.</note></term> (about which more can be seen in Becmanus's *Theological Exercises* No. 21, pages 403, 404)—is because they frequently mention *eternal love* in their Hymnbook (which among the Mystics is the same as *Sophia*) and regard it as a *Mother*. Here, it would be worthwhile to examine, among many other hymns, Hymn 51 verse 1 and 594:2, along with the addition of 669: verse 3, and to compare them with the dreams of other <term>fanatics <note>original: "Geestdryvers," a pejorative term for those claiming direct, often erratic, spiritual inspiration.</note></term> who hold *eternal love to be the Wife of God*, as seen in Micrælius's *Ecclesiastical History* Part 2, page 1419 no. 4 and 1423 no. 28. ### Of the Herrnhuters. II. Section. IV. Chapter: I. Part. ###

...had used, speak otherwise than what is spoken in this Hymn? with which so many other Hymns agree, as we shall show with abundant evidence in the following section.

<margin>The excuses of the Anonymous Writer are put to the test.</margin>
Let us now hear what our Anonymous Writer <note>This likely refers to a defender of the Moravian Brethren, possibly Count von Zinzendorf himself, who often published anonymously or under pseudonyms.</note> has to say regarding this Hymn, from which he cites nothing other than the very words we had presented in summary in the *Pastoral and Fatherly Letter*. First, on *page 21*, he will attempt to throw some simple dry sand in our eyes by saying: *The Hymn is the translation of a Latin rhyming hymn, in the style of the hymns that go by the name of* **Bernard**. <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a medieval mystic whose works were highly regarded by the Moravians for their focus on the wounds and passion of Christ.</note> Suppose we were to concede and believe that this man spoke the truth; does that serve as an excuse for the Hymn, and does it take away its **unorthodoxy**? <term>unorthodoxy</term> <note>original: "onrechtzinnigheit," referring to departures from established Dutch Reformed or Lutheran doctrine.</note> Or can errors not be propagated in Latin rhyming hymns just as well as in German ones? Or does a translation make **orthodox** that which is unorthodox in the original? Yes, but it is *in the style of those hymns that go by the name of* **Bernard**. The name of Bernard has of old been a blessing in the Church in many respects. But those hymns only go *by his name* <note>The author is suggesting the hymns are pseudepigraphal—written by others but attributed to the famous Saint Bernard to gain authority.</note>, and even if they were genuine pieces, this *71st* Hymn is only *composed in the style of those hymns.* The most unorthodox Hymns can be composed in the style of very orthodox Hymns through omissions, additions, and alterations. The Herrnhuters know this well, and their *Hymnal* <note>original: "Gezangboek."</note> testifies to it, as has already become clear to us. But besides that, the *Name of the Author* is irrelevant; it is the content and the matter itself that counts. *Even if an Angel from Heaven preached another Gospel than that which was preached by* **Jesus** *and the* **Apostles**, *let him be accursed*, we say with **Paul**. <note>A reference to Galatians 1:8.</note> We still hold to the maxim of the famous Lutheran Professor **Wernsdorf**, <note>Gottlieb Wernsdorf (1668–1729), a prominent Lutheran theologian known for his defense of orthodoxy against Pietism and "Enthusiasm."</note> whom we cited in the Preface, on the first page of the sixth leaf. But if our man knows on good grounds that this *71st* Hymn is a translation of a *Latin rhyming hymn*, why then does he not point out to us where that *Latin rhyming—*

# Enthusiasm Discovered Naked, etc. #

...if the hymn were to be found, one would have the opportunity to seek to compare the translation with the original Latin, and that in turn with the work of **Bernard**, according to whose style *it is said to have been made*. Yet, however little this pretext serves to excuse the 71st Hymn, I nevertheless have reason to think that our man is being economical with the truth, or that those Moravian Friends are in error, who have previously sought to excuse this Hymn by claiming that its creator (who must certainly be known to them) is held by them to be a singular lover of Jesus’s Divinity. For these are the words which I read some time ago, before this Anonymous Writing was published—not without agitation—in the often-mentioned written paper that was distributed among the Moravian Friends, and which I now transcribe not without a stirring of my soul; more so because I know that members of our Church <note>The author likely refers to the Dutch Reformed Church, which saw Moravian influence as a threat to orthodoxy.</note> have lent their hand and pen to it, as much to copy it out, if not to compose it, as to circulate it: *The Author of the same (namely: Hymn 71) is a singular lover of Jesus and his Divinity: If he says so much that someone might easily ask, "What is your beloved above others? Or how do you see so much in him above others?" Let him think that perhaps he was at that time somewhat drunk with love and esteem (of Jesus), etc.* 

What shall I say of such language, in which darkness is put for light, and God-dishonoring statements of an "extended divinity" <note>This likely refers to Pantheism or Panentheism, where God is seen as extending into or being one with all things—a major point of theological contention.</note> are said to be born from a heart that was drunk with the love of Jesus? He who dares to use such language, and to lend his hand and pen to write it as something that is his opinion, is also capable of placing **Van Hattem** <note>Pontiaan van Hattem (1641–1706), a Dutch theologian whose followers were often accused of fatalism and Spinozistic tendencies.</note> with **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), the philosopher whose concept of "God or Nature" was viewed by the orthodox as atheistic pantheism.</note> in the rank of the greatest Saints. God forgive those who have lent their hand to writing and distributing such notes, and may he open the eyes of those who have allowed themselves to be misled by such improper pretexts.

### Of the Moravians. Section II. Chapter IV. Part I. ###

...subjected, especially when it is read with *prejudice*. 
*That the Hymn is certainly deep, and that there are depths in it*, we readily admit, but they are the *depths of Satan and the mysteries of iniquity*. <note>A reference to Revelation 2:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2:7, suggesting the hymns contain hidden, diabolical meanings rather than divine ones.</note> It is not merely *subject to misinterpretations* when one reads it with prejudice; rather, every person who honors the true God (distinguished from a non-god) and trembles at His word—even if they held the most favorable prejudice toward the Moravians and their Songbook—who reads this Hymn with attention and understands the sense of the words, must condemn it as God-dishonoring and loathe it. And if this Hymn could be *interpreted in a good sense* by an orthodox, truth-loving, and God-fearing member of our Church, then Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher often accused of atheism or pantheism by his contemporaries.</note> and van Hattem <note>Pontiaan van Hattem (1641–1706), a Dutch theologian whose followers, the Hattemists, were accused of radical fatalism and Spinozism.</note>, along with the entire system of the <term>Enthusiasts</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiasts" referred to radical religious groups who claimed direct, emotional, and often physical experiences of the divine, often bypassing traditional scripture.</note>, could also be interpreted in a good sense, and then those people could likewise be acknowledged as Brothers. 

But our Writer himself seems to understand well enough that these excuses will not yet suffice, and therefore, look, he comes forward with a new invention to cover his Moravians, if it were possible for him. Hear him speak for himself: *The Congregation of Herrnhut*, he says, *leaves it be and makes no use of it, along with some other Hymns that are preserved by her in her Songbook, having been composed by Godly Men, but are never sung*. 

He thus counts, in the first place, *the maker of this Hymn, as well as those of other Hymns of similar nature and content, among the Godly Men*. What Heretic, however monstrous his misconceptions were, has not been honored by his followers with elevated titles of honor, and counted among the Saints of the first rank? Even Simon the Sorcerer, when he said of himself *that he was something great*, found—among those who followed him from the least to the greatest—those who said of him: *This man is the great power of God*. <note>original: "Deze is de grote kracht Gods."</note> Yet Peter pronounced a different judgment upon him, Acts 8: 9, 10, 20, 21, 22. We leave the Moravians free to boast of such "saints." But that they believe that the *Memorials of such so-called Godly ones*, which contain horrific secrets of veiled Atheism, must be so carefully *preserved*—in this, all God-

# Enthusiasm Exposed Naked, etc. #
<meta>catchword: we</meta>

Lovers of piety and truth differ from them as wide as the heavens; yet that they lend their Songbook to them, to *preserve* them therein, is not strange, for in it they show who they are and where they belong. Therefore, we also consider the Songbook of that Community to be a collection of everything belonging to corrupt <term>Mysticism</term> <note>A tradition focused on the direct, subjective experience of the divine, which the author here views as dangerously detached from scripture.</note> and <term>Enthusiasm</term> <note>In this historical context, "Enthusiasm" refers to a perceived religious frenzy or the claim of private revelation through the Holy Spirit, often used as a derogatory term for radical sects.</note>, and for a gathering place where clean and unclean, light and darkness, truth and lies are paired together—although of each latter-mentioned, the most is to be found. 

But what is the purpose of that account concerning the aim of the Songbook? It is to show that this, and other similar Hymns, should not be placed on the account of the <term>Herrnhuters</term> <note>Another name for the Moravians, derived from Herrnhut, the estate of Count Zinzendorf where the community was founded.</note>; for the Songbook is only a treasure chest in which such glorious jewels are preserved, a shop in which such poison is to be found. Yet it is a treasure that is of no use, and poison that they themselves do not ingest, but keep for others. *For they leave this Hymn there, our man will say, and make no use of it, along with several other Hymns, which are indeed preserved but never sung.* 

Few words, but full of cunning and deceit. Here is a new invention to make the Moravians immune to all arrows drawn from their Songbook, however clearly they show the deadly poison on their tips. I say it is a new invention. For until now, I do not know that any Moravian, or defender of that Sect, has made use of this invention so directly. 

The Moravians may give the credit for this to our Anonymous Writer, for he first brought forth this shield and pointed it out to them, which they already make use of—just as Mr. de Watteville <note>Johannes von Watteville (1718–1788), a prominent Moravian bishop and son-in-law of Count Zinzendorf.</note> has already tried to cover himself with it in his "Further Explanation" (which we shall put to the test in due time).

Here, one unpracticed in the secret language of the **Enthusiasts** <note>In this context, "Enthusiasts" refers to radical Pietists or groups like the Moravians who claimed direct, emotional, and mystical divine inspiration, often viewed with suspicion by the orthodox establishment.</note> might think that this **Universal Being** <note>Original: "Algemeen wezen." This term was a flashpoint for controversy, as critics argued it implied pantheism—the idea that God and the universe are the same substance.</note> signifies nothing else than that the **Three adorable Divine persons** make up no more than **one Universal Divine being**, according to 1 John 5:7 <note>The "Johannine Comma," a verse often cited in defense of the Trinity: "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one."</note>. But nothing less than that is intended here. On the contrary, the **Trinity** is regarded here in this sense as **the universal being**, insofar as it is said to be not only the **creator**, but also the **restorer of nature**. Which **creation** in the **Herrnhuter** <note>The Herrnhuters, or Moravian Brethren, were a Pietist Christian denomination known for their emotional devotion to the wounds of Christ and their distinct, often mystical, hymnography.</note> sense is not **bringing forth things from nothing**, and **calling the things which are not as though they were** (Romans 4:17). No, **Mr. Oetinger** <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782) was a prominent German theosophist and prelate who attempted to synthesize Pietism with mystical philosophy and science.</note> has taught us that this conception is a principal error among these people and that Paul's words are ambiguous; but **creating** is to them a bringing forth of **creatures out of the essence of God himself**, through **outflowing** <note>Original: "uitvloeyinge." This refers to the doctrine of emanation, where the world is seen as a literal overflow of God’s own substance rather than a separate creation made from nothing (ex nihilo).</note>. And therefore the **Godhead** is the **universal being**, because **all beings are out of him**, and **he is the essence of all essences**. And because, according to their system, the **firstborn** is the **first flowed-out being**, from whom in turn all other beings flow, according to the entire thread of the **71st Hymn**, therefore the **firstborn** is described here as **the trace of the life-well of the Godhead**, from which well all other beings have flowed out. And these conceptions of the **creation** by **outflowing from the essence of the Trinity** are the foundation why the **creator** is also called the **restorer of nature** here, since everything must return to its origin, as will become clear to us in the **3rd Part of this Chapter**.

Upon this fundamental principle it is further built that this **Universal Being** must be regarded as **the ground and the life of all beings**, since everything must be grounded therein, as we have already noted previously from the **71st Hymn**. I know well that in the **Herrnhuter Hymnal** <note>Original: "Herrnhuthsche Gezang-boek." This hymnal was the primary vehicle for Zinzendorf’s theology, often using highly eroticized or mystical language that offended traditionalists.</note> some **Hymn** or other may be found that has been taken over from orthodox and edifying **hymnals**, in which the expression where God is called **the ground and the life of all things** is used in a sound and orthodox sense by the godly author of such a **Hymn**,

...word, but since the Herrnhutters do not understand that phrase in the author’s sense, but in the sense of the Congregation, which they define elsewhere in their Hymnal, whichever it may be. For example, in the 8th Hymn in the Herrnhutter Hymnal, (when verse 2 had called Jehovah an *incomprehensible being*) in the 3rd verse of the same it is testified of Jehovah: *Ground and life of all things* <note>Original German: "Grund und leben aller dinge."</note>. The godly maker of that hymn understood this in a healthy sense. For it is the original hymn of the now blessed Neander <note>Joachim Neander (1650–1680) was a prominent German Reformed teacher and hymn-writer, most famous for the hymn "Praise to the Lord, the Almighty." He spent significant time in Bremen, the author's home city.</note>, who gave striking proofs of both his orthodoxy and his tender piety in my native city of Bremen; and it can be found in the edition of the man’s Hymns published here in the year 1725, page 14, and shows in its heading to be an expansion upon 1 John 1:7 <note>"But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin."</note>. This precious hymn the Herrnhutters have taken over into their Hymnal, yet once again not without making changes to it. Not to speak of various verbal changes I notice in verse 1 and verse 2, I say only that I observe two substantial changes, the reason for which the Herrnhutters will best know themselves. For in verse 3, the blessed Neander says, with an allusion to the *Urim* and *Thummim* <note>The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects used by ancient Israelite high priests to determine God's will; their names are often translated from Hebrew as "Lights" and "Perfections" (or "Truths").</note>: *You love the* RIGHT *and* LIGHT *that you give* <note>Original German: "Du liebest den RECHT und LICHT dir giebt." Here, "Right" (Recht) refers to justice or moral law.</note>. But in the Herrnhutter Hymnal, that is changed: *You love him who* PRACTICES IN THE LIGHT. <note>Original German: "Du liebest den der sich IM LICHTE übt."</note> And again in verse 4, Neander wrote: *Only* LIGHT *and* RIGHT *unite God and me*. <note>Original German: "Nur LICHT und RECHT vereinigt God und mich."</note> But in the Herrnhutter Hymnal: *The* LIGHT *IN THE* LORD *unites God and me*. <note>Original German: "Das LICHT IM HERRN Vereinigt God und mich."</note> Why, in both of these verses, the word *right* <note>The author implies that the Moravians deliberately removed "Right" or "Justice" (Recht) to favor a more mystical, less law-oriented faith.</note> placed alongside *light* stood so much in their way that they left it out and made changes to another man’s hymn, they may say themselves. I have my own thoughts, and remind myself of the words of the Prophet Isaiah 59:14 <note>"And judgment is turned away backward, and justice standeth afar off: for truth is fallen in the street, and equity cannot enter."</note>. (a) The Stoic Philosophers, just as they made the "Whole Universe" into God, and held God and the whole of Nature to be one and the same Being—as will be shown in § 3—were also accustomed to call the Divinity the *air* <note>original Dutch: "lucht"</note> *that surrounds everything, and in which all things live, and which is the ground of all things.* According to the testimony of Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, Chapter 14 <note>original Latin: "Cicero Lib. I. de Nat: Deor: Cap: 14."</note>; and of Diogenes Laërtius in his life of Zeno, Book 7, section 139 <note>original Latin: "Diogen: Laërtius in Zenone Lib: 7. sect: 139."</note>. This is why they also regarded the human soul as a part of that pure air, being the soul of the world. On this subject, the learned remarks of the famous Mosheim <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a pioneering German Lutheran church historian known for his objective approach.</note> deserve to be consulted, concerning Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 1038, § 3. <note>Ralph Cudworth was a prominent "Cambridge Platonist"; Mosheim translated his *True Intellectual System of the Universe* into Latin and added extensive commentary.</note>

Just as we have already heard at length regarding this from Mr. Oetinger <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782) was a prominent German theosophist and prelate who attempted to bridge the gap between science and mystical theology; the author uses him here as a representative of Moravian thought.</note>, in the sense of the Congregation. This *outflowing* <term>emanation<note>The philosophical idea that the world is not created "out of nothing," but is a literal substance flowing out from the Divine.</note></term> of all things from the Essence of God is the foundation upon which their conception of the *extension of the Divine Essence* through the whole *Universe* is built. They express this by saying that *God's Essence fulfills all things*, of which this very same Hymn gives us the correct Moravian conception in the 5th verse. This is the crucial point for which we primarily appeal to this Hymn; these are the last 6 lines:

(3) Since these propositions precede—namely, that *God is the one Universal Essence, the ground and the life of all things, yes, the air and the element in which we live and move; that He, in that manner, fills the whole Universe, as the spirit and the heart of the world, the soul and the center, animating the whole Universe*—it cannot be otherwise than that the essential distinction between God and the Creature is taken away. <margin>God's Essence and the essence of the creatures, the distinction between them.</margin> The essence of the creatures—when one separates only the form, appearance, and <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that can change without changing the essential nature of a thing, like the color of an object versus the object itself.</note> from it like the outer bark—is posited as being the same as the Essence of God Himself, as that one *Universal Essence of all Essences*. For all beings have their essence through an emanation <note>The idea that all things "flow out" from the Divine substance, a concept often associated with Neoplatonism and mysticism.</note> from the essence of the Deity, which essential part of the Deity remains in them alone, when all the *accidents* of the *outer appearance* are separated from that manifestation. This is, truth-loving reader, no groundless but in every part a well-founded deduction, grounded in the nature of the matter, according to the conception given to us in the Herrnhut Hymn-book. 

And so that no impartial person might think that one seeks to burden these people through deductions, and to charge them with propositions drawn as consequences from their words which they have never recognized as their own or expressed in words; I shall again bring forth their own words, so that you yourselves may hear them speak, and judge their sentiment therefrom. Can anyone give these words any other meaning than the one that lies in the expressions in their entire context? Namely, that the *purest spiritual beings* as well as the *bodily extended ones*, like for example a leaf, are made of *one and the same basic substance*. This substance, according to them, is the *Universal Essence of the Deity*, which is equally shared with both by the *Creator and Master of the creature and nature* through <term>emanation</term> <note>The theological theory that all things "flow out" from the essence of God rather than being created "out of nothing."</note> (for that is what *Creating* means to them). Can anyone, I say once more, give any other sound meaning to this, without violating the words as they lie there, and without hiding or twisting the true Moravian <note>original: "Herrnhutſchen"</note> meaning? We shall gladly hear him and weigh his reasons. I can as yet give no other meaning to it than the one I have stated, and all the more so when I add the language I hear in the 575th Hymn, belonging to *the worship of God*, which seems to have been composed by a member or leader of the Moravians, just like the one we just referred to; there, the words of the 17th verse are these:

There you see what it means in the Moravian <note>original: "Herrnhuthſche"</note> Hymn, that no creature shall live for us who is not God himself; namely this: that *the Essence of the creature is no true and no distinct Essence*, but the Deity is ALONE the ONLY ESSENCE, and the ONLY ALL, from which the essence of the Creatures is not essentially distinct. Instead, they are only to be regarded as so many manifestations <note>original Dutch: "wyzingen"</note>, from which, when the outward form and shape are removed, nothing remains but the one Universal Divine essence. In this view, the essence of the creature is to be regarded as nothing other than *a drop of water* drawn from the sea; though separated from the sea, it nevertheless has no distinct essence, but falling back into the sea, it forms one essence with the *Universal Element*. And in this sense, and no other, is the *Omnipresent Essence* said *to fill all things, so that all*—

# The Enthusiasm Discovered in its Nakedness, etc.
### Page 332
<meta>catchword: that</meta>

whatever floats in the heavens is an expression of that *Universal Essence of Divinity*. <note>The author is critiquing the idea that the physical world is made of God's own substance, a concept known as pantheism.</note> Has Spinoza ever spoken otherwise? Except that he made use of Philosophical, and not Enthusiastic <note>In this period, "Enthusiast" was a derogatory term for religious radicals who claimed direct, emotional inspiration from God.</note> and Moravian <note>original Dutch: "Herrnhuthsche," referring to the Moravian settlement at Herrnhut.</note> modes of speech. By this I do not mean to say that the Moravians are Spinozists, or that they learned those doctrines from Spinoza, or took them from his writings. No, I doubt whether there is more than one or another among them who has even read Spinoza; furthermore, the Enthusiasts usually try to show themselves to be great opponents of Spinoza; but I say that they have drawn that abominable doctrine from those same shops <note>The author uses "shops" metaphorically to mean the sources or schools of thought.</note> from which Spinoza took it and draped it in a Philosophical mantle, as will now become more apparent to us.

### §. III.

<margin>The origin of these abominable errors must be sought, partly in Heathen Philosophy, and partly in the corrupted Theology of the Enthusiasts.</margin>
