The notorious <term>Fanatic (Geestdrijver): literally "Spirit-driver," a pejorative Dutch term for radical reformers and mystics who claimed direct inspiration by the Holy Spirit</term> Weigel <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588) was a German theologian whose writings formed the basis of "Weigelianism," a precursor to later mystical and pietistic movements.</note>, will in many places declare himself clearly, but also godlessly enough, on this matter. > *That God births, makes, and creates nothing other than Himself. He is God, and births God. For God is the Word, and the Word is God. Therefore He has made nothing else than what He Himself is. He is all things. Therefore He makes all things, visible and invisible. Everything you see, God made it, and all that He has made through the Word, that same thing is He Himself. Instead, they decry that doctrine as a "straying heresy" while praising as orthodox truth the doctrine of Creation in which *all things are said to have flowed out from the essence of God Himself*, and which understands the *Divine essence as the Universal essence of all essences, and as the soul animating the Universe*; just as we have shown in the preceding Part of this Chapter. It is true, I would also simply take it in that sense if I did not know, and had not shown in the previous part, what *Creating* means in the *Herrnhuthian* <note>The Herrnhutters, or Moravian Brethren, were often criticized by orthodox theologians for their mystical language which seemed to blur the line between the Creator and the creation.</note> sense; not what it signifies to us—*bringing things forth out of nothing by an Almighty will*—but *a production of beings through an outflow from the Divine essence*. Does that mean that the image of God brought with it a clear light of knowledge in the understanding, and holiness in the will—according to Colossians 3:10 and Ephesians 4:24? <note>The original text cites Ephesians 4:4, but 4:24 is the standard reference regarding the "new man" created in the likeness of God.</note> Nothing less than that: but this is the meaning, that God Himself—that is, the Essence of God, shared with the soul through that birth from God—*was the light of the soul*. 

And of this the explanation given at the beginning of the 3rd verse clearly testifies for further clarification, in which it is said of the soul: That she constantly drew from her SOURCE, FROM WHICH SHE SPRUNG, or flowed: What did the soul draw? That light, which was God Himself to her. And how could she draw it from there? Because God Himself, that is, the essence of God, was the SOURCE from which she had sprung, and from which she had flowed as if from her spring <note>original: "foerſe," likely derived from the French "force," used here to mean a headwater or source.</note>. This is the reason why in Hymn 222, verse 1, *the Trinity* is called *the Universal Essence*, and *Jesus the trace of the Life-Well of the Godhead*, just as we have seen in the previous part of this chapter, section 2, page 317. ## The Moravians, Part II. Chapter IV. Section II.

Now that the high *birth of the soul out of God* has been described in such a manner, the creator of the hymn we are currently examining descends to describe the deep fall and the total ruin of the soul through sin (which, according to M. Oetinger, <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782) was a German theosopher and prelate who attempted to bridge the gap between Enlightenment science and mystical theology.</note> has caused *an internal change in the Essence of the soul*) from the middle of the 4th verse to the end of the 6th verse, *through which she has become earthly, fallen into the state of sinners, and entirely disturbed by the evil one*, etc. 

Following this, from the beginning of the 7th verse to the end of the hymn, is a prayer to God for restoration, *that He would raise the soul up again and awaken her to the new life*, etc. This is phrased with such expressions that we might partially interpret them in a healthy sense, were it not that we had learned from M. Oetinger how this *restoration of the soul—through all those stages of Creation enumerated by him—brings forth a new Essence in the soul once more*, and indeed the very same essence which she possessed in her first birth from the *Essence of God*. 

With this also agrees in every part that which a purified and restored soul, in the sense of the Moravians, testifies of herself in the 726th hymn, verse 1: **I BEGIN ANOTHER ESSENCE, WHICH CAN MIX WITH NOTHING ELSE**, which was already cited by us above on page 176. ### The Moravians Part II. Section IV. Chapter II. Page 355

If one understands it in the correct sense according to the Word of God, one can regard God in this way. But do the <term>Herrnhutters: Members of the Moravian Brethren, a pietist Christian denomination.</term> also understand it orthodoxly? Not in the least. For to them, God is the *Father of the soul*, not through the power of *re-creation*, the *renewal* of the Spirit, or gracious adoption as a child—for they are not yet speaking of spiritual restoration here, but of the *first origin* of the soul. According to this view, God is said to be her Father by virtue of procreation from His own *Essence*. That same God is her *Creator*, not because God created her out of nothing—no, for that is regarded as an error by these people—but because God brought her forth *from His own Essence* through *emanation* <note>original: "uitvloeyinge." A philosophical term meaning a flow of substance from a source, implying the soul is made of the same "stuff" as God.</note>. This God is also her *good*, because by virtue of that first Divine Birth, she possesses something of the Divine Essence, and in that sense is a partaker of the *Divine Nature*. 

These, kind reader, are not merely consequences we draw from their words, nor a meaning we assign to them at our own whim; this is the very explanation given in this 3rd and the following 4th verse regarding that testimony. It serves as the reason why God was called the *Father*, *Creator*, and the *good of the soul*. For in the last two lines of the 3rd verse, these words appear: *Therefore YOU (namely, the soul) SPRANG FORTH FROM THE DIVINE GLOW: God was your Creator, your Father and Good.* 

And so that it might not remain obscure to the soul how this is properly to be understood—that the soul is said to have *sprung from the Divine Glow*—the entire 4th verse serves as an elucidation and explanation. We shall therefore transcribe it in full, because our <note>The "Naamloze Man" (Anonymous Man) refers to an unnamed defender of the Moravians whom the author is refuting.</note> Anonymous Man only cites the first line of it. ### Of the Herrnhutters Part II. Section IV. Part II. 357

...derived, that such a *near relative of God* <note>original Dutch: "naabestaande Gods," implying a next-of-kin or blood relation.</note>, from the light and the well of eternities, should extend itself into the eternities, and become like HIS (namely: God's) FIRE. Once more, in Hymn 975, the members of the Herrnhut Congregation are addressed:
> YOU FIREBRANDS IGNITED FROM ETERNITY, <note>original German: "IHR AUS DER EWIGKEIT ENTFLAMMTE BRÄNDE."</note> that is, *You firebrands ignited from ETERNITY*.

With which the expression in the 1st verse of Hymn 714, which we shall cite in the following section, may be compared. From this it appears that this *springing of the soul from the Divine glow* expresses nothing other than the *outflow of the soul from the Essence of God*. And in this we are further confirmed by the expression of the 4th verse of this Hymn, which we are presently examining, in which that *glow* is regarded as something that is *above*, and the *springing from that glow* is explained as a *begetting* <term>begetting: translating 'telinge,' a word for biological procreation, used here to contrast with 'creation' from nothing.</term>, for the soul is there twice said to be *begotten from above*. Who ever called God’s Creation a *begetting*? And who can make any reasonable conception of a *begetting* without imagining a *communication* of something from the Essence of him *who begets*, to that which *is begotten*? And is anyone else said in the Scriptures to be *begotten* and *generated* of the Father, other than the eternal and own Son of the Father? Psalm 2; Proverbs 8. By virtue of which Divine *begetting*—incomprehensible to us—the Father is said *to have given to the Son to have life in himself, even as the Father has life in himself*. John 5:26. On which grounds the Son also cannot be regarded as anything other than *being out of and from the Father*, and consequently *of one Essence with the Father*.

---

Those who adhere to a more or less literal sense regarding the origin of the soul are accustomed to appeal to Acts 17:28 <note>"For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring."</note> and to certain expressions of the Old Church Fathers, who utilized that same manner of speaking, although they intended nothing less than the *outflow of the soul from the Essence of God*. This is certain, as seen in Hilary, *Commentary on Psalm 62*; Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, Chapter 7; Ambrose, *On Luke 6:9*; and others to be mentioned in section 4.

### Enthusiasm Discovered Naked, etc. ###

...being able to say: *I and the Father are one.* <note>John 10:30</note> Can such a thing be applied to any creature without blaspheming God? Or can this *springing forth* from a Divine glow, and this being *begotten from above*, be understood in a sense that it means nothing other than being created? Is the Son of God therefore the *firstborn* because he is the *first created*, and is he said to be *begotten by the Father* because he was brought forth by the Father and transitioned from non-being to actual being? And is it in this that the meaning lies—according to the sense of the *Herrnhutters* <note>The Herrnhutters, or Moravians, were followers of Count Zinzendorf; the author critiques their mystical language as being theologically dangerous.</note> and the contents of the previously explained *Hymn 71*—that *from the firstborn, all beings flash and flow*? The former would favor hidden *Atheism* <term>Atheism: In this 18th-century context, the author uses "Atheism" to describe pantheistic views where God and nature are the same substance, thus "destroying" the true nature of God.</term>, and the latter would favor open *Socinianism* <term>Socinianism: A rationalist Christian doctrine that denied the full divinity of Christ, viewing him instead as a perfected man.</term>. Indeed, so that we might grasp this "begetting" not in any weak sense, but in the most literal sense possible, this is what is primarily emphasized in the Hymn under discussion. Not only in that same fourth verse—where the soul is exhorted to return *to her first and true origin, through which she received her essence by begetting from above and out of the Divine glow*—holding up the example of other creatures *who, in many ways and manners, incline themselves toward their origin*; but especially in the 5th verse, in which that *begetting from above* is compared in every respect to the *begetting of actual children by and from their natural parents*. We shall present the words of the 5th verse in their entirety to our reader, together with those of the 6th verse, so they may see and judge for themselves.

See, there the begetting from above—as the *origin of the soul*, through which she *originated* <term>ontsprongen: literally "sprung forth," used here to suggest a flowing out of substance rather than a creation from nothing.</term> out of the *Divine glow*—is compared to that *begetting* by which children are *begotten* by their parents. Just as there arises from this a natural inclination of children toward their parents, from whom they (next to God) have their essence, so too must the soul incline toward *her origin*: namely, the *Being of God*, from which she *originated*. Indeed, just as every creature lives and moves *in something* as if in its own element, so too must the soul live and soar in *her element* (this being the *element and the atmosphere of the Godhead*, according to what we noted above on page 320). In that *Being and in that glow of the Godhead*, she must *live and soar*. This is what is meant in the third verse when it is said that God has given the soul *to soar above, above all other created life*. Finally, all these representations are directed solely toward this: to stir the soul, by consideration of *her Divine origin out of the Being of God*, to return again to *her origin*—that is, *to enter back into that Being from which she flowed*. Just as this exhortation is pressed home at the conclusion of the matter in the seventh and final verse: *Soul! ah, look back in earnest—consider your eternal happiness, and hasten to return again to your origin.*

# Of the Moravian Brethren. II. Section. IV. Chapter. II. Part. #

Zz

...[be]ings, passed from non-being to being? Or is this bringing forth to be understood as the *outflowing* <note>The Dutch term *uitvloeyinge* refers to emanation, the idea that the soul is a literal "flow" of God's own substance rather than a creation made from nothing.</note> of things, which now exist, *out of the Essence of God Himself?* That is truly the point of dispute, and the state of that dispute should have been clearly indicated, so as not to deceive anyone with complex and ambiguous words.

The latter, and not the former, is the true sense and the sentiment of the Moravian Brethren, as has been revealed to us thus far. And our Man has already sailed so far afield and deviated from the orthodox truth (demonstrating how much the power of error can prevail when one has first adopted favorable prejudices for the spirits of delusion themselves), that however cunningly he seeks to hide it, he chooses the side of the Moravian Brethren and their error. He not only adopts that same teaching, *concerning the origin of the soul from the Essence of God*, as his own, but also seeks to instill it in others through a faithless distortion of Scripture, when he appeals to Genesis 2:27 <note>original: "Genes: 2: 27." The author likely refers to Genesis 2:7, which describes God breathing life into Adam.</note> where it is said, *that God blew the breath of life into the nostrils of that man formed from the dust of the earth.* 

And this is for him both the explanation and the proof *of the soul's coming forth from God*, just as it is called in the 172nd Song *a springing forth from the Divine glow, and a begetting from above, just as Children are begotten by their Fathers*, and in the 171st Song *a springing from the wellspring of the Godhead, which was itself the light of the soul*, because God is said to have *blown* or *breathed* the soul into man. 

Consequently, that expression is not to be understood symbolically by him—as if God made use of some outward sign in the creation of the soul—but most literally: that God has a literal *breath* which He *blows out*, through which *something from the Essence of God* flowed out at that time when He brought forth Adam's soul, which flowed *through the nostrils* into Adam, and thus *constituted the Essence of his soul*. # Fanaticism Unmasked, etc. <note>The original Dutch title is *De Naakt ontdekte Enthusiastery*, referring to "Enthusiasm" in the 18th-century sense: a pejorative term for religious fanaticism or claims of direct private revelation.</note>

...the previous doctrine, namely: *of the Creation of all things out of the essence of God, through emanation.* <note>The author uses the term *uitvloeijinge* (outflowing), a concept central to Neoplatonism and certain mystical traditions where creation is seen as a liquid-like pouring out of God’s own substance.</note> Since some dare to view physical and material things as *emanations from the Divine essence*, one can certainly have no lower conception of the origin of the soul. Do not think that this doctrine is a new invention of the Moravians <note>original: *Herrnhuthers*</note>, or some particular opinion that this sect holds alone: No, it is a very old erroneous view, for the lie is also very old! and comes from him who was the Father of Lies from the beginning. We shall not say that there have been, from of old as well as in the present day, many different opinions regarding the origin of the human soul in general—even among the Brethren—which we do not care to recount here. (a) But we shall limit ourselves only to those who derive the origin of the soul from the essence of God. In the first book of his *The Divine Economy* <note>Pierre Poiret’s *L'Oeconomie Divine* (1687), a major work of mystical theology.</note>, in the 10th Chapter, he first declares in § 2 *that there is something in man that is of a Divine nature, and that must be a participant in the powers of the Divine nature.* The reason why he calls the soul *Divine* is given as this: *because the soul was by no means drawn by God solely out of Nothing, or merely created, but was in a Divine manner, as it were, born,* § 15. And regarding this, he defines his meaning even more clearly in § 16: *Man,* he says, *with respect to his soul and his Spirit, is not merely created by God, but born of God, just as the Divine Word itself.* — *God is not merely the Creator, but the Father of Spirits.* Thus, man is, in respect of his soul, *a true Son of God through grace,* — *the living temple, and the true possessor of the Divine Majesty.* This is because, according to him in § 19, *that which in itself must admit and possess God, can be nothing other than of Divine nature.* To this may be added the reasoning he provides in § 20 (which we have already cited previously). Finally, at the conclusion of the matter, he speaks candidly in § 24: *Some,* he says, *wonder (just as I myself also did previously, namely before I was inspired by the Spirit of Antoinette Bourignon <note>A famous Flemish mystic (1616–1680) who claimed direct revelations from God; Poiret became her most devoted follower and editor.</note>)* *that some Philosophers, both among the Heathens and among the Christians, have called the soul* a small fragment of the divine breath <note>original: "Divinæ particulam auræ" — a famous phrase from the Roman poet Horace, often used by mystics to suggest the soul is a "spark" of God.</note>, *or a tiny part or spark of the Divine breath, or spirit, or air. ->Vs. 8.<-

<note>The author provides both the original German verse (left) and his Dutch translation (right) to ensure accuracy before critiquing them. The hymn emphasizes the "inner world" of the believer’s soul.</note>

These verses can serve as some clarification to point out the ground upon which they <note>The Moravians, also known as the Herrnhuters.</note> assert that it is possible for humans *to be elevated to divine dignity*, because they *descend from God*, or *are from a Divine lineage*. I know well that believers are, in a healthy sense, *a seed of God, and born of God*, John 1:13, on account of that spiritual birth, by means of the seed of the Divine Word, and through the operation of the Holy Spirit; but not in the sense and for the reason given in this hymn, in which the *outflowing from the Divine essence* <note>The author is concerned that the Moravians are teaching "emanationism"—the idea that souls are literally pieces of God's own substance, rather than being created by Him.</note> is laid as a foundation. For this reason, they are said to be *of a Divine lineage, because God and his powerful Word begot them*. 

You could easily mistake this here, and by *this powerful Word of God* understand the *written and preached Word of God*, which Peter calls *the seed of rebirth*, 1 Peter 1:23. No, here is understood *the substantial Word, the firstborn, from whom all Beings flash forth* <note>original Dutch: "blixemen." This refers to the "Logos" or Christ, but the author implies the Moravians use it in a mystical, almost electrical sense of souls "flashing" out of the Divine.</note>, who appears here not as the means through which, but as the source from which—as well as from the essence of the Father—the soul is begotten and born, from which also its origin is first determined: *to be of a heavenly flame*, which is the same as *springing from the Divine glow*. 

And although in the Moravian sense, the soul of a righteous person has that in common with that of an unrighteous person regarding the first origin, sin has nevertheless made an *internal change in the Essence of the soul*, which change is taken away through renewal, so that a righteous person *finds his soul again*, and *commences a new being, which can mingle with nothing*. And thus the soul receives *its first origin*...

# Enthusiasm Laid Bare, etc.

THE PURE STREAM will there entirely **PENETRATE** the child (of God), and unite it with God into one spirit. Likely referring to a specific epistle or a letter addressed to the Hebrews used in their liturgy.</note> from the 7th verse: *What God enjoys, he (that Child of God) also enjoys; what God possesses, is given to him in God.* Now I ask whether the **Mystical Deification** <note>original: "Mystike Vergodinge." The controversial concept that a human being can literally become God or partake in the Divine essence, rather than just being a servant of God.</note>, which realizes the creature into the essence of the Godhead, whether in or after this life, can be puffed up any higher? ...General Epistle, concerning the *nature of animals and birds, which are tamed by human nature.* Chapter 3:7 <note>The author is citing James 3:7 to show how the word "nature" (physis) is used in the Bible to refer to the species or the beings themselves.</note>. Of this *Divine nature*, *Believers* are now said *to have become partakers*. That is the primary point of concern. *This becoming a partaker* (to become partakers <note>original Greek: κοινωνοι γινεσθαι (koinōnoi genesthai)</note>) does not only signify a *most intimate fellowship* that exists between two things of one and the same nature—the kind of *fellowship* that can never exist between things of *different natures*, such as between *light and darkness*, 2 Corinthians 6:14—but certainly exists between humans and humans, just as Christ also *partook of the human nature* when *He shared in flesh and blood with all other children*, Hebrews 2:14. 

But this *becoming a partaker* also indicates a partnership, consisting in a right to, and an enjoyment of, some good and privilege. Thus, Paul will speak of a *partaking of certain spiritual goods*, Romans 15:27. And of those *who eat the sacrifices, he will say that they have communion with the altar:* (they are partakers of the altar <note>original Greek: κοινωνοι του θυσιαστηριου εισι (koinōnoi tou thysiastēriou eisi)</note>) 1 Corinthians 10:18. In that sense which the orthodox Church gives to it, according to the *Analogy of Faith*? <note>The "Analogy of Faith" is a principle of interpretation where unclear biblical passages are explained by clearer, fundamental doctrines.</note> Then this passage favors nothing less than the Herrnhuter and Enthusiastic <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiasm" was a derogatory term for religious groups who claimed direct divine inspiration, often viewed by traditionalists as irrational or fanatical.</note> error, which elevates the creature to *the Essence of God* and to *Divine dignity*, regardless of the nature of the creature. Then he shows where he belongs, and at the same time how corrupted must be the taste of those who allow themselves to be captivated by such pretexts, and are misled by the mere sound of the words of any scriptural passage. Meanwhile, everyone who has eyes can see what the secret design may be, and what kind of Theology one is covertly seeking to introduce by such a defense of the erring Herrnhuters.

-> §. II. <-

<margin>
New proofs, in which the Mystic Deification is taught, are presented from the Hymnal and the Little Flower Garden.
</margin>
But so that no one thinks that it is only those passages which instill the error of *Deification* <term>Deification: The belief that a human being can become divine or be absorbed into the literal essence of God, a concept the author considers a dangerous heresy.</term> that we have pointed out in the Pastoral Letter, we must say that this leaven is spread throughout the entire Hymnal of the Herrnhuters, and makes itself seen and tasted by attentive and intelligent readers everywhere; though in one place it is presented more intricately, ambiguously, and craftily than in another, yet in such a way that by comparing one with another, the true sense of the Herrnhuters cannot remain hidden. We shall proceed by degrees and by way of ascent, and each time compare the expressions of the Hymnal with those which appear in the manual of the Herrnhuters, the *Spiritual Little Flower Garden* <note>original: *Geistliches Blumen-Gärtlein inniger Seelen*, a collection of mystical poetry and hymns by Gerhard Tersteegen, which was influential among the Moravians.</note>. ---

I appeal to this Hymn all the more gladly because it can clarify both the <term>Herrnhutian</term> <note>Followers of Count Zinzendorf's Moravian Brethren.</note> meaning and that of the <term>Halle Hymnbook</term> <note>The *Hallische Gesangbuch*, a central hymnal of German Pietism, which the author believes was the pure source before the Moravians altered it.</note>. For this Hymn is again taken from the Halle Hymnbook, but mutilated and corrupted according to the custom of the Herrnhuters. It is to be found there, No. 661, page 1030. I say first that the Herrnhuters have corrupted it in order to obscure the true meaning as much as possible. For in the last line of the 1st verse, the Halle Hymnbook states *AND I AM SWALLOWED UP IN GOD* <note>original German: "UND BIN IN GOTT VERSCHLUNGEN"</note>, that is, *And I am swallowed up in God*. Count Zinzendorf wanted to soften that somewhat when he expressed it as: *AND PENETRATED INTO GOD* <note>original German: "UND IN GOTT GEDRUNGEN"</note>, that is: *And penetrated into God*, although in the <term>Mystical</term> <note>Referring to the 18th-century "Mystiken," or groups seeking direct, ecstatic union with God, often viewed with suspicion by orthodox theologians.</note> sense it comes to the same thing, and teaches us that *to be penetrated into God* is the same as *to be swallowed up in God*. In the last line of the 2nd verse, the author of the Hymn says in the Halle Hymnbook, *So I remain an obedient child, AND DWELL IN YOUR NAME* <note>original German: "UND WOHN IN DEINEM NAHMEN"</note>, that is, *AND DWELL IN YOUR NAME*. But the Count changes this in the Herrnhutian Hymnbook to *And* SERVE *your Name* <note>original German: "Und DIENE deinem Nahmen"</note>, that is, *And* SERVE *your Name*. To serve God’s Name and to *dwell* in God’s Name differ greatly, yet *he who is penetrated or swallowed up in God* also *dwells* in God’s Name, for God’s Name is *God himself*. I say secondly, the Halle Hymn is mutilated by the Herrnhuters; for there it has 7 verses, but here only 3 verses. The reason for this omission of 4 entire verses will seem strange to someone who cannot see the book for themselves; but it is not so strange to us. The Herrnhuters are willing to adopt the principles of those who adhere to and propagate the errors of the Mystics; but they withhold the clear explanation of how those principles should be understood, in order to train their favorites in them through secret instruction.

### Of the Herrnhuters. Part II. Chapter IV. Section III.

The last three lines of the 3rd verse contain the foundation upon which the corrupt <term>Mystics</term> <note>Radical spiritualists in 18th-century Germany who sought direct, ecstatic experiences of God, often straying from orthodox church doctrine.</note> in Germany build the *restoration and restitution of all things, even to the salvation of the damned and the Devils*; the Herrnhuters do not shrink from adopting this, yet they prefer to keep the open declaration of it secret for a time. They do this in the hope that the simple-minded, whom they first seek to draw into their bonds, will not discover the secret so quickly, nor notice where they truly belong. But the explanation of that foundation—*how Jesus, the wellspring of life, namely the one from whom everything has flowed, must become all in all, or else his Creation, that is, that which flowed out of him, cannot again become pure and glorious as it was in its first origin and outflowing*—we find in the 4th verse of the Song, as it stands in the <term>Halle Hymnbook</term> <note>The *Hallische Gesangbuch*, a central hymnal of German Pietism, which the author uses as a point of comparison to show how the Moravians altered traditional hymns.</note>, where I read these words:

This will now appear more clearly in our second proposition.

<margin>(2) The union of the soul with God is stated such that the soul loses its own essence and takes on that of the Godhead—</margin>
(2) The second stage *of the union of the so-called believer with God* goes much further, and shall teach us *that the soul is so united with God, that she loses her own Essence and assumes that of the Godhead, and is essentialized therein, yes, becomes one common Essence with the Essence of the Godhead*. This will be clear to anyone who, without prejudice, considers not only the many passages we have already scattered throughout this entire work—specifically on the pages indicated at the beginning of this Part—but who also takes these following passages into calm consideration. It is something that gives cause for well-founded suspicion.

### Of the Moravians. Part II. Chapter V. ###

Then finally begins the 8th verse: *Lord, your flesh, (which) has come from heaven, --- may it become to us a power of God.* There you have, word for word, the entire hymn up to the 8th verse, which is the last. We make no other remarks about all those verses, but ask anyone who is unbiased whether this hymn is a Communion Hymn <note>original: "Avontmaals Lied," referring to the Lord's Supper</note>? And if not, what is to be judged of someone who dares to lie so shamelessly to give his slander the appearance of truth and find entry among the simple-minded, and of what such a person might not be capable? (2) Let us now also see what his second reason is, which he derives from the words of the 8th verse itself, *in which he says, that regard is given to the hidden consumption of Christ’s flesh and blood.* This has some appearance of truth, all the more because the four middle lines of this verse are somewhat obscure and ambiguous in the High German <note>original: "Hoogduitsch"</note>, which the Anonymous Writer, through his vile translation, makes even more ambiguous. Anyone who has understanding and judgment easily sees that the first and the last lines belong together in this manner: *Lord, your flesh, having come from heaven (or that has come from heaven), may it become to us a power of God.* But the four middle lines, which stand between them, are somewhat broken, and make it somewhat doubtful whether they should be applied to Jesus himself and to his *flesh come out of heaven*, or whether they must be applied to the believers. The Anonymous Writer chooses the latter because it best serves his purpose, though it shall avail him nothing. We had several things to note regarding the sense and the proper translation of those four middle lines, yet it will not matter much here, and we have no desire to dispute over the nature of the language with someone who has forgotten much of the peculiar character of both languages. Let me be liberal <note>here meaning "generous in argument"</note> and grant our man *that those lines refer to the believers, and that through this is seen the hidden consumption of Christ’s flesh and blood.* Then the question is, which flesh and blood of Christ is it that, according to this hymn, *is hiddenly or mystically <term>Mystiek: relating to a direct, internal experience of the divine</term> consumed?* It is not the flesh and blood that Jesus took from Mary—

### §. III.

<margin>(3) The third error is that the Moravians <note>The Moravians, or *Herrnhutters*, are a Pietist Christian denomination that emphasized an emotional, personal relationship with Christ, often using vivid and mystical language that drew criticism from more traditional Reformed theologians.</note> claim that Jesus is still physically born in the believer and takes on human nature.</margin>
The third error, which is born from the preceding one *concerning the double body of Christ*, is this: *that Jesus is still physically born in the believer, and takes on human nature within them*. -> *Some short Appendices serving the matter.* <-

When I found myself compelled for weighty reasons, at the beginning of August of the past year, to publish in advance the Preface along with the first Section and the first two Chapters of the second Section of this my work, and to share them with the eager, truth-loving Reader, I declared that I would not—and also could not—make such haste with the continuation, in consideration of various obstacles that I then anticipated. All those hindrances not only came to pass, but even more occurred besides; others of much greater weight and importance, which I had not foreseen and which it is unnecessary to mention here, although they are not unknown <note>The author likely refers to local ecclesiastical disputes or personal challenges that would have been common knowledge among his contemporary readers in the Reformed Church.</note>. It is for this reason that, with one hindrance following upon another, I have been unable to lay a hand on this work at all for a full three months, to do anything of any substance toward its continuation. It was not until the month of November that I could think of the work with any regularity, at which time I soon found my desire and zeal awakened with redoubled urgency to set my hand to the work in the fear of the Lord, and to "redeem the time" <note>A biblical reference to Ephesians 5:16, "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil," meaning to make the most of every opportunity.</note> for it as much as the doubled duties of my other ministerial service allowed. Is it outrageous to write in public against public wandering spirits, whose own writings are made public by themselves? <note>The term "wandering spirits" (dwaal geeſten) refers to those perceived as spreading heretical or heterodox doctrines, common in 18th-century religious polemics.</note> He can count on the fact that it is truly expected, and is still expected—not that he should merely do something, but that he should publicly answer, distinctly, clearly, and in good faith, not to one or another, but to all the grievances and well-founded accusations brought publicly against him and his **Herrnhuters**. <note>The Herrnhuters, or Moravian Brethren, were a Pietist Christian denomination led by Count Zinzendorf. They faced significant opposition from the established Reformed Church in the Netherlands.</note> He could not have been ignorant that such was expected of him and his fellow advocates. For the **Very Reverend Gentlemen Deputies** of the **Christian Synod of South Holland**, held in *The Hague* in the year 1738, urged this with all persistence in person to **Mr. de Watteville** and his fellow advocate, as well as calling for a public and open-hearted **Confession** from the entire Congregation. And when, after long waiting, those Gentlemen Deputies were informed that no other Confession was to be expected from the **Herrnhuters** than that which **Mr. de Watteville** had already issued (being the so-called *Declaration* of that gentleman, which appeared as early as the end of the year 1738, and which was extensively and thoroughly refuted last year, both by the **Highly Noble Mr. Professor van den Honert**, as well as by the **Right Honorable Mr. Kuipers**, and also in several places by me), the **Christian Synod of South Holland**, held in **WOERDEN** in the year 1739, took this unanimous resolution: *That the Herrnhuters are not orthodox, and thus do not belong to our Church, but hold harmful and destructive false-grounds, as several public writings by renowned men demonstrate. — Likewise, this did not remain obscure, as they have answered essentially nothing until now in their defense regarding the Grievances brought against them in the Synod of The Hague. Also, because they refuse to give a complete, open-hearted, and clear Confession of their Faith upon Synodal request.* And lest anyone think that this little leaf and pamphlet from the **Lord Count**, and the reasons contained therein, were judged sufficient by that **Most Reverend Assembly**, it is added in the Synodal resolution: *That certain two delivered papers (being the two we are examining here) are not sufficient; the one from the Count of Zinzendorf being but a copy of no use, and intended only to seek delay and procrastination, and to hold up the Synodal deliberations concerning them,* etc. Of that opinion were also their **Noble Mightinesses the Gentlemen Political Commissioners**, as can be seen from that same Synodal Act.

# Of the Herrnhuters. Account: I. Appendix. 483

...cannot now think that the State is concerned with the continuation of a Theological and Moravian <note>The original Dutch "Theo-logi- en Moravers" likely refers to "Theological and Moravian affairs" or "Theological Moravianism."</note> enterprise, it is not our business to investigate. (1) The opinion of the Lord Count himself is easily discerned from his own Declaration, which we have already noted previously on pages 114 and 115, and wish to repeat here: *That a Christian Authority, WHEN IT WANTS TO BE CALLED A CHRISTIAN AUTHORITY, cannot forbid private Gatherings and Conversations; and if it should want to forbid them, then A CHRISTIAN SUBJECT CANNOT obey.* This is the explanation of that restriction which the Count makes here with these words: *in all things, where they are not restricted by their conscience.* Meanwhile, it has been urged in the Christian Synods that the Herrnhuter **Conventicles** <note>Private religious meetings held outside the official state church, often viewed with suspicion by authorities.</note> must be prevented, and that the help of the Authorities should be requested for this purpose. (2) One matter that affects the constitution of the entire Congregation itself, and from which it can be seen how far their submission to the Authority goes—where they introduce a **Hierarchy** among themselves far more sovereign than that which the Pope of Rome exercises—I cannot omit to raise here. I find in the first volume of *Isaac Le Long's Memorable Historical Accounts, page 104 et seq.*, certain *Herrnhuter Statutes*, which are called *The Lord’s Commandments and Prohibitions*, published for *Herrnhut* on May 12, 1727. It is indeed said in the 7th Article; *that every inhabitant in Herrnhut shall acknowledge themselves bound to be submissive to the Authority, etc.*

But Article 9 states: *He who wants to build his own house shall first apply to the* ELDERS *regarding this, to plan the work; and wait so long until the place is assigned to him, etc.* In this country, that is the work of the **Sovereign** <note>Meaning the local civil government or building magistrates.</note>, but among the Herrnhuters, it is the work of the Elders of the Congregation. Likewise Article 18: *He who wants to take up residence in Herrnhut shall first apply to the* ELDERS; *yet no one shall be tolerated there without their knowledge, even if it were for only one night.* Article 20: *In Herrnhut, no one shall change their profession without the knowledge of the* ELDERS; *much less leave their Master during their apprenticeship without his permission and the prior knowledge of the* ELDERS. Article 21: *No dispute within Herrnhut may last longer than eight days; nor shall anyone be complained about until the same [dispute] cannot be [settled] in an amicable way (and specifically within these 8 days)—*

Now, as little as the Count can expect it from that side, so little can he expect it with any ground from any other side. And consequently, the promise he makes is nothing other than a vain beating of the air, and a promising of something that one never had the intention to pay.

### 3. In—

<margin>(l)</margin> We sincerely wish that the *Lord Count* <note>The "Lord Count" refers to Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader of the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuters).</note> might be gripped in his heart by *Divine* operation, to have mercy on so many poor souls whom he has so miserably misled with his helpers—doing so to satisfy his own ambition, and to burn incense and sacrifice to his own net and yarn <note>Original: "aan zyn eigen net en garen te roken en te offeren." <margin>(m)</margin> I hold the *Lord Count* here to his word of Honor, which he is obligated to keep sacredly, not only as one who calls himself a *Right Reverend Bishop*, but principally as a *Man* of that *High Birth* and of that *Character* which we in no way dispute. I, for my part, accept that condition, and appoint all the *Synods* and all the *Theological Faculties* of our *Netherlands*, as well as the most prominent <term>Classes<gloss>Regional governing bodies in the Reformed Church structure, composed of ministers and elders.</gloss></term> and *Consistories* as *Judges*, and subject myself fully to the sentence which they shall pass; provided that by the *Protestant Churches* one understands nothing other than the *True Reformed* and those *Lutheran Churches* that adhere firmly in all respects to their *Symbolical Books* <note>Symbolical Books: The official confessions of faith (symbols) that define a church's doctrine.</note>, and not such persons from the *Protestant Church* who, more or less, secretly or openly, favor the *Enthusiasts* <note>Enthusiasts: A derogatory term used in this period for those who claimed direct, emotional divine inspiration outside of established scripture and church order.</note>. I mean those *Protestant Churches* that adhere firmly in all respects to the *Orthodox Doctrine* contained in the *Public Symbolical Books* and in the <term>Forms of Unity<gloss>The three standards of the Dutch Reformed Church: The Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort.</gloss></term>.

<margin>(n)</margin> I also accept this condition; and if that happens which the *Lord Count* expects (though no one but he and his following can expect it, without any ground), then I release the *Lord Count*, as far as I am concerned, from his promise which he makes here, and give him the freedom to continue his *Triumph*, and to boast of the victory throughout all *Europe*.

<margin>(p)</margin> In the year 1739, a small book was published, bearing this title: *Church History of the Bohemian Brethren, under J. Amos Comenius <note>Jan Amos Comenius (1592–1670) was a famous Czech philosopher and pedagogue, and the last bishop of the original Unity of the Brethren.</note>, the last Bishop of the Brethren’s Congregation in Bohemia, along with a confession of faith, letters, and church order.* <note>Original German title: *Kirchen Historie der Böhmischen Brüder, unter J. Amos Comenius letzten Bischoff der Brüder Gemeine zu Böhmen, nebst einen Glaubens bekäntnis, briefen und Kirchen-ordenung.*</note> That Bohemian Brother Congregation, which has built a church in Berlin by the permission of the King of Prussia and has its own Teachers, declares in a writing—which has been placed in the bud of wrath <note>A metaphorical expression suggesting the document was born out of conflict or is the source of burgeoning controversy.</note>—to be descended from that Congregation over which Comenius was the last Bishop. The Lord Count could also publish our Heidelberg Catechismus, and that of Luther; will anyone therefore conclude that the Herrnhut Congregation adheres in all parts to the true sentiments of the Reformed or Lutherans?

<margin>(q)</margin> Who will reassure us in this regard? The Lord Count certainly cannot do so, for his testimony cannot be valid in this matter. However, truth-loving Reader, I cannot hide from you the deceit that I have discovered lurking behind these words. In that transcript which I possessed, which was signed by the Lord Count's own hand, there were these words following *shall give to the light*: *And which we are willing to let be regarded as a Confession of Faith only insofar as one can be assured that we כך <note>Original Hebrew: "so" or "thus"</note> believe and teach, but by no means as a Formula or definition of the only Rule of Holy Scripture, in which our Doctrine is entirely contained, which we profess.* All these words were omitted in this printed paper. Each person who has understanding and judgment can easily determine the reason for themselves, especially those who know anything of the answer that the Lord de Watteville <note>Johannes von Watteville (1718–1788), a prominent Moravian bishop and Zinzendorf's son-in-law.</note> gave to the Right Honorable Gentlemen Deputies of the South Holland Synod (when they asked whether the Confession which the Lord Count had delivered to the King of Sweden was to be held as the Confession of the Congregation?). His answer essentially amounted to this: *that the Congregation could bear that confession, but in the sense of the Congregation, which it was not bound to explain.* I leave the judgment of this entire transaction to anyone who knows how resolute and sincere people act, and must act, if they do not wish to be considered deceivers.

# I I.

## The True Sentiments of the Moravian Brethren, regarding various Principal Articles; drafted by Frederick de Watteville. (a)

->§. I.<-

The Brethren hold the Word of God, contained in the Holy Scriptures, 
->to be<-

(a) The kind reader will please note that this *Declaration* is merely an *explanation* given by Mr. de Watteville as a private individual regarding the views of the Herrnhuters <note>A name for the Moravian Brethren, derived from their settlement at Herrnhut ("The Lord's Watch") in Saxony.</note>, whom he calls *Moravian Brethren*. This Declaration cannot and should not be viewed as anything more authoritative, and the Herrnhut congregation cannot be held accountable for it. At the very least, there is not the slightest evidence that the Herrnhuters outside of IJsselstein <note>A town in the Netherlands where the Moravians had a community.</note>, or those in Germany, much less the Holy Count himself <note>Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader of the Moravian Church.</note>, the Brethren's so-called Bishop, have consented to or approved it. In the first Declaration, which was signed on October 1, 1738, the title was: *Declaration of the Herrnhut Brethren, etc.* and the signature was: *on behalf of the Brethren outside IJsselstein and in Amsterdam, as their* **ADVOCATE**, **FREDERICK DE WATTEVILLE**. Attached to it was a so-called "handwritten **APPROBATION**" by the Count of Zinzendorf and Pottendorf, the **HIGHLY REVEREND BISHOP** of the Bohemian and Moravian Brethren. But here, Mr. de Watteville only mentions his name, both at the beginning and the end of the writing, stating that he is the Author, without mentioning in what capacity he does so; and here, nothing less than a so-called Episcopal *Approbation* is added. Anyone may guess the reasons for this, though that gentleman himself will know best. We make no other observation about it than that which the most recent Christian Synod of South Holland <note>The governing body of the Reformed Church in the region.</note> made regarding it, in these words: *The second (namely: paper, being what we are now examining) containing only some confession points, and thus not all; and also only signed by a Baron van Watteville, and not submitted as a confession of all*, both of which were required of them. Therefore, this paper, as well as the previous one from the Lord Count, was judged to be insufficient. Consequently, we have not intended to put Mr. de Watteville’s particular views to the test, but only to point out, in part, where he [omitted] the *True sentiments of the Herrnhuters*, as they are found in the Hymnbook...

### §. V.

The Brethren profess God to be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, according to the revelation of Himself and His Word; just as Baptism among us is always performed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. (m)

### §. VI.

...[Spi]nozism <note>The text likely completes the word "Spinozistery" (Spinozism) from the previous column, referring to the philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, often accused of equating God with nature.</note> God in the creature or in matter. Although Enthusiasm <note>term: "Enthusiastery" (Enthusiasm); in the 18th century, this referred to a perceived religious delusion where individuals claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit, often viewed by critics as a path to heresy.</note>, he says, differs greatly from Atheism, and even appears to oppose it, it can nonetheless happen that it shifts into Atheism when, through an *apotheosis* <note>original: "αποθεωσις," meaning deification or the elevation of a human or thing to divine status.</note> or Deification, everything (it is said) returns into the Essence of God. (m) Whether the Herrnhutters hold an orthodox or unorthodox view regarding the adorable Trinity, that most weighty doctrine, we raised no objection in the *Pastoral Letter*. Not only does he fail to do that, but in this Article he presents his Declaration—with which he wishes to prove the orthodoxy of the Herrnhutters—in such a way that he makes himself and his Brethren much more suspect by that very act. For everything he says in this Article could also be said and signed by any Socinian <note>Socinian: a follower of a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, viewed as a major heresy by the author’s contemporaries.</note>, and yet they would remain a Socinian. If things were entirely pure among the Herrnhutters regarding this fundamental doctrine, why does he not speak more clearly and distinctly? But perhaps he believes that the following Article will be able to remove all our concerns.

### § XIII.
...stouthearted people, who wish to show the world that they are pure and orthodox. Meanwhile, I cannot let it pass unnoticed that here the Lord Baron <note>Referring to Baron Friedrich von Watteville, a prominent leader in the Moravian movement.</note> takes a wonderful pleasure in that beloved Moravian way of speaking: that *someone must truly become a sinner* in order to receive forgiveness of sins, and *enter into the sinner-state, and order of sinners*, according to the following 12th Article. These are queasy expressions. What someone already is, they do not need to first become. Indeed, what every human being is by nature, they do not become through Grace. I well know that as long as an unconverted person goes along in their blindness and insensitivity, they do not see, feel, or acknowledge that they are an unconverted sinner, damnable before God. But when they are convicted by the grace of God, by means of the Word of God and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, then they see and acknowledge that they *are a sinner*; but they do not then first *become* a sinner, and they do not then first *enter into the state and order of sinners*, but rather become aware that they have lived in *that* state up until now. When we speak of people who are *in the state, and order, or among the number of sinners*, we mean by that the unconverted, who still live in their *natural state*. But the Moravians, who have a language of their own, mean by this the *graced ones*, *who receive forgiveness of sin*.

This Hymn-book is their *principal sanctuary*; for in part the Baron places it in the same rank as the Gospel that was preached by the Apostles, and thus it undergoes the same fate as the Gospel; in part because it is to them *the Song of Moses and of the Lamb*, of which Revelation 15 verse 3 speaks, which shall be sung by those who shall stand by *the sea of glass, who shall have the victory over the beast, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, having the harps of God. verse 2.* By which *Harp-players* <note>original: "Cyther-Speelders"</note> the Herrnhuters must then be understood, according to their own application which they make in the 56th Song, verse 3, and the 968th (the second of that number) verse 2. To which also belongs that entire collection of songs standing under the title *Of the City of God and the Song of the Lamb*, from numbers 963—967. And then this Hymn-book is *the Song of Moses and of the Lamb*, which the Herrnhut Harp-players sing, standing at the Sea of Glass, after the achieved victory over the Beast—which for them is the Protestant Church. (3) Regarding the charges taken from that Hymn-book, which had only just come to his ears when that first Declaration was published (by whom, he knows best), he and his Brothers wish for nothing more than that the songs in which those matters are found were named to them, whereupon *we*, he says, *shall defend ourselves*. His and his Brothers' wish is fulfilled; a few of those songs were pointed out to them in our Pastoral Letter, and thereafter others by the Honorable Professor Voget <note>Albert Voget (1695–1771), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Utrecht who was a sharp critic of the Moravians.</note>, which are proofs...

(2) It is, with good reason, very much in question whether the *Approbation* <note>term: Approbation. For on one hand, the personally signed *Approbation* of that *Gentleman* is not printed in the *Hymn-book*, but we are merely expected to believe that the book is *Censored*; we are not so gullible here in this Country. On the other hand, that *Approbation*, if it is even available, is handled deceitfully: For in that *edition* of the *Hymn-book* of the *Congregation* at *Herrnhut*, which was released in the year 1737, that same *Preface* stands word for word, and therein that same *Declaration* regarding the named *Approbation* of *Mr. GUDE*, which was placed before the *edition* of the year 1735, being signed December 9, 1734. Yet in that latest edition, there are far more than a hundred *Hymns* extra. For in the first one from the year 1735, there are no more than 1075 numbers, but in the latest one from the year 1737, there are 1254 *Hymns*. How does it appear to us now that *Mr. GUDE* also *Censored* and *Approved* those new *Hymns*? If such a transaction took place in our midst, those who granted the *Approbation* would complain about it as a breach of trust. ## §. XVI.

From page 295 to 300, to which we refer the truth-loving reader back.

(bb) Everything the Baron says here is partly proof that he has nothing substantial to bring forward in *defense of the Songs cited in the Pastoral Letter* <note>original: "Herd: Brief," referring to the *Herderlyke Brief* or Pastoral Letter, a common form of official communication in 18th-century Dutch churches.</note>, that he yields the case, and that his previous boasting was nothing more than bluster and slander; and partly, it all results in deception. Let us examine his words a little more closely. (1) He says: *we do not wish to dispute over any Songs*. In the Pastoral Letter, we also had no intention of *disputing* with the Herrnhuters, nor do I have it in this book; rather, I demonstrate as clear as day that the greatest bulk of those Songs contains not only all sorts of dangerous errors, but the most extravagant, abominable mysteries of iniquity and the *depths of Satan* <note>original: "dieptens des Satans" — a reference to Revelation 2:24, used here to imply that the Moravian hymns contained hidden, demonic heresies.</note>, as dishonoring to God as any ever driven by the most dangerous Enthusiasts <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiast" was a derogatory term for those claiming direct, emotional, and often irrational divine inspiration.</note>. These are *Songs* which the Baron has publicly taken upon himself to *defend* in the name of all his Brethren residing here in this Country. He is not released from this obligation, which he himself undertook, by this excuse; rather, we hold him to his word of Honor, either to defend the Songs without exception if he can, or to publicly confess his guilt regarding his slander and to loathe the abominable errors found in the Congregation's Hymn-book. He must give us proof that the entire Congregation loathes them and condemns and rejects the Hymn-book that has been their Symbolic book until now. (2) He says doubtfully: *if there are (namely Songs in the Hymn-book) which are judged to contain offenses*. This is as if the Baron and his Brethren had never known this, and as if we here in the Netherlands were the first to express our well-founded concerns about it and to show the danger. ### §. XVI.

## That which, as a *Report from Germany*, in a public writing un-

Theological Faculties and Churches in Germany have complained about and condemned the offenses and dangerous errors found in the Hymnbook? And if the Baron <note>Referring to Count Zinzendorf, who held the title of Baron of Pollendorf.</note> might have conducted himself according to the maxim and the unholy alliance of the Herrnhuters—to let himself be deterred by no speaking or writing of the opposing party—did he then not know that trusted friends of the Herrnhuters warned and cautioned Count Zinzendorf and the Congregation about this in a friendly manner? To convince my reader of the contrary, I shall only appeal to what I find in the High German *Acta Historico-Ecclesiastica* <note>original: "Acta Histor: Eccles:" — A prominent 18th-century journal documenting contemporary church history and theological disputes.</note>, the 15th volume, where on page 423 it is mentioned that the third question proposed to Count Zinzendorf by a friend of the Herrnhuters, the legal scholar in Frankfurt, Mr. van Loen <note>Johann Michael von Loen (1694–1776), a prominent German jurist and relative of Goethe, who was initially sympathetic to the Moravians.</note>, was this: *Whether their Songs, because several among them appear offensive, strange, and obscure, should not better be omitted from being sung in gatherings where all sorts of people are present?* To this, the answer of the Lord Count was: *Offensive Songs should not be sung at all. Those that appear offensive must be allowed to pass, when the offense is similar to those found in the Bible, and because such offense lies only in the reader. The entire teaching of Jesus Christ may be something strange. The Bohemian Brethren <note>original: "Boheemsche Broederen" — The 15th-century proto-Protestant group from which the Herrnhuters claimed spiritual descent.</note> must be content that their clearest expressions are not understood, as the matters are mysteries.* To this answer, Mr. van Loen again remarked the following: *That, although beautiful Songs are to be found in the Herrnhuter Hymnbook, there were nonetheless some offensive, strange, and obscure ones among them: That Magister Oetinger <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782), a famous Lutheran theosophist who briefly defended the Moravians before distancing himself.</note> had not removed the offensiveness in his defense. A thing that is offensive to the weak, if it is not changed when it could easily be changed without harming the truth, becomes a given scandal.* This already took place at the end of the year 1737 and the beginning of the year 1738, and thus a year earlier than any movement regarding the Herrnhuter Hymnbook was made here in this Country <note>Referring to the Netherlands.</note>. (3) When the Baron says: *We want to be so upright as to omit them (namely: the Songs that contain offenses) in the first reprint, or to improve them.* To that I must answer: (a) That the uprightness of the Herrnhuters, by all those who love truth above lies and true simplicity above hypocrisy and deceit, is valued no higher than that of convicted deceivers. (b) That the Baron does not keep his word, which he gave so boldly in the first Declaration, accompanied by insults and slander against all those who came too close to that sanctuary of the Herrnhuters, their Hymnbook—

### §. XVI.

From page 295 to 300, to which we refer the truth-loving reader back.

(*bb*) Everything the Baron <note>Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader of the Moravian Brethren, who also held the title of Baron of Pollendorf.</note> says here is, in part, proof that he has nothing substantial to bring forward *in defense of the Songs* cited in the Pastoral Letter <note>original: "Herd: Brief" — Short for *Herderlijke Brief*, a formal letter of warning or guidance issued by the Dutch Reformed church authorities regarding the Moravians.</note>; that he gives up the case; and that his former boasting was nothing other than hot air and slander; and in part, everything ends in deception. Let us look at his words a little more closely. (1) He says: *we do not wish to argue about any Songs.* In the Pastoral Letter, we also had no intention to *dispute* with the Herrnhuters <note>The Moravian Brethren, followers of Zinzendorf, who settled in Herrnhut, Germany.</note>, nor do I have it in this book; but I demonstrate as clearly as the noonday sun that the vast majority of those *Songs* contain not only all sorts of dangerous errors, but the most extravagant, abominable secrets of unrighteousness and depths of Satan <note>A biblical reference to Revelation 2:24, used here to accuse the Moravians of heresy or hidden immoral doctrines.</note>—so dishonoring to God as have ever been promoted by the most dangerous <term>Enthusiasts</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiasm" (Enthousiastery) was a derogatory term for religious movements accused of prioritizing emotionalism and claims of direct divine inspiration over rational scripture.</note>. And we find these soul-destroying errors not in a common songbook, but in a *censored and approved Hymnbook*, which is the *Hymnbook of the Congregation of Herrnhut*; indeed, it is a <term>Symbolic book</term> <note>An official document containing the authorized doctrines and confessions of a church, similar to a creed.</note> accepted by the entire Congregation, from which they not only sing in the Assembly, but which is used for public teaching and catechizing, as if from a *System* of Herrnhutist Theology—just as the Hymnbook is said in the Preface to contain a *Hymn-Theology*. These are *Songs* that the Baron has publicly taken upon himself to *defend* in the name of all his Brethren residing here in this Country. He is not released from this obligation, which he himself took on, by this excuse; but we hold him to his word of Honor: either to defend the Songs without distinction, if he can, or to publicly confess guilt for his slanders, and to loathe the abominable errors found in the Congregation's Hymnbook, and to give us proof that the entire Congregation loathes them and condemns and rejects the Hymnbook that has been their Symbolic book until now. (2) He says doubtfully: *if there are (namely, Songs in the Hymnbook) which are judged to contain offenses.* As if the Baron and his Brethren had never known that, and as if we here in the Netherlands were the first to express our well-founded concerns about it and show the danger. ## §. XVI.
# That which, as a report from *Germany*, in a public writing un-

Theological Faculties and Churches in Germany have complained about and condemned the offenses and dangerous errors found in the Hymnbook? And if the Baron behaved according to the principle and the unholy alliance of the Herrnhuters, *to let oneself be drawn away by no speech or writing of the opposing party*; did he then not know that trusted friends of the Herrnhuters kindly admonished and warned Count von Zinzendorf and the Congregation about this? To convince my reader of the contrary, I shall only appeal to what I find in the High German *Historical Ecclesiastical Acts* <note>original: "Acta Histor: Eccles:" — referring to the *Acta Historico-Ecclesiastica*, a significant 18th-century journal documenting church history and controversies.</note>, the 15th volume, where on page 423 it is mentioned that the 3rd question, which the friend of the Herrnhuters, the jurist at Frankfurt, Mr. von LOEN <note>Johann Caspar von Loen (1694–1776), a German noble and writer who was initially sympathetic to Zinzendorf but later became critical.</note>, posed to Count von Zinzendorf, was this: *Whether their Songs—since several among them appear offensive, strange, and obscure—might not better be left unsung in Gatherings where all sorts of people are present?* To this, the answer of the Lord Count was: *Offensive Songs should not be sung at all. Those that appear to be offensive must be allowed to pass, when the offense is similar to those found in the Bible, and because such offense lies only within the reader. The entire teaching of Jesus Christ is something rare and strange. The Bohemian Brethren had to be content that people did not understand even their clearest ways of speaking, as the matters themselves are mysteries.* Upon this answer, Mr. von LOEN again remarked the following: *That, although beautiful Songs are found in the Herrnhuter Hymnbook, there were nonetheless also some offensive, strange, and obscure ones among them; that Magister Oetinger <note>Friedrich Christoph Oetinger (1702–1782), a prominent German Lutheran theologian and theosophist who attempted to bridge the gap between Pietism and Enlightenment science.</note>, in his defense, had not removed the offensiveness. A matter that is offensive to the weak—if one does not change it when it could easily be changed without harming the truth—becomes a given offense <note>A "given offense" (scandalum datum) is a theological term for a stumbling block created by someone's actions or words that leads others into doubt or sin.</note>.* This already occurred at the end of the year 1737 and the beginning of the year 1738, and thus a year earlier, before any stir was made over the Herrnhuter Hymnbook here in this Country <note>Referring to the Netherlands.</note>. (3) When the Baron says: *We intend to be so sincere as to omit or correct them (namely: the Songs containing offenses) in the first reprint.* To that I must answer: (a) That the sincerity of the Herrnhuters, by all those who love truth over lies and true simplicity over hypocrisy and deceit, is held at a higher value than that of convicted deceivers. (b) That the Baron does not keep his word, which he [gave] so boldly in the first Declaration, with added insults and slanderous words against all who dared touch that sanctuary of the Herrnhuters, their Hymnbook...

### II. TO THE-

reader, notice is given that these two writings were delivered to the Most Reverend Synods of South and North Holland. The Herrnhuters <note>A common name for the Moravian Brethren, named after their community 'Herrnhut' (The Lord's Watch) in Saxony.</note> must take a particular pride in this, and must have some special purpose for it, in order to instill a prejudice in the reader, whether in our Country or primarily in Germany. But why does the publisher not mention the fate that befell these papers at those two Most Reverend Synodical Meetings? I make no secret of it, and shall share it with the reader. The resolution regarding these two small papers in the Christian Synod of South Holland is this: *Also because they (the Herrnhuters) refuse to give a full, frank, and clear confession of their faith upon Synodical request: Since certain two delivered papers are not sufficient, the one from the Count of Zinzendorf <note>Nikolaus Ludwig, Count von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader and benefactor of the Moravian Brethren.</note> being but a copy of no use, and intended only to seek postponement and delay, and to hold up the Synodical Deliberations concerning them; the second containing only some points of confession, and thus not all: and also only signed by a Baron von Watteville <note>Friedrich von Watteville, a prominent Moravian leader.</note>, and not submitted as a confession of all, which both were required of them.* And a little thereafter it is said: *that they (the Herrnhuters) differ from us has become sufficiently apparent even in this Synod — — from various terms in the Letter, delivered yesterday to this Assembly by the above-mentioned Baron de Watteville.* How these papers were received in the Christian Synod of North Holland is recorded in the Acts of the Assembly: *The Most Reverend Lord Praeses <note>The presiding officer or moderator of the Synod.</note> reports that upon his entrance into the Most Reverend Assembly, some copies of a booklet, under which stood the name of the Baron de Watteville, and another written paper, were shoved into his hand in an intrusive manner by an unknown person.* The Most Reverend Synod has judged, as much for that informal treatment as for other circumstances, to lay those things aside and to make no reflection upon them. That unknown person, who had stealthily slipped those papers into the Lord Praeses's hand, was discovered by one of the respective Members of the Assembly, and being asked in a decent manner for his name and the purpose of delivering these papers, he refused to answer either, whereupon he was ordered to leave the Church. Yet having the boldness to come back in through another door, and being discovered once more, he was shown out of the Church by order of their Noble Mightinesses <note>original: "Ed: Mog:" — the secular representatives of the government who attended the Synods.</note> and ordered not to come in again. ## II. APPENDIX.

### *Containing the Resolutions taken in several Synodal Assemblies of our Country in the matter of the Herrnhuters, in the Year 1739.*

Since the publishers of those two papers, which we examined in the preceding Appendix, appeal to the delivery of those writings to two Highly Reverend Synodal Assemblies held last year in South and North Holland; and since it is not known to everyone what these and other Christian Synods <note>A Synod is a formal council of a church, gathered to decide on issues of doctrine or administration.</note> of our country have decided in the matter of the Herrnhuters <note>A common name for the Moravian Brethren, followers of Count von Zinzendorf, named after their settlement Herrnhut ("The Lord’s Watch").</note>, I have judged it useful, indeed necessary, to share some of those decisions with my reader—as many as I have been able to obtain from authentic copies. This is done not only so that the members of our Church might know what those Highly Reverend Church Assemblies have judged in the matter of the Herrnhuters, which has caused so much stir, but also so that no deceptive <note>original: "abusive," meaning erroneous or misleading reports common in 18th-century polemics.</note> reports might gain ground in Germany to the detriment of the entire Church of the Netherlands—much like the lying reports regarding the actions of the Reverend Consistory <note>term: Consistory <gloss>The local governing council of a Dutch Reformed congregation, made up of the minister and elders.</gloss></note> of Amsterdam, which have found far too much belief, to the detriment of our Assembly. Behold then the resolution of four Highly Reverend Synods of our Blessed Netherlands.

---

outcome of the delivery of these leaves <note>referring to the pages of the confession or petition</note> to the Christian Synodal Assembly. Can a sensible person now judge that there lies therein so much cause for boasting for the Herrnhuters? Yet if they wish to flaunt it, we can grant it to them as well as to anyone who, with the note upon which his crime and sentence is written hanging upon his breast, dares to show off. Nevertheless, it would be better if they behaved as those legally condemned, and humbled themselves before God and men, and sincerely renounced their dangerous errors, and embraced the sanctified truth with an unfeigned heart. Which we wish for the Baron <note>likely referring to Baron von Watteville</note> and his Brethren, together with their Bishop <note>referring to Count von Zinzendorf, who was consecrated a bishop of the Moravians.</note>.

### I.

->The resolution of the Christian Synod of South Holland, regarding<-
->the matter of the <term>Herrnhuters</term><note>A religious group also known as the Moravian Brethren, followers of Count von Zinzendorf.</note>, held within Woerden in July<-
->of the Year 1739.<-

Upon the questions posed by the Presiding Officer <note>original: "D. Præses," the leader of the church council.</note>: 1. *How should one regard these people?* 2. *And, if they are harmful, what means should then be used to prevent them from misleading the members of our Church?* Their Noble Mightinesses requested the Classes <note>term: Classes <gloss>Regional governing bodies within the Dutch Reformed Church, composed of ministers and elders from a specific district.</gloss></note> to submit their considerations on the matter; after which Their Noble Mightinesses would state their own conclusions.

**I.** When the question was put regarding their doctrine, the Lords Deputies, Directors, and respective Classes were essentially in agreement with one another: that the <term>Herrnhuters</term> are not orthodox <note>original: "regtzinnig," meaning holding the correct, established beliefs of the Dutch Reformed Church.</note>, and thus do not belong to our Church, but hold harmful and destructive false principles. This is shown in various public writings by renowned men, such as the Professors vanden Honert Junior, Voget, Drieffen, and Gerdes, as well as the Pastoral Letter from the Reverend Consistory of Amsterdam, written to warn everyone against their errors. Various members of this Christian Synod have also demonstrated this extensively in person. Furthermore, the matter was made even clearer because they have, until now, provided no substantial answer in their defense against the Grievances brought against them in the Synod of The Hague <note>original: "Synodo Hagana"</note>. They also refuse to give a full, candid, and clear Confession of their faith upon the Synod’s request. The two papers they delivered are insufficient: the first, from the Count of <term>Zinzendorf</term>, is merely a copy of no use, intended only to seek delay and stalling to hold up the Synodal deliberations concerning them; the second contains only some points of Confession, and thus not all of them. It was also signed only by a Baron von <term>Watteville</term> <note>Johannes von Watteville was a close associate and son-in-law of Zinzendorf.</note> and was not submitted as a confession on behalf of the whole group, both of which had been demanded of them.

...be mindful to prevent this evil seed, so that the members of our congregations might no longer be led astray by it; and those who are wavering might be set right once more.

Among the various means that had been devised by the respective members, Their <term>Noble Mightinesses</term><note>original: "Ed: Mog." (Edel Mogende), a formal title for high-ranking administrative or governing officials in the Dutch Republic.</note> judged:

✠. ->*In which various objections of the Mennonites*<-

When, in the first two chapters of this my work, I mentioned the name of <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>A term often used derisively for radical reformers who rejected infant baptism; here referring to the spiritual ancestors of the Mennonites.</note> and <term>Mennonites</term> <note>A pacifist Protestant group following the teachings of the reformer Menno Simons.</note> in more than one place, and demonstrated in various ways the agreement of the <term>Herrnhuters</term> <note>The Moravian Brethren, followers of Count von Zinzendorf.</note> with the views or practices of some within that denomination, it first came to my ears through rumors that some among those "Friends" <note>A respectful term the author uses for the Mennonites.</note> took great offense at this. They believed my intent was to make the Mennonites suspect, as if they were fundamentally in agreement with the Herrnhuters. Others, who judged more calmly, lamented that I had involved the Mennonite cause in the matter of the Herrnhuters, because the uninformed might conclude from this that the cause of the Herrnhuters and that of the Mennonites is one and the same. This was especially concerning because, in the beginning, the greatest following of <term>Count von Zinzendorf</term> consisted of those who call themselves Mennonites or <term>Doopsgezinden</term> <note>The Dutch name for Mennonites, literally meaning 'baptism-minded.'</note>, or specifically <term>Collegiants</term> <note>A Dutch religious movement that emphasized individual study and rejected formal church hierarchies.</note>. Others accused me of not acting in good faith and of charging these people with something that neither could nor should be charged to them.

Meanwhile, this story circulated through various circles, and everyone judged according to their own disposition. The rumor that I must have written something I could not justify found more belief the stronger the assurances given that among the Mennonite <term>Ministers</term> one (though now no longer unknown to me who) had already taken up the pen to refute me on these points; of which a kind of draft, in the form of a letter, was read in several circles. For my part, I heard these loose rumors without much emotion, as it is no longer unusual for me, and many with me, to be the subject of gossip <note>Original: "over de tonge te rollen." Literally, "to roll over the tongue," meaning to be talked about or slandered.</note>, and to be judged, even condemned, by those who either do not understand the matter they judge, or who content themselves with viewing it from only one side.
