The second who appeals to this Sebastian Franck is ARNOLDUS MESHOVIUS (whom I have not yet been able to obtain, but whose words I take over from Becmanus’s *Theological Exercises* XXI, page 360), who speaks in his *History of the Anabaptists*, Book 3, Chapter 21, thus:

> *Sebastian Franck, although he himself led a group among the Anabaptists, yet in order to sell smoke to the Magistrate <note>meaning: to deceive or mislead the authorities</note> so that he would not be expelled, he recounted their errors and sects as distinctly as he could; and thereafter, freely lashing out at the errors of those who disagreed, he was the first to record for posterity that more than 44 sects flourished among them.* <note>original Latin: "Sebastianus Franck, licet ipse familiam inter Anabaptistas duceret, ut tamen fumos Magistratui, ne pelleretur, venderet, errores ipsorum & sectas, quam potuit distincte recensuit, ac subinde liberius dissentientium errores perstringens, ultra 44 sectas inter eos vigere, primus Anabaptistarum memoriæ prodidit."</note>

That is:

> *Sebastian Franck, although he himself was at home among the Anabaptists (a), in order to sell some smoke to the Magistrate, so that he might not be banished, has enumerated their errors and sects as distinctly as he could; and by sometimes freely combing <note>critiquing or examining</note> the errors of those differing from him, he, as the first among the Anabaptists, has left behind in writing that THERE ARE MORE THAN 44 SECTS to be found among them.* Here may yet be add-

(a) Whether Sebastian Franck should be counted among the Anabaptists, I know not; but I have clearly been able to notice in leafing through his book that he declares himself for no specific Denomination. Nevertheless, he shows quite clearly where he belongs: namely, with the Enthusiasts <term>Enthusiasts: 17th-century term for those believing in direct personal inspiration by the Holy Spirit, often prioritizing it over established church doctrine</term> and Fanatics <term>original: "Geestdryvers," literally 'spirit-drivers'; a derogatory term for radical reformers who claimed direct spiritual revelation</term> who exalt the inward Word above the written Word, of which I shall cite but one sample. > *Therefore let no one be made a fool of or bewitched by the letter of Scripture, but let him first consider and test the Scripture, how it compares with his heart. ## IV. APPENDIX.

### Containing several samples from a new Herrnhuter Translation of the New Testament.

Just as the Herrnhuters most clearly—and directly contrary to their own claims—demonstrate that they are a particular and distinct sect unto themselves, they also seem intent on nothing more than having nothing in common with any other denominations, and especially with the Protestant Church, regarding anything that touches upon public worship. David’s Psalms are sung as little in their meetings as the proven orthodox and pious hymns that have been introduced and used for edification in the Reformed and Lutheran congregations in Germany; instead, the Herrnhuters must have their own Hymnbook, filled with Enthusiastic <term>Enthusiastic: In the 18th century, "Enthusiasm" (from the Greek 'enthousiasmos') was a pejorative term used by established churches to describe groups claiming direct, private divine inspiration or emotional revelation that bypassed traditional scripture and reason.</term> errors, which is titled *the Hymnbook of the Congregation at Herrnhut*. Now it is beginning to reach the point where these people must also have a special Herrnhuter Bible, and a new translation that differs from nothing more than it does from those used in the Protestant Churches. The way for this has been paved now that Count von Zinzendorf <note>Nikolaus Ludwig, Count von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), was the primary benefactor and spiritual leader of the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuters).</note>, the so-called Bishop of the Herrnhuter sect, has presumed to bring to light a new High German translation of the New Testament in the past year of 1739. He released it as an "untimely birth" <note>original: "ontydige geboorte"; the author likely uses this phrase to imply the work was rushed, ill-conceived, or monstrous.</note>, printed in Büdingen in two volumes. The first volume contains the Historical Books, namely: the four Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles; the second volume contains the Apostolic Epistles and the Revelation of John. Before each volume, a special Preface by the publisher is placed.

*The first is signed on December 16, 1738, during the voyage to St. Thomas <note>A Caribbean island, then part of the Danish West Indies, where the Moravians established a famous mission to enslaved people.</note>, on board the ship St. Martin: The second on the return voyage from St. Thomas, on board the ship Aletta, at the latitude of Lizard <note>The Lizard Peninsula in Cornwall, England, a common navigational landmark for ships entering the English Channel.</note>, in the beginning of April 1739.*

This signature serves in place of the publisher's name, as it is well known from these details that the author is Count von Zinzendorf. Whether there is some other secret hidden beneath the fact that these circumstances are noted for us so precisely, on that everyone can form their own—

One might conclude from this that the Publisher and the Writer of the Preface is also the Author of this Translation; however, whether that conclusion corresponds with the truth remains to be seen, for in the Prefaces the Author is not clearly defined. Nevertheless, the Count does occasionally make it appear that one should take him for the author, though not without giving cause for counter-arguments. Even before I knew of a Herrnhuter translation, I read in the High German *Historical Ecclesiastical Acts* <note>original: "Acta Historico Eccles:"</note> printed in Weimar, in the 15th part, page 416, about a certain Mr. **Gottfried Polycarpus Muller**, a learned man who, after resigning his service as Director of the Gymnasium <note>In the German tradition, a Gymnasium is a prestigious secondary school focusing on classical learning.</note> at Zittau, departed with his wife for Herrnhut. Regarding him, the writer of these *Acts* says:

> *Some believe that he is working there (namely: at Herrnhut) on a new translation of the Bible for the Herrnhuter Brethren, but others cast it into doubt.*

Who the Translator may be remains a riddle to us, but it is certain that this Translation is intended for the service of the Herrnhuters. In the first Preface, the Publisher calls this translation *a trial* <note>original: "ein Versuch"</note> *for a new translation of the New Testament:* regarding which he has nothing yet to say, but that it will only then become clear whether he has anything to say when those—who lack neither understanding <note>original: "an Sinn"</note> nor the ability to handle these holy matters—have let him know what they have to remark upon. At that time, his first task will not be the defense of his work, but its improvement; for he says he wishes to be treated as nothing other than **A PUPIL RECITING HIS LESSON.** This appears to be spoken with eminent humility, when a Count and Bishop speaks in such a manner about a work that he wants to be regarded as his own labor; yet time will tell. Humble expressions do not always testify to a humble heart. The Roman High Bishop also calls himself *Servant of the Servants* <note>original: "Servus Servorum" — a traditional title of the Pope (Servus servorum Dei).</note>. He continues, saying that no one can take it ill of him that he makes this translation public through the press, for he believes he will thus find, in the best and most innocent <note>original: "unſchuldigſten"</note> way, those who can be helpful to him in his weighty yet childlike intention.

He even saw seven or eight German translations <note>original: "Duitsche Overzettingen"</note> in the past, yet he guarded himself against any foreign additions, out of fear they might confuse rather than help him. That in Germany various wandering spirits <term>Dwaal-Geeften: literally "error-spirits," referring to religious dissenters or those deemed heretical</term>, each from their own principles and for their own ends, have emboldened themselves to translate the Bible, either in whole or in part, to support their errors, is all too true—to the sorrow of all who love truth and godliness, and to the disturbance of many congregations. This I had to report beforehand concerning this translation, from the publisher’s own Prefaces.

As soon as it came to my knowledge that such a Translation by the Count <note>Count Nicholas Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), the leader of the Moravian Brethren.</note> was at hand, I made every effort to obtain it, which I finally succeeded in doing. When I began to open it here and there, I soon discovered with shock the most base sacrilege in the twisting, mutilation, and corruption of the Scripture, of which the Translator had made himself guilty—partly out of deep ignorance of the Greek language, partly out of inexcusable negligence, and partly with a cunning and wicked intent. I found myself compelled, while this work of mine was coming to an end and the progress of the printing press was hindered for some time by the bitter cold, to apply myself with more attention to the investigation, so as to be able to share something of it with my Reader. Time did not permit me to go through the entire New Testament piece by piece and put this Translation to the test. I only took three Historical Books from the first Volume, namely: the Evangelists Matthew and John, and the Acts of the Apostles; and from the second Volume, two Epistles, namely: those of Paul to the Romans and to the Hebrews, and to those I added the Revelation of the same John. To share everything with the Reader would be tedious, and yet to report too little might make it seem as if there were not many errors, but only a few minor faults that could be excused. Therefore, I have selected several samples from my notes to submit to the judgment of everyone, but particularly the Theologians in our country, just as they appear, without—for the time being—adding any of my own remarks or drawing any conclusions from them. For the convenience of the Reader, I divide each page into three columns: in the first stands the Moravian translation in High German <note>original: "Hoogduitſch"</note>; in the second, the High German translation of Luther and our Dutch Translation; in the third, those words from the Greek text which are at issue. Let everyone test and judge for themselves.

(a) The Reader is requested to note once and for all that the Moravian Translator generally translates the word <term>Theos</term> <note>original Greek: "Θεος", meaning God</note> as *God the Lord* when it is used for the Father, but when it is applied to the Son and Holy Spirit, he uses only *God*; for example in this Chapter verse 3, Chapter 6: 27, 29, 46, Chapter 8: 40, 41, 42, 47, and so on throughout. <note>The author is highlighting what he perceives as a subtle Arian or subordinatist tendency in Zinzendorf’s translation, where the Father is given a more distinct title than the Son.</note>

*Luther:* And takes me prisoner in the law of sin, which is in my members.
*Dutch:* And takes me prisoner under the law of sin, which is in my members.

*Luther:* Who will deliver me from the body of this death?
*Dutch:* Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?

*Luther:* There is now nothing damnable in those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.
*Dutch:* There is then now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.

*Luther:* For the law of the Spirit, who makes alive in Christ Jesus,
*Dutch:* For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus.

*Luther:* So that the righteousness required by the law might be fulfilled in us,
*Dutch:* So that the right of the law should be fulfilled in us,

<column-break/>

### *The Moravian Translation of Romans*

— **8:27.** For he prays in a Divine manner for the saints. <note>original German: "Denn er betet auf eine Göttliche art vor die heiligen." The Moravian text emphasizes the "manner" of prayer rather than the intercession itself.</note>

**9:5.** All this belongs to them, yes, the Messiah, the God over all things, is himself from their midst. May he be praised for eternity, Amen. <note>original German: "Das gehöret ihnen alles, ja der Meffias, der Gott über alle dinge, ift felbft aus ihrem mittel. Er fey gelobet in ewigkeit Amen."</note>

— **6.** For not all those who are of the people of Israel are therefore also children of God.

**10:1.** is omitted. <note>The author notes that Zinzendorf's version skips the first verse of Chapter 10, which expresses Paul's desire for Israel's salvation.</note>

— **8.** The matter is so near to you in your mouth and in your heart, (namely the subject of faith of which we preach.)

— **10.** For faith in the heart helps toward righteousness, and when one confesses with the mouth, then one becomes well. <note>original German: "Denn der glaube im hertzen hilfft zur gerechtigkeit, und wenn man mit dem munde bekennet, fo wird einem wohl." The use of "wohl" (feeling well or comfortable) is a significant departure from the traditional "saved" or "blessed."</note>

### *Luther and the Dutch*

*Luther:* For he intercedes for the saints according to what pleases God. <note>original German: "Den er vertritt die heiligen, nach dem das Gott gefället."</note>
*Dutch:* Since he prays for the saints according to God. <note>original Dutch: "Dewyl hy na God voor den heiligen bidt."</note>

*Luther:* Whose also are the fathers, from whom Christ comes according to the flesh, who is God over all, praised in eternity, Amen. <note>original German: "Welcher auch find die Väter, auff welchen Chriftus herkömt nach dem fleifch, der da ift Gott über alles, gelobet in ewigkeit, Amen."</note>
*Dutch:* Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is as far as the flesh is concerned, who is God above all to be praised in eternity, Amen. <note>original Dutch: "Welker zyn de Vaders, en de uit welke Chriftus is fo veel het vleefch aangaat, dewelke is God boven alle te pryzen in der eeuwigheit, Amen."</note>

*Luther:* For they are not all Israelites who are of Israel.
*Dutch:* For they are not all Israel who are out of Israel.

*Luther:* I entreat God. <note>original German: "Ich flehe auch Gott."</note>
*Dutch:* That I [make] to God. <note>original Dutch: "Dat ik tot God [doe.]"</note>

*Luther:* The word is near you, namely in your mouth, and in your heart. *This is the word of faith that we preach.*
*Dutch:* Near you is the word in your mouth and in your heart. *This is the word of faith which we preach to you.*

*Luther:* For if one believes from the heart, one becomes righteous, and if one confesses with the mouth, one becomes saved. <note>original German: "Denn fo man von hertzen glaubet, fo wird man gerecht, und fo man mit dem munde bekennet, fo wird man feelig."</note>
*Dutch:* For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation. <note>original Dutch: "Want met der herten gelooft men ter rechtveerdigheit, en met den monde belydt men ter zaligheit."</note>

*Hebrews*

XI. 5. for before his transformation, <note>original German: "verwandelung". In standard versions, this is "translation" or "taking away," referring to Enoch.</note>

XIII. 20. But the God of peace, who has led our Lord Jesus on high from the dead—he who is so great in the blood of the eternal testament, the shepherd of the sheep, <note>original German: "in die höhe geführet" (led on high) instead of "brought back" or "raised."</note>

### Luther and the Dutch
[VI. 18. Regarding the] offered hope.
*Dutch:* [Namely we] who have taken refuge, to hold fast to the proposed hope.

*Luther:* And considers the blood of the Testament unclean, through which he is sanctified,
*Dutch:* And has considered the blood of the Testament unclean, through which he was sanctified,

*Luther:* for before his taking away,
*Dutch:* For before his removal,

*Luther:* For she considered him faithful who had promised it.
*Dutch:* Since she considered him faithful who had promised it.

*Luther:* But God of peace, who brought from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal Testament, our Lord Jesus,
*Dutch:* Now the God of Peace, who through the blood of the eternal Testament brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, [namely] our Lord Jesus Christ,

(a) I cannot understand how the Translator could read and translate without trembling the words that stand in the 22nd Chapter of this Revelation, vs. 18, 19; <note>These verses contain a famous warning: "If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues... and if any man shall take away from the words of the book... *To words*; that which is found in the 3rd line of the 3rd verse, means nothing other than "to words" in <term>High German<note>Original: *Hoogduits*. Refers to the German language as spoken in the southern uplands and used in Luther's Bible translation.</note></term>, where *worte* is the plural form <note>Original: *meerder-getal*. The author is making a grammatical point: the hymn uses the plural "words" (human speech) rather than the singular "Word" (divine scripture).</note>. This is a fact that may be asked of anyone who understands the German language and does not allow themselves to be carried away by a rush of prejudice to bear witness against the truth. A soul filled with the inner peace of God testifies here that she does not know how to express her experience with any words. And how indeed could that be expressed with words which, according to <note>Original: *Phil: 4: vs: 7*. "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus."</note> Philippians 4:7, *surpasses all understanding*? Or, if one wishes to see here a reference to some prescription or prescriptions of words? Then they would be human prescriptions, to which such a soul declares she cannot bind herself.

This is the classic King James phrasing of the verse. The author is using it to argue that a childlike state is a requirement for the Kingdom.</note> These were indeed newly born little children who were carried to Jesus in people's arms, which the word *Little Children* <note>original: "Kinderkens"</note> indicates in the parallel passage of Luke 18: verse 16, and as translated in 1 Peter 2: verse 2: *newborn babes*. In this way, Jesus, expressing himself regarding such *little children* with the words *of such is the kingdom of heaven*, wishes to make known the necessity of coming to the state of those little children, in being also so manageable and submissive.

> *Until he turns himself entirely toward annihilation,* <note>original German: "vernichtung". In the mystical tradition, this refers to the total surrender of the self-will so that God may act through the person.</note>
> *Yes, lead him freshly to your altar,*
> *Let the old Adam find rest nevermore.* <note>The "old Adam" refers to human nature in its fallen state, which must be overcome by spiritual rebirth.</note>

It is pitiable that a complete turning toward annihilation—which some would interpret as a merely passive and idle existence—is being inferred here; yet this pertains entirely to the *old man*, just as he must be brought to nothing in the death of *Christ*. Romans 6: verse 6: *knowing this, that our old man is crucified with (him), that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.* Indeed, what else is intended by this prayer? For the final verse of this hymn reveals that the goal is that one may be:

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of Moravian hymns against theological critics. And plunge me wholly and entirely into your baptism;
SO THAT THE SINFUL FORM MAY BE WHOLLY AND ENTIRELY LOST,
AND NOTHING UNCLEAN MAY BE FOUND IN ME.
<note>The first three lines are translated from the original German: "Und tauch mich gantsz und gar in deine tauf hinein; DAMIT DIE SUNDLICHE GESTALLT SICH GANTSZ UND GAR VERLIERE, UND NICHTS UNREINES AN MIR MOG SU FINDEN SEIN."</note>

->This is verse 1.<-

> *O Spirit of pure fear! come, lead the holy anointing;*
> *And baptize me wholly and entirely into your baptism;*
> *So that the sinful form may be wholly and entirely lost,*
> *And nothing unclean may be found in me.*

It is not easy to determine how some have read here of being baptized into *Jesus's Baptism*, since the prayer is directed toward the Holy Spirit. However, this baptism is also the baptism of Jesus, as the Spirit-baptism <note>The "baptism of the Spirit" refers to an internal spiritual transformation or "sealing" by God, distinct from the outward water ritual of baptism.</note> that belongs to Him; according to the words of John the Baptist in Matthew 3 verse 11: *He who comes after me... He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* But that is not the inquiry here: some criticize such a prayer—asking that the sinful form <note>original: "zondige gestalte". This refers to the corrupt nature or "shape" of the soul influenced by sin.</note> be wholly and entirely lost, and nothing unclean remain. 

But how then should one pray? Is one permitted to continue loving any part of the sinful form? Should one desire to retain something unclean? Must one not, in the pursuit of holiness <term>Heiligmaaking: The theological process of sanctification, where a believer is made holy through divine grace.</term>, strive to rid oneself of everything that is sinful and unclean? And must one not then pray against it without any exception? What of the promise in Ezekiel 36 verse 25: *Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols <note>original: "drek-goden", literally "dung-gods," a derogatory biblical term for idols.</note>, will I cleanse you.* Indeed, what promises that pledge sanctification make an exception here? One should also see what Paul says concerning the duty of believers in 2 Corinthians 7 verse 1: *Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.*

Hymn 376, verse 7—the one they wish to have compared—contains the following, derived from what was sung regarding the Father’s drawing [of souls] to the Son, and the Son’s drawing [of souls] back to the Father:

If one imagines this prayer itself, what impropriety does it contain? In the *Reformed baptismal form* <note>The official liturgy used by the Dutch Reformed Church for the sacrament of baptism.</note> it is prayed, *that the children may be buried with Christ in His death, and may rise with Him in a new life.* But can such a thing happen without being enveloped in Christ’s image, and without the subduing of the sinful nature? The Moravians <note>term: "Hernhutters," the followers of Count von Zinzendorf, known for their emotional and Christ-centered piety.</note> do not have so much concern about it.

*Which in enshrouded Majesty,* <note>original: "gewond'ne Majesteit"; the word "gewonden" refers to being wrapped or swaddled, echoing the swaddling clothes of the infant Jesus in the manger.</note>
*Is in Jesus, the humble child.*

Here is the body that God is said to have built for himself; it is not only clearly distinguished from the creation <term>Creature: In this theological context, "the creature" (Creatuur) refers to the whole of the created world or nature as distinct from the Creator.</term>, but it is clearly and uniquely pointed to the child *Jesus*. *The Father has prepared the Son a body*, Heb. 10 : vs. 5. *So God is revealed in the flesh*; 1 Tim. 3 : vs. 16. *So in Christ dwells the fullness of the Godhead bodily*; Col. 2 : vs. 9. *And he who has seen him, has seen the Father*. John 14 : vs. 9, 10.

That everything must be grounded in *Christ*, that everything must find Him again, become in Him and DISAPPEAR <note>The capitalization in the original suggests an emphasis on the mystical absorption or total submission of all things into Christ's sovereignty.</note>, He who is the RESTORER (namely of all things); that everything must gather itself in Him, and fold itself together in Him, as the GENERAL BUILDING <note>original: "Algemene Gebouw"; a metaphorical term used by some mystics to describe Christ as the architectural foundation and living structure of the entire spiritual and physical universe.</note>. That He may increase according to His pleasure, and yet not be changed in all of that, and that however many things flow out of Him, He nevertheless remains the same; that He penetrates through all manner of forms; Yes, that this ALL knows no bounds, even though it swiftly penetrates through the whole and walks through all parts; Hymn 71. Vs. 11, 12, 13. 16, 17.

The hymn is the translation of a Latin rhymed poem, after the style of the hymns that go by the name of Bernard <note>Referring to Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a medieval monk and mystic famous for his intense, emotional devotion to the physical humanity and sufferings of Jesus.</note>.

It is certainly deep, and subject to misunderstanding, especially if it is read with prejudice. The congregation of Herrnhut <term>Herrnhut: The central community of the Moravian Church in Saxony, known for its focus on the "Blood and Wounds" of Jesus and its extensive hymnody.</term> leaves it as it is and makes no use of it, along with several other hymns; these are preserved by them in their hymnal as composed by God-fearing men, but are never sung.

Furthermore, what is brought forward here can all be understood in a good sense, if one takes it according to Rom. 11 : vs. 36. *From Him, through Him and to Him are all things*. Col. 1 : vs. 16, 17. *By Him all things are created, which are in the heavens and which are on the earth, which are visible and which are invisible, whether they be thrones, whether they be dominions, whether they be principalities, whether they be pow—*

Here the body, which God is said to have built for Himself, is not only clearly distinguished from the Creation <term>Creature: original "Creatuur," meaning all created things as distinct from the Creator</term>, but it is also clearly and uniquely pointed toward the child Jesus. The Father has prepared the body for the Son, Hebrews 10:5; thus God is revealed in the flesh, 1 Timothy 3:16; thus in Christ the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9; and he who has seen Him, has seen the Father, John 14:9, 10.

*That everything must base itself upon Christ, that everything must find itself again in Him, become in Him and* DISAPPEAR, *He who is the* RESTORER <note>original: "WEDERBRENGER"; often refers to the "Restoration of All Things" or apocatastasis, the belief that all creation will eventually be reconciled to God.</note> (*namely of all things*); *that everything must gather itself together in Him, and nestle itself together in Him, as the* UNIVERSAL EDIFICE. *That He may increase according to His pleasure, and yet not be changed in all that, and that, however many things flow from Him, He nevertheless remains the same; that He may penetrate through all kinds of forms; yes, that this* ALL *knows no bounds, even if it rapidly penetrates through the whole and walks through all parts;* Song 71. Verses 11, 12, 13. 16, 17.

The song is a translation of a Latin rhymed hymn <note>original: "Latyns Rym-lied"</note>, in the style of the songs attributed to Bernard <note>Presumably St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic famous for his devotion to the humanity and suffering of Jesus.</note>.

It is certainly profound, and subject to misinterpretation, especially when read with prejudice. The congregation of Herrnhut <note>The Moravians, a Pietist community led by Count Zinzendorf, known for their emotional and mystical hymnody.</note> leaves it be and makes no use of it, along with some other hymns; these are preserved by them in their hymnbook as having been composed by godly men, but they are never sung.

Furthermore: what is added here can all be understood in a good sense, if one takes it according to Romans 11:36: *From Him, through Him, and to Him are all things.* Colossians 1:16, 17: *By Him were all things created, that are in heaven and that are on earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or pow—* <note>The Dutch text ends with "mag-", a fragment of "magten" (powers), leading to the next page.</note>

and lovers <note>original: "lief hebbers." In this context, it refers to those who love the truth or the spiritual life.</note>, will be subject. One might also ask, in passing, that if so little ground for accusation can be found in the evidence presented—which anyone can examine for themselves to test its validity—what respect can one have for such accusations which are merely adopted from private accusers as if they were proven truths? In the meantime, it is wished for the Author of this H. & V. B. <note>likely an abbreviation for "Heilige en Vermakelyke Berijmingen" (Holy and Pleasant Versifications), the title of the hymn book under discussion.</note> that the Lord does not hold against him the harm they may cause, nor the offense they have already given to many pious souls; that they may humble themselves before the Lord for their lack of caution, and remember the Counsel of Gamaliel, *Acts 5: vs. 38, 39: Stay away from these men, - - for if this [plan or work is of men, it will come to nothing; but if it is of God, you cannot overthrow it] etc.* <note>original Latin reference: "Actor: 5." Gamaliel was a respected teacher of the law who advised the Jewish authorities to be cautious in their persecution of the apostles, suggesting that God’s will would ultimately be revealed through the success or failure of their mission.</note>

<summary>The author concludes the defense by questioning the validity of the accusations against the hymn book and calls for humility and biblical caution based on the advice of Gamaliel.</summary>
<keywords>Gamaliel, Acts 5, hymn book defense, accusations, piety, theological controversy, humility</keywords>
